source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: Three zero-objective scalar blocks have unique attained updates and unique zero primal/dual solution, yet one rational start has an unbounded recurrence.
selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 Write the columns of $A$ as $a_1=(1,1,1)^T$, $a_2=(1,1,2)^T$, $a_3=(1,2,2)^T$. Their squared norms are $3,6,9$, so every scalar block subproblem has a strictly positive quadratic coefficient and a unique attained minimizer. Also $det A=-1$, so $Ax=0$ has only $x=0$. The dual function is $d(y)=inf_x\langle y,Ax\rangle$: it is $0$ when $A^Ty=0$ and $-\infty$ otherwise. Since $A$ is invertible, $A^Ty=0$ only for $y=0$, so the dual optimum is unique. [A1, F1, given, algebra]

2.1 For $z=e^{it}$, direct expansion gives $\operatorname{Im}(e^{-2it}q(e^{it}))=\frac{\sin t(22\cos t-21)}{81}$. If this vanishes because $\sin t=0$, substitution gives $q(1)=1/162$ and $q(-1)=775/54$, both nonzero. Otherwise $\cos t=21/22$, and substitution into the real part gives $\operatorname{Re}(e^{-2it}q(e^{it}))=19/19602\ne0$. Thus $q$ has no unit-circle zero. [A1, step 1.2, algebra, cases]

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Assume Countable Choice and the Galerkin and adjoint hypotheses of [[thm-elliptic-fe-gradient-error-in-energy-norms]]. Suppose the adjoint regularity and dual approximation assumptions of [[cor-aubin-nitsche-h-r-plus-s-rate-under-primal-and-dual-approximation]] hold separately for the state and adjoint equations, giving
$$\|u-u_h\|_{L^2}\le C_u h^{r+s},\qquad \|p-p_h\|_{L^2}\le C_p h^{r+s}$$
for $0<h\le1$, $r\ge1$, and $s\in(0,1]$. Assume the parameter derivative operators satisfy
$$|\ell_\theta'[\eta](v)|\le M_\ell^0\|\eta\|_2\|v\|_{L^2},\qquad |a_\theta'[\eta](v,w)|\le M_a^0\|\eta\|_2\|v\|_{L^2}\|w\|_{L^2}.$$
Assume the discrete derivative maps in [[thm-elliptic-fe-gradient-error-in-energy-norms]] have compatible $L^2$ extensions and constants $C_J,C_\ell,C_a$ independent of $h$ give, for every $\|\eta\|_2\le1$, a direct-objective derivative defect at most $C_Jh^{r+s}$, an $L^2$-dual load-derivative defect at most $C_\ell h^{r+s}$, and a bilinear derivative defect at most $C_ah^{r+s}\|v\|_{L^2}\|w\|_{L^2}$. Then the reduced-gradient error is $O(h^{r+s})$. This rate requires those extra $L^2$-bounded parameter derivative maps; the energy-norm result alone does not imply it.

actualproofparagraphs.3.1: Apply the exact gradient subtraction in [F2]. The direct-objective and derivative-data defects contribute their assumed $O(h^{r+s})$ bounds; step 2.1 bounds the state- and adjoint-dependent terms by constants times $h^{r+s}$. Taking the supremum over $\|\eta\|_2\le1$ proves the asserted rate. If the $L^2$ derivative bounds or either dual approximation hypothesis fails, this rate has not been proved. [A1, F2, step 2.1] ∎

For the finite-basis data on the model's open Hermitian domain in
[[def-finite-basis-projector-energy-model]], the Hermitian response
$$F(P)=h+G(P)+\nabla E_{xc}(P)$$
is $C^1$ on the model's open domain. At every $P_0$ with an occupied/unoccupied
gap, the occupied-projector map $\Phi(P)=\Pi_r(F(P))$ is $C^1$ on a sufficiently
small neighborhood of $P_0$ where that gap persists.

actualproofparagraphs.2.1: Continuity of $F$ gives a neighborhood $V$ of $P_0$ on which $\|F(P)-F(P_0)\|_F<g/4$, where $g$ is the gap at $P_0$. By [F6], the operator-norm difference is also less than $g/4$. By [F5] this image lies in a common gap-preserving ball; [F3] makes its block projector $C^1$ there and [L1] identifies it with the defined occupied projector. By [F4], $\Phi=\Pi_r\circ F$ is $C^1$ on $V$. [step 1.1, F3, F4, F5, F6, L1, choose] ∎

Put $V:=H^1_0(0,1)$ with its $H^1$ norm, and let $V_h\subseteq V$ be a finite-dimensional conforming piecewise-linear space on an interval partition with maximum cell width $h$. Let $u\in C^2([0,1])\cap V$ and assume its nodal interpolant $I_hu$ belongs to $V_h$. Let $A\in C^2([0,1])$ satisfy $0<\alpha\le A(x)\le M$, and write $C_A:=\|A''\|_{L^\infty(0,1)}$. Define $a(v,w)=\int_0^1A v'w'$ and let $a_h$ use one midpoint quadrature sample per cell. Let $F$ and $F_h$ be bounded exact and discrete loads, and put $\delta_{F,h}:=\sup_{w_h\ne0}|F(w_h)-F_h(w_h)|/\|w_h\|_{H^1}$. Then the exact and discrete solutions satisfy

$$\|u-u_h\|_{H^1}\le(1+2M/\alpha)\sqrt2h\|u''\|_\infty+\frac2\alpha\left(\frac{C_Ah^2}{24}(\|u'\|_2+h\|u''\|_\infty)+\delta_{F,h}\right).$$

The explicit $\delta_{F,h}$ is the data/source oscillation term; no rate or vanishing of it is asserted without an additional load approximation hypothesis. Here coercivity follows directly because every sampled coefficient satisfies $A(m_K)\ge\alpha$; this special argument does not infer stability from quadrature exactness.

Assume Countable Choice and let $d\in\{2,3\}$. Let $\mathcal T_h$ be a matching shape-regular affine simplicial mesh as in [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]. Let $V_h$ be a conforming zero-boundary P1 Lagrange subspace of a Hilbert space $V$, with $V_h\subseteq V$, and let $I_hu\in V_h$ be the global nodal interpolant of $u\in H^2(\Omega)\cap C(\overline\Omega)$ whose boundary nodal values vanish. Assume $\|z\|_V\le C_V|z|_{H^1(\Omega)}$ for $z=u-I_hu$. The reference nodal functionals are bounded on $W^{2,2}$, and the exact/discrete variational problems satisfy the hypotheses of [[thm-first-strang-lemma-for-conforming-perturbed-galerkin]], with discrete coercivity $\alpha_h>0$. Then a constant $C_I$ depending only on the reference P1 element and shape-regularity bound satisfies

$$\|u-u_h\|_V\le(1+M/\alpha_h)C_VC_Ih|u|_{H^2(\Omega)}+\frac{\delta_{a,h}(I_hu)+\delta_{F,h}}{\alpha_h}.$$

If $\alpha_h\ge\alpha_*>0$ uniformly, the displayed approximation contribution is $O(h)$; the geometry, quadrature, and load defects remain separate terms and require their own estimates.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
For the autonomous split problem $y'=a(y)+b(y)$ of [[def-additive-ode-and-partition]], set
$$\gamma:=1-\frac1{\sqrt2},\qquad \delta:=-\frac1{\sqrt2}.$$
The explicit tableau and the lower-triangular implicit tableau, using the separate stage conventions of [[def-explicit-runge-kutta-tableau-and-stage-map]] and [[def-implicit-runge-kutta-stage-equations]], are
$$\widetilde A=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0\\\gamma&0&0\\\delta&1-\delta&0\end{pmatrix},\quad \widetilde b=(\delta,1-\delta,0),\quad \widetilde c=(0,\gamma,1),$$
$$A=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0\\0&\gamma&0\\0&1-\gamma&\gamma\end{pmatrix},\quad b=(0,1-\gamma,\gamma),\quad c=(0,\gamma,1).$$
For a step $h>0$ from $y$, the method is defined by
$$Y_1=y,\qquad Y_2=y+\gamma h a(Y_1)+\gamma h b(Y_2),$$
$$Y_3=y+h\bigl[\delta a(Y_1)+(1-\delta)a(Y_2)\bigr]+h\bigl[(1-\gamma)b(Y_2)+\gamma b(Y_3)\bigr],\qquad y^+=Y_3.$$
Thus there are two implicit solves per step, one for each nonzero diagonal implicit stage. The unscaled stage-equation residual uses the update-residual convention of [[def-implicit-residual-and-algebraic-error-units]]. The tableaus and stages alone assert neither branch existence nor stability.
source_evidence.case_anchor: The first implicit tableau row is zero and its first stage is explicitly Y1=y; the later two diagonal entries are the positive constant gamma, not a rank assumption on a full tableau.

literal_source_anchor.description: the positive-order integral formula and strict Caputo-order domain
literal_source_anchor.quote:
Let $T>0$ and $\beta>0$. For $g\in L^1(0,T)$, its left fractional
integral of order $\beta$ is, for almost every $t\in(0,T)$,

$$I^\beta g(t):=\frac{1}{\Gamma(\beta)}\int_0^t(t-s)^{\beta-1}g(s)\,ds.$$

The definition uses Lebesgue integration, with
[[def-indefinite-lebesgue-integral-on-a-compact-interval]] and
[[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]. The kernel is integrable and
$$\int_0^t(t-s)^{\beta-1}\,ds=\frac{t^\beta}{\beta}$$
by [[lem-fractional-integral-kernel-power-integral]]. Tonelli's theorem
[[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] therefore gives
$$\int_0^T\int_0^t(t-s)^{\beta-1}|g(s)|\,ds\,dt =\int_0^T|g(s)|\int_s^T(t-s)^{\beta-1}dt\,ds \le \frac{T^\beta}{\beta}\|g\|_{L^1(0,T)}<\infty,$$
so the defining integral is finite for almost every $t$. For continuous $g$,
it is finite at every $t\in[0,T]$ and
$$|I^\beta g(t)|\le \frac{t^\beta}{\beta\Gamma(\beta)}\|g\|_\infty =\frac{t^\beta}{\Gamma(\beta+1)}\|g\|_\infty,$$
using [[thm-real-gamma-functional-equation]].

For $0<\alpha<1$ and an absolutely continuous function
$u:[0,T]\to\mathbb R$ whose almost-everywhere derivative belongs to
$L^1(0,T)$, its Caputo derivative of order $\alpha$ is the
almost-everywhere defined function

$$D_C^\alpha u:=I^{1-\alpha}u'=\frac{1}{\Gamma(1-\alpha)}\int_0^t(t-s)^{-\alpha}u'(s)\,ds.$$

Here absolute continuity is as in
[[def-absolutely-continuous-function]]. Under Countable Choice
([[def-countable-choice]]), every such absolutely continuous $u$ has
$u'\in L^1(0,T)$ by
[[thm-absolutely-continuous-functions-have-integrable-derivatives]], so the
Caputo derivative is defined on the whole absolutely continuous class under
that assumption. Without Countable Choice, the same formula is defined for
each absolutely continuous $u$ whose derivative is separately known to be in
$L^1(0,T)$. The Gamma factors are the positive real Euler Gamma function
[[def-real-gamma-function-by-the-euler-integral]].

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $M,d\ge1$, let $0\le c_1<\cdots<c_M\le1$ be distinct collocation nodes, and let $\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_M$ be their cardinal polynomials from [[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]]. Define
$$Q_{ij}:=\int_0^{c_i}\ell_j(s)\,ds,\qquad b_j:=\int_0^1\ell_j(s)\,ds.$$
The matrix $Q\in\mathbb R^{M\times M}$ and vector $b\in\mathbb R^M$ are the collocation tableau coefficients. For an IVP $y'=f(t,y)$ on the open domain of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]], write
$$F_j(U):=f(t+c_jh,U_j),\qquad QF(U):=\left(\sum_{j=1}^M Q_{ij}F_j(U)\right)_{i=1}^M.$$
All displayed integrals use the oriented Riemann convention of [[def-oriented-integral]]. In particular $Q_{ij}=0$ when $c_i=0$, and the integral in $u_h$ vanishes at $\tau=0$. The collocation stages and endpoint are the implicit Runge–Kutta equations of [[def-implicit-runge-kutta-stage-equations]] with $A=Q$, nodes $c$, and weights $b$:
$$U=\mathbf1u+hQF(U),\qquad \Psi_h(t,u)=u+h\sum_{j=1}^M b_jF_j(U).$$
The associated collocation polynomial on normalized time $\tau\in[0,1]$ is
$$u_h(\tau):=u+h\int_0^\tau\sum_{j=1}^M\ell_j(s)F_j(U)\,ds.$$
Thus $u_h(c_i)=U_i$, $u_h'(c_i)=hF_i(U)$, and $u_h(1)=\Psi_h(t,u)$ whenever $U$ is an admissible solution. This definition alone asserts no branch existence or uniqueness.

For interpolation estimates define the **Lebesgue constant** of this fixed node set by
$$\Lambda_M:=\max_{0\le s\le1}\sum_{j=1}^M|\ell_j(s)|.$$
For a real matrix $A$, write $\|A\|_\infty:=\max_i\sum_j|a_{ij}|$. These constants depend on the nodes and on $M$; no uniform-in-$M$ bound is part of the definition.
source_evidence.case_anchor: Definition requires M>=1 distinct nodes, so its tableau, cardinal sum and Lebesgue-constant sum are nonempty. At c_i=0 or normalized time tau=0 the oriented integral is zero as explicitly stated; no node or polynomial is selected from an empty list, and branch existence is not asserted.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $\mathcal H=\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$, with square-summability as in [[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]. Define the diagonal operator $A$ by
$$D(A)=\left\{u\in\mathcal H:\sum_{k\ge1} k^4|u_k|^2<\infty\right\},\qquad (Au)_k=-k^2u_k.$$
Let $g\in\mathcal H$ be the fixed sequence $g_k=1/k$ for odd $k$ and $g_k=0$ for even $k$; membership follows from [[thm-p-series-real-exponents]] with exponent $2$. The split evolution is $u'=Au+g$. For $t\ge0$, define the exact diagonal subflow $E_tu=(e^{-k^2t}u_k)_{k\ge1}$ and the exact translation subflow $B_tu=u+tg$. By [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]] and [[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $0<e^{-k^2t}\le1$, so each $E_t$ maps $\mathcal H$ to itself; each $B_t$ does so because $g\in\mathcal H$. The associated Strang modal step is
$$S_h=E_{h/2}\circ B_h\circ E_{h/2},\qquad h>0,$$
where the rightmost map is applied first. Each coordinate of $E_t$ solves $u_k'=-k^2u_k$, and each coordinate of $B_t$ solves $u_k'=g_k$. This is a precisely defined sequence-space model; it records one Dirichlet sine-mode boundary mismatch and makes no general convergence assertion for unbounded PDE operators.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $a,b:U\to\mathbb R^d$ be $C^3$ fields on an open set, and restrict attention to points and time intervals for which the unique local solutions of $x'=a(x)$ and $x'=b(x)$ remain in $U$. Denote their exact solution maps by $\Phi_a^t$ and $\Phi_b^t$. The **Lie split map** applies $a$ and then $b$:
$$L_h:=\Phi_b^h\circ\Phi_a^h.$$
The **Strang split map** applies half of $a$, then $b$, then half of $a$:
$$S_h:=\Phi_a^{h/2}\circ\Phi_b^h\circ\Phi_a^{h/2}.$$
Define the vector-field Lie bracket convention
$$[a,b](y):=Db(y)a(y)-Da(y)b(y).$$
This definition is finite-dimensional. It asserts neither that an unbounded operator has a common invariant domain nor that its commutators are bounded.
source_evidence.case_anchor: If a or b is zero or the bracket vanishes, the same composition/bracket formulas remain defined; the Definition makes no nonzero-error assertion.

Let $a,b:U\to\mathbb R^d$ be $C^3$ fields on an open set, and restrict attention to points and time intervals for which the unique local solutions of $x'=a(x)$ and $x'=b(x)$ remain in $U$. Denote their exact solution maps by $\Phi_a^t$ and $\Phi_b^t$. The **Lie split map** applies $a$ and then $b$:
$$L_h:=\Phi_b^h\circ\Phi_a^h.$$
The **Strang split map** applies half of $a$, then $b$, then half of $a$:
$$S_h:=\Phi_a^{h/2}\circ\Phi_b^h\circ\Phi_a^{h/2}.$$
Define the vector-field Lie bracket convention
$$[a,b](y):=Db(y)a(y)-Da(y)b(y).$$
This definition is finite-dimensional. It asserts neither that an unbounded operator has a common invariant domain nor that its commutators are bounded.
source_evidence.case_anchor: The Definition fixes composition order and bracket Db a-Da b on admitted local-flow intervals; it asserts no converse solvability or unbounded-operator claim.

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$. Its **Fenchel conjugate** is the
extended-real function on the same Euclidean space
$$f^*(s):=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\{\langle s,x\rangle-f(x)\}.$$
When $f(x)=+\infty$, the corresponding term is $-\infty$ and does not increase
the supremum. Its effective domain is
$\operatorname{dom}f^*=\{s:f^*(s)<+\infty\}$.
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: The extended-real conjugate is a supremum over the Euclidean domain, with infinite primal values contributing negative infinity rather than undefined subtraction.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $S=S^*\succ0$ be an $n\times n$ finite-basis overlap matrix and supply its
Cholesky factor $L$ with $S=LL^*$, $L$ invertible
([[def-cholesky-factorisation-with-positive-diagonal]],
[[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]]).
If $h_0=h_0^*$ is the coefficient-basis one-body matrix, set
$h=L^{-1}h_0L^{-*}$, where $L^{-*}=(L^*)^{-1}$; this is the Cholesky
whitening whose generalized Ritz quotient is preserved by
[[prop-positive-definite-overlap-whitening-preserves-generalized-ritz-pencil]].
For coefficient vectors use $y=L^*c$; the interaction map and chosen
exchange-correlation functional below are supplied in these orthonormal
coordinates. Fix $1\le r<n$ and the
projector domain $\mathcal P_r$ of [[def-rank-r-orthogonal-projector-domain]].

Supply a Hermitian matrix $h$, a real-linear self-adjoint map
$G:\mathbb H_n\to\mathbb H_n$ for the Frobenius inner product, and a real-valued
$C^2$ functional $E_{xc}$ on an open neighborhood of $\mathcal P_r$. Define
$$E(P):=\operatorname{tr}(hP)+\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(P G(P))+E_{xc}(P),\qquad F(P):=h+G(P)+\nabla E_{xc}(P).$$
Here $F(P)$ is the Hermitian Frobenius-gradient formula justified by
[[prop-finite-projector-energy-reality-and-gradient]].

The finite-basis Hartree–Fock model is the special case $E_{xc}=0$ with a
supplied symmetry-compatible Coulomb/exchange tensor defining $G$. A
Kohn–Sham-like model supplies its density map and chosen differentiable
exchange-correlation functional. These are finite-dimensional mathematical
models; this definition makes no assertion that the selected functional is an
exact continuum physical energy.

literal_source_anchor.description: the explicit admitted-domain restriction of the local drift and three shears
literal_source_anchor.quote:
Let $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, let $V\in C^1(Q,\mathbb R)$, and let $M$ be a real symmetric positive-definite matrix. Use the force-kick $K_a$ and drift $D_b$ already defined in [[def-leapfrog-step-map]], with $U$ there replaced by $V$. The local kick is the restriction of $K_a$ to $Q\times\mathbb R^d$. The local drift is the restriction of $D_b$ to
$$\{(q,p):q\in Q,\ q+bM^{-1}p\in Q\}.$$

For a signed step $h$, the local leapfrog map is the restriction of $K_{h/2}\circ D_h\circ K_{h/2}$ to the states for which all three intermediate configurations lie in $Q$. Its output is defined only on that admitted set. This definition changes the configuration domain of the published map; it does not redefine the global leapfrog map or assert that the local map is complete.

review_basis.full_actual_interface:
Assume AC. Fix a finite horizon $T>0$, finite dimensions $d,m\ge1$, and an
open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$. Use a complete usual filtered probability
space and an adapted standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion whose increments
after time $s$ are independent of $\mathcal F_s$, as in
[[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]] and
[[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]. Let $b:[0,T]\times U\to\mathbb R^d$
and $\sigma:[0,T]\times U\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}$ be Borel maps. Require
that they are bounded on every compact subset of $[0,T]\times U$ and locally
Lipschitz in the state uniformly in time: for every compact $K\subset U$ there
is $L_K<\infty$ such that, for every $t\in[0,T]$ and $x,y\in K$,
$$|b(t,x)-b(t,y)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(t,y)\|_F\le L_K|x-y|.$$
Let $\xi$ be $\mathcal F_0$-measurable, take values in $U$ almost surely, be
independent of the future Brownian increments, and satisfy $\mathbb E|\xi|^2<\infty$.

For $n\ge1$, set
$$K_n=\{x\in U: |x|\le n,\ \operatorname{dist}(x,U^c)\ge n^{-1}\}.$$
When $U=\mathbb R^d$, interpret $\operatorname{dist}(x,U^c)=+\infty$.
The compact sets $K_n$ are nested and their interiors exhaust $U$. A **local
strong solution up to exit** is the compatible family of stopped adapted
continuous processes $X^{(n)}$ and stopping times $\tau_n$ such that
$$\tau_n=\inf\{t\in[0,T]:X^{(n)}_t\notin\operatorname{int}K_n\}\wedge T, \qquad X^{(n)}_{t\wedge\tau_n}=\xi+\int_0^{t\wedge\tau_n}b(s,X^{(n)}_s)\,ds+ \int_0^{t\wedge\tau_n}\sigma(s,X^{(n)}_s)\,dW_s,$$
with the equation holding indistinguishably and with $X^{(n)}$ constant after
$\tau_n$. Empty early $K_n$ simply give $\tau_n=0$. Compatibility means that
for $m\ge n$, $X^{(m)}$ stopped at $\tau_n$ equals $X^{(n)}$ up to
indistinguishability. The maximal lifetime is $\zeta=\lim_n\tau_n$; for
$t<\zeta$, the common value of $X^{(n)}_t$ for sufficiently large $n$ defines
the maximal local solution $X_t$.

This definition records a local integral equation; it does not assert that a
solution exists or that $\zeta=T$. Those are separate theorem obligations.
The local coefficient conditions allow superlinear growth; global Lipschitz
hypotheses will be imposed only on the coefficient truncations used in the
existence proof.

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Fix $n\in\mathbb N$ and the Euclidean space $E=\mathbb R^n$ with inner
product and norm from [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. A **relation** $A$ on
$E$ is a subset of $E\times E$; write $a\in A(x)$ exactly when
$(x,a)\in A$. Its graph is this subset. The relation is **monotone** if
$$\langle x-x',a-a'\rangle\ge0\quad\text{for all }(x,a),(x',a')\in A.$$
It is **maximal monotone** if it is monotone and no strictly larger subset of
$E\times E$ is monotone. This definition is finite-dimensional and makes no
claim about infinite-dimensional spaces.
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: Monotonicity quantifies graph pairs in a finite-dimensional Euclidean relation; maximality forbids any larger monotone graph rather than assuming every relation has full domain.

literal_source_anchor.description: the B_0 assignment and predecessor coefficient recursion
literal_source_anchor.quote:
Define polynomials $B_m\in\mathbb R[X]$ recursively. Put $B_0(X)=1$. If $m\ge1$ and $B_{m-1}(X)=\sum_{q=0}^{m-1}\beta_{m-1,q}X^q$, set
$$B_m(X):=m\sum_{q=0}^{m-1}\beta_{m-1,q}\left(\frac{X^{q+1}}{q+1}-\frac{1}{(q+1)(q+2)}\right).$$
Natural numbers in real denominators mean their canonical real images from [[def-canonical-natural]]; these images are positive by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and therefore invertible in $\mathbb R$ by [[thm-reals-field]]. Every sum is finite. Write $B_m:=B_m(0)$ for the Bernoulli number of index $m$.

literal_source_anchor.description: the endpoint summands and interior range1 through n-1
literal_source_anchor.quote:
Let $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\ge1$ and let $y=(y_0,\ldots,y_n)\in\mathbb R^{n+1}$. In real-valued formulas, each natural index denotes its canonical real image ([[def-canonical-natural]]). Since $n>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]], division by $n$ is defined in $\mathbb R$ ([[thm-reals-field]]). The type-I discrete cosine transform, in the Lobatto convention used here, is the vector $X=(X_0,\ldots,X_n)$ defined by
$$X_k:=y_0+(-1)^k y_n+2\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}y_j\cos\!\left(\frac{j k\pi}{n}\right),\qquad 0\le k\le n.$$
Here $(-1)^k$ is the natural power of the real number $-1$ from [[def-integer-power]], and the sum is the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]], empty when $n=1$. The data $y_j$ are ordered from the right endpoint toward the left endpoint at nodes $\cos(j\pi/n)$. This definition fixes the unnormalised DCT-I convention; the transform is not defined at $n=0$.

literal_source_anchor.description: the affine pullback m+d t and zero-degree midpoint branch
literal_source_anchor.quote:
Let $a<b$, $m=(a+b)/2$, $d=(b-a)/2$, and $f\in C[a,b]$. For $n\ge1$, set $g(t):=f(m+dt)$ on $[-1,1]$, let $y_j=g(\cos(j\pi/n))$, and form $a_0,\ldots,a_n$ from the DCT-I coefficients in [[thm-na-clenshaw-curtis-interpolation-coefficients]]. With the Chebyshev moments $\mu_k$ of [[lem-na-chebyshev-integral-moments]], define
$$Q_{n,[a,b]}(f):=d\sum_{k=0}^{n}a_k\mu_k.$$
For $n=0$, define instead
$$Q_{0,[a,b]}(f):=(b-a)f(m),$$
the midpoint rule. This is the explicit endpoint and zero-degree convention for Clenshaw–Curtis quadrature. The sums and coefficients are exact real quantities; finite-precision evaluation is a separate algorithm.

literal_source_anchor.description: the separate r=1 indicator and Darboux-integrability paragraph
literal_source_anchor.quote:
Let $a<b$, let $x_1,\ldots,x_s\in[a,b]$ be a finite indexed list (repetitions are allowed), and let $w_1,\ldots,w_s\in\mathbb R$. For every Riemann-integrable $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$, define the quadrature value and residual by
$$Q(f):=\sum_{i=1}^{s}w_i f(x_i),\qquad L(f):=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx-Q(f).$$
For a natural $r\ge1$, say that $Q$ is exact through degree $r-1$ if $L(p)=0$ for every formal real polynomial $p$ of degree at most $r-1$ ([[def-real-polynomial-degree-leading-coefficient-and-monic]]). Here $r-1$ is the natural predecessor specified by [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]]. For any natural $q$, the factorial $q!$ in a real-valued formula denotes its canonical real image under [[def-canonical-natural]]. This denominator is nonzero: $q!\ne0$ by [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], every nonzero natural is a successor by [[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]] and therefore is at least $1$ in the natural order [[def-nat-order]], and its canonical real image is positive by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]], hence invertible by [[thm-reals-field]]. For $t\in[a,b]$ define
$$g_{r,t}(x):=\begin{cases}\dfrac{(x-t)^{r-1}}{(r-1)!},&x>t,\\0,&x\le t,\end{cases}\qquad K_r(t):=L(g_{r,t}).$$
The power is the natural power of [[def-integer-power]]. For $r\ge2$, $g_{r,t}$ is polynomial and continuous on each side of $t$ by [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]]; the polynomial branch extends to $t$ with value $0$ because $r-1\ge1$, agreeing with the zero branch. Thus it is continuous on $[a,b]$ and Riemann-integrable by [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]. For $r=1$ it is the indicator of $(t,b]$; if $t=b$ it is zero, and if $t<b$, for each $\varepsilon>0$ choose $s\in(t,b)$ with $s-t<\varepsilon$ and use the partition with breakpoints $a,t,s,b$ after deleting repeated endpoints. The indicator is constant on all panels except $[t,s]$, where its oscillation is $1$, so its upper-minus-lower sum is at most $s-t<\varepsilon$; [[thm-riemann-criterion]] makes it integrable. At $r=1$ the denominator is $0!=1$. Once $K_1$ is shown integrable, changing its values at the finitely many quadrature nodes does not change its integral by [[lem-changing-a-function-at-finitely-many-points]].

source_evidence.fullclaim: Let $V$ be a real Hilbert space, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and write $V^*$ for the continuous real dual. A parameter-dependent coercive elliptic variational problem is a family of bounded bilinear forms $a_\theta:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ and bounded linear functionals $\ell_\theta\in V^*$ such that, on each parameter neighborhood under discussion, $\|a_\theta\|\le M$ and $a_\theta(v,v)\ge\alpha\|v\|_V^2$ for fixed $M<\infty$ and $\alpha>0$. Operator-norm $C^1$ data means that the maps $\theta\mapsto A_\theta\in\mathcal L(V,V^*)$, $A_\theta u:=a_\theta(u,\cdot)$, and $\theta\mapsto\ell_\theta\in V^*$ are continuously Fréchet differentiable. A state at $\theta$ is a vector $u_\theta\in V$ satisfying $a_\theta(u_\theta,v)=\ell_\theta(v)$ for every $v\in V$. When a state is specified, a $C^1$ objective $J:V\times\Theta\to\mathbb R$ defines the reduced objective $j(\theta)=J(u_\theta,\theta)$. This definition alone asserts neither state existence nor uniqueness of an optimizer.
source_evidence.case_anchor: Coercivity requires alpha>0; a noncoercive parameter value is outside this data class, while a zero solution is not excluded.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, let $N\ge1$, and for $0\le n\le N$ let $U_n\subseteq\mathbb R^{d_n}$ be open. A finite parameterized state-step graph consists of a $C^1$ initial map $x_0:\Theta\to U_0$ and $C^1$ step maps $\Psi_n:U_n\times\Theta\to U_{n+1}$ for $0\le n<N$, such that the recursion $x_{n+1}(\theta)=\Psi_n(x_n(\theta),\theta)$ is defined for every $\theta$ in the chosen parameter neighborhood. A $C^1$ running objective consists of maps $\ell_n:U_n\times\Theta\to\mathbb R$ and a terminal objective $\phi:U_N\times\Theta\to\mathbb R$, all $C^1$. Its reduced objective is
$$J(\theta)=\phi(x_N(\theta),\theta)+\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\ell_n(x_n(\theta),\theta).$$
The maps and objective define one finite real-arithmetic graph. A gradient of this graph is the derivative of this finite composition; it is not the derivative of an exact implicit solution unless the step map itself is that solution map.
source_evidence.case_anchor: The step maps may have singular Jacobians: this is a finite composition definition, without an inverse-Jacobian hypothesis or optimizer-existence assertion.

$$J(\theta)=\phi(x_N(\theta),\theta)+\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\ell_n(x_n(\theta),\theta).$$
The maps and objective define one finite real-arithmetic graph. A gradient of this graph is the derivative of this finite composition; it is not the derivative of an exact implicit solution unless the step map itself is that solution map.

$$F_p(\mu;\lambda)=h^{-1}J(q_1)M^{-1}p_1=0,$$

$$p_{1/2}=p-\frac h2\nabla V(q)-hJ(q)^T\lambda,\qquad q_1=q+hM^{-1}p_{1/2},$$
$$p_1=p_{1/2}-\frac h2\nabla V(q_1)-hJ(q_1)^T\mu.$$
The position and momentum equations are respectively $c(q_1)=0$ and $J(q_1)M^{-1}p_1=0$. At $h=0$ define the step to be the identity.

Use the data of [[def-regular-holonomic-phase-space-and-dynamics]]. For a consistent input $(q,p)\in\mathcal M$, put $v=M^{-1}p$ and
$$\lambda_* =\mu_* =\frac12A(q)^{-1}\bigl(D^2c(q)[v,v]-J(q)M^{-1}\nabla V(q)\bigr).$$
For nonzero signed $h$, form the sequential scaled residual equations
$$F_q(\lambda)=h^{-2}c\!\left(q+hM^{-1}\left(p-\frac h2\nabla V(q)-hJ(q)^T\lambda\right)\right)=0,$$
$$F_p(\mu;\lambda)=h^{-1}J(q_1)M^{-1}p_1=0,$$
where $q_1,p_{1/2},p_1$ are given by the updates below. The selected multiplier pair, when it exists uniquely, is the local root branch whose limits as $h\to0$ are $\lambda_*$ and $\mu_*$. This defines a partial exact step map; no root-existence assertion is part of this definition.

For such a selected pair $\lambda,\mu\in\mathbb R^m$, define
$$p_{1/2}=p-\frac h2\nabla V(q)-hJ(q)^T\lambda,\qquad q_1=q+hM^{-1}p_{1/2},$$
$$p_1=p_{1/2}-\frac h2\nabla V(q_1)-hJ(q_1)^T\mu.$$
The position and momentum equations are respectively $c(q_1)=0$ and $J(q_1)M^{-1}p_1=0$. At $h=0$ define the step to be the identity.

Here $\lambda,\mu$ are force-level multipliers: the corresponding constraint impulses are $hJ^T\lambda$ and $hJ^T\mu$. This scaling keeps the limiting multiplier equations nonsingular as $h\to0$. The position equation is SHAKE; the final momentum equation is the RATTLE tangency correction.

additional_source_clauses.text:
Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, let $c:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be smooth (that is, $C^\infty$) with $1\le m<d$, let $M$ be a constant symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix, and let $V:U\to\mathbb R$ be smooth. A **holonomic constraint** is the position condition $c(q)=0$. Write $J(q)=Dc(q)$, let $Q=\{q\in U:c(q)=0\}$, and define its regular part by $Q_{\mathrm{reg}}=\{q\in Q:\operatorname{rank}J(q)=m\}$. For $q\in Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$, $A(q)=J(q)M^{-1}J(q)^T$ is positive definite. On a compact regular chart $K\subset Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$, $A^{-1}$ is uniformly bounded: $\sup_{q\in K}\|A(q)^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}<\infty$.

A position-momentum pair $(q,p)$ is **consistent** when $q\in Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$ and $J(q)M^{-1}p=0$. The **regular constrained phase manifold** is
$$\mathcal M=\{(q,p)\in U\times\mathbb R^d:c(q)=0,\ J(q)M^{-1}p=0,\ q\in Q_{\mathrm{reg}}\}.$$
The ambient canonical two-form is $\omega_0=\sum_{i=1}^d dq_i\wedge dp_i$; its restriction to $\mathcal M$ is denoted $\omega_{\mathcal M}$.

For $v=M^{-1}p$, the constrained Hamilton equations are
$$\dot q=v,\qquad \dot p=-\nabla V(q)-J(q)^T\lambda,$$
with multiplier
$$\lambda=A(q)^{-1}\bigl(D^2c(q)[v,v]-J(q)M^{-1}\nabla V(q)\bigr).$$
Here $D^2c(q)[v,v]\in\mathbb R^m$ has components $v^TD^2c_j(q)v$. This multiplier is the one that keeps both $c(q)=0$ and $J(q)M^{-1}p=0$ satisfied.

review_basis.full_actual_interface:
Fix a semi-explicit presentation $x'=f(t,x,z)$, $0=g(t,x,z)$ as in [[def-semi-explicit-index-one-dae-and-consistent-initial-data]] and a sufficiently differentiable consistent local solution. Differentiate the algebraic constraint along the differential equation, substituting $x'=f(t,x,z)$ and any previously obtained derivative relations at each stage. The **differentiation index in this convention** is the least positive integer $k$ for which the original constraint and its first $k$ differentiated equations locally determine $z$ and $z'$, with the equation for the highest derivative of $z$ having an invertible square Jacobian on a neighborhood of the solution. If no such finite $k$ exists, this local index is undefined. This convention counts through the first derivative of the algebraic variables and is local to the fixed presentation; it is not a universal index theory for arbitrary implicit systems.

If $g_z$ is invertible, one differentiation gives

$$
g_t+g_x f+g_z z'=0,
$$

which determines $z'$, so the index is one. If $g_z$ is singular, the index must be checked from the actual differentiated equations; no index-one conclusion follows from this definition alone.

Let $V\in C^4(U,\mathbb R)$, using the $C^k$ convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], and let $a,b\in U$. A **regular path with fixed endpoints** is $R\in C^1([0,1],U;\mathbb R^d)$ such that $R(0)=a$, $R(1)=b$, and $R'(s)\ne0$ for every $s\in[0,1]$ (with one-sided derivatives at the endpoints). $$P_{t(s)}^\perp\nabla V(R(s))=0\qquad(0\le s\le1),$$

where $\nabla V$ is the gradient in [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. Thus the gradient is tangent to the path; at points where it vanishes the equation still holds. The endpoints are fixed data and need not be local minima unless that is added as a hypothesis. This is a conditional mathematical definition and makes no claim about reaction rates, physical mechanisms, or uniqueness.

For a relation $A\subseteq E\times E$ and $\rho>0$, define its resolvent as
the inverse relation
$$J_{\rho A}:=(I+\rho A)^{-1},\qquad J_{\rho A}(y)=\{x\in E:y-x\in\rho A(x)\},$$
where $\rho A(x)=\{\rho a:a\in A(x)\}$. Its domain is the set of $y$ for
which this value set is nonempty. At this point it may be partial and
set-valued; full domain and single-valuedness are separate conclusions of
[[thm-maximal-monotone-resolvent-is-firmly-nonexpansive]].

$$A_{\gamma,h}(\widetilde J):=I_d-\gamma h\widetilde J.$$
When this matrix is invertible, the **one-stage Rosenbrock step** uses the stage slope $k$ and update
$$A_{\gamma,h}(\widetilde J)k=f(t,y),\qquad \Phi_{\gamma,h}^{\widetilde J}(t,y):=y+hk.$$
The **exact-Jacobian branch** sets $\widetilde J=D_yf(t,y)$, where $D_yf$ is the Jacobian in the state variables as in [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. An approximate-Jacobian branch may supply a different $\widetilde J$; the equation requires the chosen shifted matrix to be invertible. The name **Rosenbrock–Euler** here refers to the case $\gamma=1$. This definition specifies one linearized step and does not say that it solves the full backward-Euler nonlinear equation.

Let $X,Y$ be nonempty subsets of finite-dimensional real Euclidean spaces and
let $\Psi:X\times Y\to[-\infty,+\infty]$ be an extended-real function. A
pair $(x_*,y_*)$ is a
**saddle point** of $\Psi$ if $\Psi(x_*,y_*)$ is finite and
$$\Psi(x_*,y)\le \Psi(x_*,y_*)\le \Psi(x,y_*)\qquad(x\in X,\ y\in Y).$$
The inequalities must be defined at the arguments they display. For an
equality-constrained problem the primal set may be a product set of
finite-valued pairs $(x,z)$.

review_basis.full_actual_interface:
Let $d,m\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$ and $g:\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$. A **semi-explicit differential-algebraic equation (DAE)** on $\Omega$ is

$$
x'(t)=f(t,x(t),z(t)),\qquad 0=g(t,x(t),z(t)).
$$

The $x$-coordinates are the **differential variables** because their derivatives occur in the first equation. The $z$-coordinates are the **algebraic variables** because their derivatives do not occur. A solution on an interval $I$ is a pair of functions $x:I\to\mathbb R^d$, $z:I\to\mathbb R^m$ whose graph lies in $\Omega$, with $x$ differentiable, satisfying both displayed equations at every $t\in I$. An initial pair $(x_0,z_0)$ at $t_0$ is **algebraically consistent** when $g(t_0,x_0,z_0)=0$. On the regular index-one branch below this is the algebraic initial condition used for reduction. For higher-index systems, algebraic consistency is only necessary: differentiated constraints may impose additional initial conditions.

At a point with $g(t_*,x_*,z_*)=0$, the presentation is **regular index one** when $f,g$ are $C^1$ near the point and the square Jacobian $g_z(t_*,x_*,z_*)=D_zg(t_*,x_*,z_*)$ is invertible. The [[thm-index-one-dae-implicit-function-reduction]] then supplies a unique local branch $z=\psi(t,x)$ through that point. Only that selected branch is used in local numerical claims. Higher-index systems and points with singular $g_z$ are outside this index-one interface.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Fix a dimension $d\ge1$. A finite set $\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb N_0^d$ is
**downward closed** if, whenever $\ell\in\Lambda$ and $\ell_j>0$, the index
$\ell-e_j$ also belongs to $\Lambda$; here $e_j$ is the $j$th coordinate unit
vector. In this pair an admissible Smolyak set is a nonempty finite downward-
closed $\Lambda$ that contains $0$.

For a level hierarchy from [[def-smolyak-univariate-level-hierarchy]], define
the **Smolyak cubature functional**
$$Q_\Lambda(f):=\sum_{\ell\in\Lambda}(\Delta_{\ell_1}^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes\Delta_{\ell_d}^{(d)})(f).$$
Each summand is a finite signed weighted sum. Expanding all differences and
adding coefficients at equal points gives one finite signed weight for each
distinct node in
$$\mathcal N_\Lambda:=\bigcup_{\ell\in\Lambda}X_{\ell_1}\times\cdots\times X_{\ell_d}.$$
The **node-union work count** for this direct evaluation convention is
$W(\Lambda):=|\mathcal N_\Lambda|$, so shared nodes are counted once. A
combined weight may be negative or zero; no positivity claim follows from the
definition.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $Q:[0,1]\to\mathbb R$ be a finite quadrature functional of the form
$$Q(g)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i g(x_i),$$
where $m\ge1$, the nodes $x_i\in[0,1]$ are distinct, and $w_i\in\mathbb R$.
A one-dimensional **nested level hierarchy** is a sequence
$(Q_\ell)_{\ell\in\mathbb N_0}$ of such functionals, with node sets
$X_\ell=\{x_{\ell,i}:1\le i\le m_\ell\}$ satisfying
$X_{\ell-1}\subseteq X_\ell$ for every $\ell\ge1$.
Set $Q_{-1}:=0$, the zero functional, and define the **detail functional**
$$\Delta_0:=Q_0,\qquad \Delta_\ell:=Q_\ell-Q_{\ell-1}\quad(\ell\ge1).$$
Finite sums are as in [[def-finite-sum]]. For each $d\ge1$, the integration
functional used below is $I_d(f):=\int_{[0,1]^d}f$, with the multiple Riemann
integral convention of [[def-multidimensional-darboux-integral]].

The convergence and rate results in this pair use the **dyadic composite-
Simpson hierarchy**
$$Q_\ell(g):=Q_S(g;0,1,2^{\ell+1}),\qquad X_\ell=\{k/2^{\ell+1}:0\le k\le2^{\ell+1}\},$$
where $Q_S$ is the even-panel rule of [[alg-composite-simpson-rule]]. The
number of panels is even and at least two. The sets are nested because
$k/2^{\ell}=2k/2^{\ell+1}$, and their weights are nonnegative with total
weight one: each two-panel block has nonnegative weights $H(1,4,1)/6$
summing to its length $H$, and the blocks partition an interval of length one.
Level zero has nodes $0,1/2,1$ and weights $1/6,4/6,1/6$.

For a multi-index $\ell=(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_d)\in\mathbb N_0^d$, any tensor
product $R_{\ell_1}^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes R_{\ell_d}^{(d)}$ of these
finite functionals means the finite weighted functional obtained by multiplying
the coordinate weights and evaluating on the corresponding node tuples. In
particular, $\Delta_\ell:=\Delta_{\ell_1}^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes
\Delta_{\ell_d}^{(d)}$. No exactness or error property is implied by the
notation alone.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Use the smooth program, dimensions, gradient conventions, and Lagrangian
$L(x,\nu,\lambda)=f(x)+\nu^Th(x)+\lambda^Tg(x)$ of
[[def-inequality-constrained-program-and-kkt-geometry]]. Let $\rho>0$,
$\nu\in\mathbb R^p$, and $\lambda\in\mathbb R^m_+$. The equality
augmented Lagrangian is
$$\mathcal L^E_\rho(x,\nu)=f(x)+\nu^Th(x)+\tfrac{\rho}{2}\|h(x)\|_2^2.$$
For inequalities, with $[z]_i^+=\max\{z_i,0\}$, the projected
(Powell–Hestenes–Rockafellar) augmented Lagrangian is
$$\mathcal L_\rho(x,\nu,\lambda)=f(x)+\nu^Th(x)+\tfrac{\rho}{2}\|h(x)\|_2^2+ \frac{\|[\lambda+\rho g(x)]_+\|_2^2-\|\lambda\|_2^2}{2\rho}.$$
After an inner candidate $x^+$ is produced, the multiplier update is
$$\nu^+=\nu+\rho h(x^+),\qquad \lambda^+=[\lambda+\rho g(x^+)]_+.$$
The bracket is componentwise. A **declared inner stationarity residual** is
$\|\nabla_x\mathcal L_\rho(x^+,\nu,\lambda)\|_2$; an inner procedure must
report the residual it achieved or an explicit failure status.

The equality and inequality formulas are distinct branches. For an inequality
with $\lambda_i+\rho g_i(x)>0$, its summand equals
$\lambda_i g_i(x)+\rho g_i(x)^2/2$; when
$\lambda_i+\rho g_i(x)\le0$, its summand is constant in $x$.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Use the nonlinear program and SQP subproblem conventions of
[[def-sqp-linearized-quadratic-subproblem]]. For $\rho>0$, define the
nondifferentiable L1 merit function
$$\psi_\rho(x)=f(x)+\rho\left(\|h(x)\|_1+\|[g(x)]_+\|_1\right).$$
For a subproblem step $p$ at $x$, its linearized predicted decrease is
$$D_\rho(x,p)=-\left[\nabla f(x)^Tp+\rho\left(\|h(x)+Dh(x)p\|_1-\|h(x)\|_1+ \|[g(x)+Dg(x)p]_+\|_1-\|[g(x)]_+\|_1\right)\right].$$
A trial fraction $t\in(0,1]$ satisfies the Armijo test with coefficient
$\sigma\in(0,1)$ when
$$\psi_\rho(x+tp)\le\psi_\rho(x)-\sigma tD_\rho(x,p).$$
The definition alone does not assert $D_\rho(x,p)>0$, existence of an
accepted fraction, or convergence of a sequence of accepted SQP steps.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Use the smooth nonlinear program convention of
[[def-inequality-constrained-program-and-kkt-geometry]]: minimize a $C^2$
objective $f:U\to\mathbb R$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, subject to
$h(x)=0$ and componentwise $g(x)\le0$. Fix a current point $x\in U$ and a
symmetric positive-definite matrix $B\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$. The
**SQP quadratic subproblem** is
$$\min_{p\in\mathbb R^n}\quad \nabla f(x)^Tp+\tfrac12p^TBp \quad\text{subject to}\quad h(x)+Dh(x)p=0,\quad g(x)+Dg(x)p\le0.$$
The variable $p$ is the proposed displacement. Its feasible set is the
polyhedron defined by the displayed affine constraints. A constraint index
$i$ is **active at $p$** when $g_i(x)+Dg_i(x)p=0$. For equality multiplier
$\nu$ and inequality multipliers $\lambda\ge0$, a **KKT tuple** for the
subproblem satisfies primal feasibility,
$$Bp+\nabla f(x)+Dh(x)^T\nu+Dg(x)^T\lambda=0, \qquad \lambda_i\bigl(g_i(x)+Dg_i(x)p\bigr)=0\quad(1\le i\le m).$$
Rows of $Dh(x)$ and active rows of $Dg(x)$ are stacked in that order in the
subproblem KKT matrix $\begin{bmatrix}B&A^T\\A&0\end{bmatrix}$.

All inequality signs and multiplier signs here agree with the source program:
$g_i\le0$ and $\lambda_i\ge0$.

Let $V$ and $U$ be as in [[def-regular-minimum-energy-path-in-a-collision-free-tube]], let $x\in U$, and let $H=\nabla^2V(x)$ use the convention of [[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]]. Since $V\in C^4(U)$, it is $C^2$; [[cor-hessian-is-symmetric]] gives $H^T=H$. In the standard Euclidean inner product this makes the endomorphism represented by $H$ self-adjoint. Therefore the real spectral theorem [[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]] applies, and $H$ has ordered eigenvalues $\lambda_1(H)\le\cdots\le\lambda_d(H)$.

A **validated ordered eigenvalue enclosure** is a list of intervals $I_j=[\ell_j,u_j]$ together with an independently checked certificate proving $\lambda_j(H)\in I_j$ for every $j$ and preserving the stated ordering. The exact Hessian $H$, interval arithmetic or another validated spectral method, and all rounding assumptions used by the certificate are part of that external certificate; a Ritz value or residual alone is not, by definition, such a certificate.

For $d\ge2$ and $\gamma>0$, the enclosure certifies **index one with gap $\gamma$** when $u_1\le-\gamma$ and $\ell_j\ge\gamma$ for every $j\ge2$. For $d=1$, the condition is $u_1\le-\gamma$, with no positive-eigenvalue clauses. A validated enclosure records the input evidence; this definition does not assert that any particular eigensolver produces it.

## Definition

Let $V$ and $U$ be as in [[def-regular-minimum-energy-path-in-a-collision-free-tube]], let $x\in U$, and let $H=\nabla^2V(x)$ use the convention of [[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]]. Since $V\in C^4(U)$, it is $C^2$; [[cor-hessian-is-symmetric]] gives $H^T=H$. In the standard Euclidean inner product this makes the endomorphism represented by $H$ self-adjoint. Therefore the real spectral theorem [[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]] applies, and $H$ has ordered eigenvalues $\lambda_1(H)\le\cdots\le\lambda_d(H)$.

A **validated ordered eigenvalue enclosure** is a list of intervals $I_j=[\ell_j,u_j]$ together with an independently checked certificate proving $\lambda_j(H)\in I_j$ for every $j$ and preserving the stated ordering. The exact Hessian $H$, interval arithmetic or another validated spectral method, and all rounding assumptions used by the certificate are part of that external certificate; a Ritz value or residual alone is not, by definition, such a certificate.

For $d\ge2$ and $\gamma>0$, the enclosure certifies **index one with gap $\gamma$** when $u_1\le-\gamma$ and $\ell_j\ge\gamma$ for every $j\ge2$. For $d=1$, the condition is $u_1\le-\gamma$, with no positive-eigenvalue clauses. A validated enclosure records the input evidence; this definition does not assert that any particular eigensolver produces it.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
For a continuous $f$ on $[-1,1]$, define its Chebyshev coefficients by
$$a_0(f)=\frac1\pi\int_0^\pi f(\cos\theta)\,d\theta,\qquad a_n(f)=\frac2\pi\int_0^\pi f(\cos\theta)\cos(n\theta)\,d\theta\quad(n\ge1).$$
For the analytic function $f_a(x)=1/(2-x)$, these coefficients are $a_0=1/\sqrt3$ and $a_n=2(2-\sqrt3)^n/\sqrt3$ for $n\ge1$, a geometric decay. For the nonsmooth function $f_s(x)=|x|$, they are $a_0=2/\pi$, $a_{2m}=4(-1)^{m-1}/(\pi(4m^2-1))$ for $m\ge1$, and $a_{2m+1}=0$; the nonzero coefficients decay algebraically like $m^{-2}$.
source_evidence.case_anchor:
For a continuous $f$ on $[-1,1]$, define its Chebyshev coefficients by
$$a_0(f)=\frac1\pi\int_0^\pi f(\cos\theta)\,d\theta,\qquad a_n(f)=\frac2\pi\int_0^\pi f(\cos\theta)\cos(n\theta)\,d\theta\quad(n\ge1).$$
For the analytic function $f_a(x)=1/(2-x)$, these coefficients are $a_0=1/\sqrt3$ and $a_n=2(2-\sqrt3)^n/\sqrt3$ for $n\ge1$, a geometric decay. For the nonsmooth function $f_s(x)=|x|$, they are $a_0=2/\pi$, $a_{2m}=4(-1)^{m-1}/(\pi(4m^2-1))$ for $m\ge1$, and $a_{2m+1}=0$; the nonzero coefficients decay algebraically like $m^{-2}$.

proofparagraphs.text: The function $f_s(x)=|x|$ is not differentiable at $0$: for $h>0$ its difference quotient is $1$, while for $h<0$ it is $-1$, so the two-sided limit in [F11] does not exist. By [F7], $|\cos\theta|=\cos\theta$ on $[0,\pi/2]$ and $|\cos\theta|=-\cos\theta$ on $[\pi/2,\pi]$. The subtraction identity [F9] gives $\cos(n(\pi-\theta))=(-1)^n\cos(n\theta)$, so reflection makes each odd coefficient integral its own negative. Therefore $a_0(f_s)=\frac1\pi\int_0^\pi|\cos\theta|\,d\theta=\frac2\pi.$ For odd $n$, that reflection makes $a_n(f_s)=0$. [given, F6, F7, F9, F11, algebra]

Put $q=2-\sqrt3$. Then $0<q<1$, $q^{-1}=2+\sqrt3$, $q+q^{-1}=4$, and $1-q^2=2\sqrt3q$. By [F8], $z=qe^{i\theta}$ has modulus $q$. For $m\ge1$, put $S_m(z)=\sum_{n=1}^m z^n$. Multiplying the finite sum by $1-z$ cancels consecutive terms and gives $(1-z)S_m=z-z^{m+1}$. The triangle inequality in [F3] gives $|1-z|\ge1-q>0$, so $$\left|S_m(z)-\frac z{1-z}\right|=\frac{|z|^{m+1}}{|1-z|}\le\frac{q^{m+1}}{1-q}.$$ Induction using the addition formulas in [F5] and Euler's identity in [F8] gives $z^n=q^n(\cos(n\theta)+i\sin(n\theta))$. Thus $C_m(\theta):=1+2\sum_{n=1}^m q^n\cos(n\theta)$ differs from $1+2\operatorname{Re}(z/(1-z))$ by at most $2q^{m+1}/(1-q)$, uniformly for $\theta\in[0,\pi]$. [F3, F4, F5, F8, algebra, induction]

Multiplying the finite sum by $1-z$ cancels consecutive terms and gives $(1-z)S_m=z-z^{m+1}$. The triangle inequality in [F3] gives $|1-z|\ge1-q>0$, so $$\left|S_m(z)-\frac z{1-z}\right|=\frac{|z|^{m+1}}{|1-z|}\le\frac{q^{m+1}}{1-q}.$$ Induction using the addition formulas in [F5] and Euler's identity in [F8] gives $z^n=q^n(\cos(n\theta)+i\sin(n\theta))$. source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Take $f(x)=\tfrac12(x-1)^2$, $g(z)=\tfrac12(z+1)^2$, constraint $x-z=0$,
$\rho=1$, and scaled initial values $z^0=u^0=0$. The primal optimizer is
$x_*=z_*=0$ with value $p_*=1$; $y_*=1$ is a saddle and dual optimizer. The
first two exact scaled ADMM sweeps are
$$(x^1,z^1,u^1)=\left(\tfrac12,-\tfrac14,\tfrac34\right),\qquad (x^2,z^2,u^2)=\left(0,-\tfrac18,\tfrac78\right).$$
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: The fixed two scalar quadratics with unit penalty have zero consensus optimizer and the displayed two exact rational sweeps.
selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.2 Differentiating the first strictly convex quadratic in [F1] gives $2x^{k+1}=1+z^k-u^k$. At $k=0$ this yields $x^1=1/2$. Differentiating the second gives $2z^{k+1}=x^{k+1}+u^k-1$, hence $z^1=-1/4$ and then $u^1=u^0+x^1-z^1=3/4$. [A1, F1, given, algebra]

3.1 The same two equations give $x^2=(1-1/4-3/4)/2=0$, $z^2=(0+3/4-1)/2=-1/8$, and $u^2=3/4+0-(-1/8)=7/8$. Each subproblem is a strictly convex quadratic, so both minimizers in each of these sweeps are attained and unique. The recurrence values are exact rationals. [A1, F1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

$$M_1(\mu_t)=M,\qquad M_0(\mu_t)=\frac{N_0}{1+\kappa N_0t/2}.$$

proofparagraphs.text: With $\varphi(x)=x$, the coagulation increment is $(x+y)-x-y=0$. The integral equation therefore gives $M_1(\mu_t)=M$ on the solution interval. [given, F1, algebra]

With $\varphi=1$, the increment is $1-1-1=-1$, so $N'(t)=-\kappa N(t)^2/2$. If $N_0>0$, differentiating $1/N(t)$ gives $(1/N)'=\kappa/2$ and hence the displayed formula. If $N_0=0$, positivity gives $N(t)\ge0$ and the differential equation gives $N'(t)\le0$, so $N(t)=0$, again the formula. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

additional_source_clauses.text:
Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, let $c:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be smooth (that is, $C^\infty$) with $1\le m<d$, let $M$ be a constant symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix, and let $V:U\to\mathbb R$ be smooth. A **holonomic constraint** is the position condition $c(q)=0$. Write $J(q)=Dc(q)$, let $Q=\{q\in U:c(q)=0\}$, and define its regular part by $Q_{\mathrm{reg}}=\{q\in Q:\operatorname{rank}J(q)=m\}$. For $q\in Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$, $A(q)=J(q)M^{-1}J(q)^T$ is positive definite. On a compact regular chart $K\subset Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$, $A^{-1}$ is uniformly bounded: $\sup_{q\in K}\|A(q)^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}<\infty$.

A position-momentum pair $(q,p)$ is **consistent** when $q\in Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$ and $J(q)M^{-1}p=0$. The **regular constrained phase manifold** is
$$\mathcal M=\{(q,p)\in U\times\mathbb R^d:c(q)=0,\ J(q)M^{-1}p=0,\ q\in Q_{\mathrm{reg}}\}.$$
The ambient canonical two-form is $\omega_0=\sum_{i=1}^d dq_i\wedge dp_i$; its restriction to $\mathcal M$ is denoted $\omega_{\mathcal M}$.

For $v=M^{-1}p$, the constrained Hamilton equations are
$$\dot q=v,\qquad \dot p=-\nabla V(q)-J(q)^T\lambda,$$
with multiplier
$$\lambda=A(q)^{-1}\bigl(D^2c(q)[v,v]-J(q)M^{-1}\nabla V(q)\bigr).$$
Here $D^2c(q)[v,v]\in\mathbb R^m$ has components $v^TD^2c_j(q)v$. This multiplier is the one that keeps both $c(q)=0$ and $J(q)M^{-1}p=0$ satisfied.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $D=(-\pi/4,\pi/4)\times(-1/4,1/4)$ and define

$$X(s,n)=(1+n)(\cos s,\sin s),\qquad U:=X(D).$$

This is an open annular sector: its points have radius $3/4<\|x\|_2<5/4$, positive first coordinate, and angular coordinate in $(-\pi/4,\pi/4)$. The displayed polar map is one-to-one on $D$ with smooth inverse $s=\arctan(y/x)$ and $n=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}-1$. Let $a=\pi/6$, $W(s)=(s^2-a^2)^2$, and define $V(X(s,n))=W(s)+n^2/2$ on $U$. The curve $R(t)=X(-a+2at,0)$, $0\le t\le1$, is a regular MEP joining the two minima $X(-a,0)$ and $X(a,0)$. Its image is the circular arc of radius one. The point $X(0,0)$ is an index-one saddle.

By [F3], $\nabla V(X(s,n))\cdot T(s)=W'(s)/(1+n)$ and $\nabla V(X(s,n))\cdot N(s)=n$. At $n=0$, the path tangent is $T(s)$ and its unit normal is $N(s)$, so the normal gradient component vanishes. The path is regular because $\|R'(t)\|_2=2a>0$; hence it is a regular MEP by [F1]. [F1, F3, given, algebra]

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $P_0=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$, $P_1=\operatorname{diag}(0,1)$, and
$X=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$. In the finite-basis model choose
$S=L=I_2$, $h=0$, $E_{xc}=0$, and the real-linear map
$$G(P)=\bigl(\langle P,P_0\rangle_F-\langle P,P_1\rangle_F\bigr)X+\langle P,X\rangle_F(P_0-P_1).$$
At $P_0$ and $P_1$ the commutator residuals are equal and nonzero, making the
two-vector Gram matrix singular. A solver that reports this singular system
uses the specified baseline fallback, even though the exact capped minimizer
exists.

actualproofparagraphs.2.1: Substitution gives $G(P_0)=X$ and $G(P_1)=-X$. The matrices $X$ and $-X$ have eigenvalues $-1,1$, so both iterates have gap $2$. Direct multiplication gives $[G(P_0),P_0]=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}=[G(P_1),P_1]\ne0.$ [step 1.1, algebra]
actualproofparagraphs.3.1: Writing the common residual as $J$, the Gram matrix is $B_{ij}=\langle J,J\rangle_F=2,\qquad B=\begin{pmatrix}2&2\\2&2\end{pmatrix},$ which is singular. The equality-constrained bordered system has matrix $\begin{pmatrix}2&2&1\\2&2&1\\1&1&0\end{pmatrix}$, whose first two rows coincide, so a solver that reports singularity takes the prescribed fallback. With $C=2$, $c=(1/2,1/2)$ is feasible and minimizes the objective; the objective is constant on $c_1+c_2=1$, so [F2] selects this unique minimum-norm minimizer. If a rank-revealing solver returns it instead of reporting singularity, then $F_{mix}=\tfrac12X-\tfrac12X=0$ has no strict gap, and the proposal algorithm again falls back by its candidate-gap branch. Thus either outcome of this configured solve uses the baseline. [step 2.1, F2, F3, algebra] ∎

source_evidence.case_anchor: The two explicitly supplied residual matrices are equal and nonzero in Proof step 2.1. Proof step 3.1 exhibits the feasible coefficient pair(1/2,1/2), so no empty history or feasible coefficient set is involved.

source_evidence.fullclaim: On $\mathbb R^2$, let $V(x,y)=x^4/24+y^2/2$, take the point $(0,0)$ and direction $v=e_1$. The exact Hessian action is $\nabla^2V(0,0)e_1=0$. With exact gradients, the central dimer estimate is $D_\epsilon=(\epsilon^2/6)e_1$. If the two gradient evaluations have errors $+\eta e_1$ and $-\eta e_1$, each of norm $\eta$, the computed estimate becomes $\widehat D_\epsilon=(\epsilon^2/6+\eta/\epsilon)e_1$. The truncation bias decreases with $\epsilon$, while this permitted noise contribution increases as $\epsilon$ shrinks.
source_evidence.case_anchor: For fixed $\eta>0$, the deterministic term $\epsilon^2/6$ tends to zero as $\epsilon\to0$, but the permitted error term $\eta/\epsilon$ grows without bound. Therefore reducing the dimer separation does not monotonically improve the Hessian-vector estimate when force evaluations are inexact. [step 2.1, algebra] ∎

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Use the sequence-space Dirichlet heat model in [[def-dirichlet-sine-mode-heat-splitting-model]] with zero initial state and forcing coefficients $g_k=1/k$ for odd $k$, zero for even $k$. The generator-domain and boundary mismatch are certified by [[lem-diagonal-heat-semigroup-generator-domain]] and [[lem-dirichlet-forcing-coefficients-exceed-the-generator-domain]]. At a fixed time $T>0$, the exact coordinatewise solution and the Strang approximation with $N=T/h$ steps satisfy
$$c_T h^{5/4}\le\|\widetilde u_N-u(T)\|_{\ell^2}\le C_T h^{5/4}$$
for all sufficiently small $h=T/N$, with constants $c_T,C_T>0$. This is a rigorously specified modal example of boundary-induced order reduction. It is not a convergence theorem for general unbounded PDE operators.

actualproofparagraphs.1.1: For each mode, solving $u_k'=-k^2u_k+g_k$, $u_k(0)=0$, gives $u_k(t)=\frac{g_k}{k^2}(1-e^{-k^2t}).$ Differentiating verifies the equation and initial value. Also $|u_k(t)|\le |g_k|/k^2\le k^{-3}$, so [F4] shows the reference state belongs to $\ell^2$ for every $t\ge0$. [F1, F4, F5, algebra]
actualproofparagraphs.1.2: Put $x=k^2h$. By [F1], each Strang coordinate obeys $\widetilde u_{n+1,k}=e^{-x}\widetilde u_{n,k}+h e^{-x/2}g_k.$ Starting from zero and summing this scalar recurrence gives $\widetilde u_{N,k}=h e^{-x/2}\frac{1-e^{-Nx}}{1-e^{-x}}g_k,$ where the finite geometric identity follows by multiplying the sum by $1-e^{-x}$; the denominator is positive because $x>0$ and the exponential is strictly increasing. [F1, F5, algebra]
actualproofparagraphs.2.2: Since $Nx=k^2T$, the identity $\frac{h e^{-x/2}}{1-e^{-x}}=\frac{1}{k^2}\frac{x}{e^{x/2}-e^{-x/2}}$ turns the numerical value into the exact modal value times $x/\sigma(x)$, where $\sigma(x):=e^{x/2}-e^{-x/2}$. Therefore for odd $k$, $|\widetilde u_{N,k}-u_k(T)|=k^{-3}(1-e^{-k^2T})q(k^2h),\qquad q(x):=1-\frac{x}{\sigma(x)},$ and the error is zero for even $k$. [F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]
actualproofparagraphs.4.1: For sufficiently small $h$, $H\ge8$ and $h\le T$. The interval $[H,2H]$ contains at least $H-1$ integers, and among any $m$ consecutive integers at least $(m-1)/2$ are odd; hence it contains at least $H/4$ odd integers. For each such $k$, $1\le k^2h\le4$, $k^{-6}\ge(2H)^{-6}$, $q(k^2h)\ge q(1)$ by step 2.3, and $1-e^{-k^2T}\ge1-e^{-T/h}>1/2$ since $T/h\ge1$ and $e=1+1+\sum_{n\ge2}1/n!>2$. Therefore the sum of squared errors over these modes is at least $\frac H4\,(2H)^{-6}\,\frac{q(1)^2}{4}=cH^{-5}=c h^{5/2}$ for a constant $c>0$. Taking square roots of the upper bound in step 3.1 and this lower bound proves the claimed two-sided $h^{5/4}$ error rate. [F5, step 2.3, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

source_evidence.case_anchor: Even modal errors are exactly zero by Proof step 2.2, while Proof step 4.1 obtains its strictly positive lower bound from odd modes; zero initial state is explicitly used in Proof step 1.1 and1.2.

Take $J(u)=\int_0^1u\,dx$. On a neighborhood of each fixed $\theta>-1$, the form is uniformly coercive in the $H^1$ norm, so this is a parameterized coercive elliptic problem in the sense of [[def-parameterized-elliptic-variational-problem]].

By the product rule [F7], $(w'v_\varepsilon)'=w''v_\varepsilon+w'v_\varepsilon'$; since $v_\varepsilon$ vanishes at both endpoints, [F6] gives $\int_0^1w'v_\varepsilon'=\int_0^1v_\varepsilon$. By [F8], the difference between the two sides with $v$ in place of $v_\varepsilon$ is at most $(\|w'\|_{L^2}+1)\varepsilon$, so the weak identity $\int_0^1w'v'=\int_0^1v$ follows as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. Also, [F4] gives $a_\theta(v,v)\ge(1+\theta)\|v\|_{H^1}^2/2$; on a neighborhood of each $\theta>-1$ this is a uniform coercivity bound. Hence $u_\theta=w/(1+\theta)$ solves the state equation and is unique. Finally $\int_0^1w=1/12$, so $j(\theta)=1/(12(1+\theta))$. [A1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, F7, F8, given, algebra]

Realify $\mathbb C^2$ as $\mathbb R^4$ and let
$$H_K=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad V=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad A=-iH_K,\quad B=-iV.$$
Here $H_K$ is a two-level kinetic matrix and $V$ is a Hermitian potential coupling. The finite-dimensional Schrödinger equation is $\psi'=(A+B)\psi=-i(H_K+V)\psi$. Each exact kinetic or potential subflow preserves the Euclidean norm, so every exact Lie or Strang composition does as well. The local errors are nonzero for suitable initial data because the two generators do not commute; no spatial PDE or unbounded-operator conclusion is claimed.

Applying [F2] shows the exact subflows retain norm while the Lie and Strang maps have their respective nonzero local splitting defects. [F2, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

actualproofparagraphs.1.1: Solving the scalar residual gives $(1+hk)Y=u_0$, hence $Y=u_0/(1+hk)$. Since $1+hk>0$, this is the unique root in the stated interval and agrees with the branch in [F1]. [F1, F3, given, algebra]

review_basis.full_actual_interface:
Let $v(t)$ be the capacitor voltage and $i(t)$ the series current in a circuit with capacitance $C>0$, resistance $R>0$, and source voltage $u(t)$. Kirchhoff's current law and voltage law give the semi-explicit system

$$
C v'=i,\qquad 0=R i+v-u(t).
$$

The algebraic equation determines $i=(u(t)-v)/R$. With $C=R=1$, $u(t)=1$, and $v(0)=0$, the consistent initial current is $i(0)=1$, and the reduced ODE is $v'=1-v$. One backward-Euler step of size $h$ gives

$$
v_1=\frac{h}{1+h},\qquad i_1=\frac1{1+h}.
$$

For $h=1$, this is $(v_1,i_1)=(1/2,1/2)$. The pair $v(0)=0,i(0)=0$ is inconsistent for this same source.
review_basis.source_specific_focus: The scalar resistor/capacitor constraint yields an explicit current branch and the paired backward-Euler voltage/current values, rejecting the wrong initial current.

For $q,v\in\mathbb R^2$, multiplier $\lambda\in\mathbb R$, length $\ell>0$, and gravitational acceleration $g_0>0$, consider

$$
q'=v,\qquad v'=-g_0 e_2-\lambda q,\qquad 0=\frac12(q^\mathsf Tq-\ell^2),
$$

where $e_2=(0,1)^\mathsf T$. The position constraint, tangency condition, and acceleration constraint determine the allowed initial position, velocity, and multiplier. On the constraint manifold the multiplier is

$$
\lambda=\frac{\|v\|_2^2-g_0q_2}{\ell^2}.
$$

This is a regular index-three DAE in the convention of [[def-regular-differentiation-index]].

review_basis.full_actual_interface:
For $q,v\in\mathbb R^2$, multiplier $\lambda\in\mathbb R$, length $\ell>0$, and gravitational acceleration $g_0>0$, consider

$$
q'=v,\qquad v'=-g_0 e_2-\lambda q,\qquad 0=\frac12(q^\mathsf Tq-\ell^2),
$$

where $e_2=(0,1)^\mathsf T$. The position constraint, tangency condition, and acceleration constraint determine the allowed initial position, velocity, and multiplier. On the constraint manifold the multiplier is

$$
\lambda=\frac{\|v\|_2^2-g_0q_2}{\ell^2}.
$$

This is a regular index-three DAE in the convention of [[def-regular-differentiation-index]].

review_basis.full_actual_interface:
Consider the scalar semi-explicit system

$$
x'=z,\qquad 0=g(x,z):=x.
$$

Its algebraic Jacobian is $g_z=0$, so it is not regular index one. In the convention of [[def-regular-differentiation-index]], differentiating $x=0$ once gives $z=0$, and differentiating again gives $z'=0$; the system has differentiation index two. The algebraic residual is $g(x,z)=x$: at every candidate $(0,M)$, it is zero for any $M$, although the algebraic variable of a solution must be $z=0$. Thus no residual-to-$z$-error bound holds near $(0,0)$. The initial pair $(0,1)$ satisfies the algebraic equation but is not consistent with a solution, while $(1,0)$ violates the algebraic equation and cannot be an initial value.

literal_source_anchor.quote: For $n>m$, the truncated version of [F3] retains exactly the $m$ terms with index lag $j=0,\ldots,m-1$. Since $u^k-u^{k-1}=h$, $$\widetilde\delta_h^\alpha u^n =\frac{h^{1-\alpha}}{\Gamma(2-\alpha)}\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}a_j =\frac{h^{1-\alpha}m^{1-\alpha}}{\Gamma(2-\alpha)},$$ where the sum telescopes. The full sum through $j=n-1$ likewise telescopes to $n^{1-\alpha}$ and equals the exact derivative from step 1.2. This gives the bias stated. [step 1.2, F3, algebra]

literal_source_anchor.quote: The direct full-history step $n$ uses one term for each increment $k=1,\ldots,n$. Let $S=\sum_{n=1}^N n$. Reindexing by $n\mapsto N+1-n$ using [F8] also gives $S=\sum_{n=1}^N(N+1-n)$. Adding these equalities termwise gives $2S=\sum_{n=1}^N(N+1)=N(N+1)$ by [F7], so the full-history term count is $N(N+1)/2$. Retaining the sequence requires $N+1$ nodal values. [given, F7, F8, algebra]

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Let $K=\operatorname{diag}(1,2)$ and start exact symmetric Lanczos at the unit
vector $b=e_1=(1,0)^T$. At $m=0$, $K_0(K,b)=\{0\}$ and there is no Ritz value. For every $m\ge1$, $K_m(K,b)=\operatorname{span}\{e_1\}$,
so its only Ritz value is $1$, while the induced Euclidean operator norm is
$\|K\|_2=2$. The Ritz value from this start does not certify the PDHG upper
step-size bound.
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: The chosen diagonal matrix and first-coordinate start keep every positive-dimensional Krylov subspace one-dimensional, so the only Ritz value misses the larger matrix norm.
selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 Since $Kb=e_1=b$, every power $K^j b=b$. For $m=0$, the spanning list is empty and its span is $\{0\}$, with no nonzero vector on which to evaluate a Rayleigh quotient. For every $m\ge1$, the spanning set in [F1] consists of repetitions of the single nonzero vector $e_1$, and the Rayleigh quotient on this one-dimensional subspace is $e_1^TKe_1/(e_1^Te_1)=1$. Exact Lanczos terminates after one vector with Ritz value $1$. [A1, F1, given, algebra]

2.1 For $x=(x_1,x_2)$, $\|Kx\|_2^2=x_1^2+4x_2^2\le4(x_1^2+x_2^2)$, with equality at $e_2$, so [F4] gives $\|K\|_2=2$. The top eigenspace is $\operatorname{span}\{e_2\}$ and $Pb=0$; [F2] identifies exactly this degenerate branch and supplies no top-eigenvalue convergence bound. Therefore the Ritz value $1$ is not the norm upper bound $2$ required by [F3]. [A1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

actualproofparagraphs.1.1: The function $u(t)=e^{\theta t}s$ satisfies $u'=\theta u$ and $u(0)=s$. Conversely, for any solution $v$ with this initial value, the product and chain rules give $(e^{-\theta t}v(t))'=0$. By [F4] this product is constantly $s$ on its solution interval, and positivity and the reciprocal identity in [F3] imply $v(t)=e^{\theta t}s$. Thus the displayed solution exists globally and is unique. [F3, F4]
actualproofparagraphs.2.1: Verify the actual common-tube hypotheses locally at any $(s_*,\theta_*)$. Fix $\varepsilon,\delta,\eta>0$ and restrict the parameters to $|s-s_*|<\varepsilon$, $|\theta-\theta_*|<\delta$. For $-\eta\le t\le\tau+\eta$, $$|e^{\theta t}s|\le B:=(|s_*|+\varepsilon)\exp((|\theta_*|+\delta)(\tau+\eta)).$$ Treat $(s,\theta)$ as the flow parameter, with initial map $(s,\theta)\mapsto s$ and field $(t,u,s,\theta)\mapsto\theta u$ on $\mathbb R^4$. The bounded convex open set $$(-\eta,\tau+\eta)\times(-B-1,B+1)\times(s_*-2\varepsilon,s_*+2\varepsilon)\times(\theta_*-2\delta,\theta_*+2\delta)$$ has compact closure inside that field's domain and contains all these trajectories for $0\le t\le\tau$ and the restricted parameters. The field and initial map are $C^1$. Step 1.1 supplies existence and uniqueness, so [F1] applies. Each shooting interval uses this same argument with its own initial node; since there are two intervals, a common finite bound may also be taken. [F1, F3, step 1.1]

$$H_\delta=\begin{pmatrix}-\delta&0\\0&\delta\end{pmatrix},\qquad E_\delta=\begin{pmatrix}0&\delta\\\delta&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \widehat H_\delta=H_\delta+E_\delta.$$

Thus an absolute perturbation tolerance alone cannot guarantee a mode error tending to zero as the spectral gap collapses.

$$H_\delta=\begin{pmatrix}-\delta&0\\0&\delta\end{pmatrix},\qquad E_\delta=\begin{pmatrix}0&\delta\\\delta&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \widehat H_\delta=H_\delta+E_\delta.$$

The exact lowest eigenvector is $e_1$. The perturbation has Euclidean operator norm $\delta$, which tends to zero with the gap, but the lowest eigenvector of $\widehat H_\delta$ remains at angle $\arctan(\sqrt2-1)>0$ from $e_1$. Thus an absolute perturbation tolerance alone cannot guarantee a mode error tending to zero as the spectral gap collapses.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
For $0<\epsilon\le1$, take $M=I_3$ and
$$c_\epsilon(q)=(q_3,q_3+\epsilon q_2).$$
The Jacobian has full row rank for every fixed $\epsilon>0$, but
$$A_\epsilon=J_\epsilon J_\epsilon^T=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1+\epsilon^2\end{pmatrix}$$
has smallest eigenvalue $2\epsilon^2/(2+\epsilon^2+\sqrt{4+\epsilon^4})\sim\epsilon^2/2$. Thus the inverse multiplier bound in the RATTLE residual estimate is not uniform as the constraints approach dependence. At $\epsilon=0$ the rank hypothesis fails.
source_evidence.case_anchor:
For $0<\epsilon\le1$, take $M=I_3$ and
$$c_\epsilon(q)=(q_3,q_3+\epsilon q_2).$$
The Jacobian has full row rank for every fixed $\epsilon>0$, but
$$A_\epsilon=J_\epsilon J_\epsilon^T=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1+\epsilon^2\end{pmatrix}$$
has smallest eigenvalue $2\epsilon^2/(2+\epsilon^2+\sqrt{4+\epsilon^4})\sim\epsilon^2/2$. Thus the inverse multiplier bound in the RATTLE residual estimate is not uniform as the constraints approach dependence. At $\epsilon=0$ the rank hypothesis fails.

proofparagraphs.text: The two rows $(0,0,1)$ and $(0,\epsilon,1)$ of $J_\epsilon$ are linearly independent exactly when $\epsilon>0$. Their Gram matrix is the displayed $A_\epsilon$, whose trace is $2+\epsilon^2$ and determinant is $\epsilon^2$. [given, F1, algebra]

Consequently no single residual-to-multiplier constant works for this family as $\epsilon\downarrow0$; this is consistent with [F2], whose uniform estimates assume a fixed compact chart with uniformly bounded $A^{-1}$. At $\epsilon=0$ the two rows coincide, so [F1]'s full-rank hypothesis fails. [F1, F2, step 2.1] ∎

Consider the mean-square stable scalar SDE
$$dX_t=-2X_tdt+\sqrt3X_t\,dW_t,\qquad X_0=1.$$

$h=1/2$, explicit Euler–Maruyama has one-step mean-square amplification
$3/2>1$, even though the deterministic Euler multiplier is zero. The
drift-implicit Euler–Maruyama update has one-step mean-square factor
$5/8<1$.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
On $\mathbb R^2$, let $a(x)=Ax$ and $b(x)=Bx$, where
$$A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad B=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix}.$$
The fields are smooth and their exact flows exist globally. With the bracket convention in [[def-exact-split-flows-lie-strang-and-bracket]], the Lie split has a nonzero $h^2$ local defect and the symmetric Strang split has a nonzero $h^3$ local defect at $x=e_1=(1,0)^T$.

actualproofparagraphs.1.1: By [F4], the linear fields have global exact flows. Direct multiplication gives $BA=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\quad AB=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\quad C:=BA-AB=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.$ By [F1], $[a,b](x)=Cx$. [F1, F3, F4, algebra]
actualproofparagraphs.2.1: Multiplying once more gives $CA-AC=\begin{pmatrix}0&-2\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad CB-BC=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\2&0\end{pmatrix}.$ These are the matrices of $[a,[a,b]]$ and $[b,[a,b]]$ under the same convention. [F1, F3, step 1.1, algebra]
actualproofparagraphs.2.2: At $e_1$, $Ce_1=-e_1\ne0$, so [F2] gives Lie local defect $-\frac12h^2e_1+O(h^3)$, whose leading coefficient is nonzero. Thus its local error has exact order two. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]
actualproofparagraphs.3.1: The Strang leading matrix from step 2.1 is $-\frac1{24}(CA-AC)-\frac1{12}(CB-BC)=\begin{pmatrix}0&1/12\\-1/6&0\end{pmatrix}.$ It sends $e_1$ to $(0,-1/6)^T\ne0$, so [F2] gives a nonzero cubic leading local defect and exact local order three. [F2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Encode a one-dimensional zero-boundary function by its derivative. The exact Hilbert space is the mean-zero subspace $V:=\{g\in L^2(0,1):\int_0^1g=0\}$, with $a(g,h)=\int_0^1gh$. Its associated function is $U_g(x):=\int_0^xg(t)\,dt$. The source functional is $F(h):=\int_0^16xU_h(x)\,dx$. Its exact solution is $g_u(x)=1-3x^2$, whose associated function is $U_{g_u}(x)=x-x^3$.

For the nonconforming discrete space, take broken piecewise-affine functions on $[0,1/2]\cup[1/2,1]$ that vanish at $0$ and $1$, with no continuity imposed at $1/2$. Identify each such function with its two cellwise slopes, a two-dimensional space $V_h$ of piecewise-constant fields. For $\omega_h=s_L\mathbf1_{[0,1/2]}+s_R\mathbf1_{(1/2,1]}$, define its associated broken function by $U_{\omega_h}(x)=s_Lx$ on the left cell and $U_{\omega_h}(x)=s_R(x-1)$ on the right cell. Use $\widetilde a_h(g,\omega_h):=\int_0^1g\omega_h$ and $F_h(\omega_h):=\int_0^16xU_{\omega_h}(x)\,dx$. The left basis function $\phi_L(x)=2x$ on the first cell and $0$ on the second corresponds to slope field $\omega_L=2\mathbf1_{[0,1/2]}$; it has residual $F_h(\omega_L)-\widetilde a_h(g_u,\omega_L)=-1/4$. Thus the exact solution does not satisfy the broken discrete equation on $V_h$: its consistency residual is nonzero. This is the term retained by the second Strang estimate in place of an exact Galerkin identity. The conforming Céa hypothesis $V_h\subseteq V$ is also false.
source_evidence.case_anchor: The associated broken function for $\omega_L$ is $\phi_L$. Thus $F_h(\omega_L)=\int_0^{1/2}12x^2dx=1/2$, whereas $\widetilde a_h(g_u,\omega_L)=\int_0^{1/2}2(1-3x^2)dx=2[x-x^3]_0^{1/2}=3/4$, by [F9]. The residual is $-1/4$ and $\|\omega_L\|_h=\sqrt2$, so $\delta_h^{\mathrm{nc}}(g_u)\ge1/(4\sqrt2)>0$. [A1, A2, F9, step 1.2, algebra]

Fubini [F4] gives $F(h)=\int_0^1h(t)3(1-t^2)dt=\int_0^1h(t)(1-3t^2)dt=a(g_u,h)$, since $\int h=0$. The form is the $L^2$ inner product, so [F5] confirms the unique exact solution is $g_u$. source_evidence.full_current_interface:
On the annulus $U=\{(x,y):1/2<\sqrt{x^2+y^2}<3/2\}$ consider
$$
\dot x=(1-r)x-y,\qquad \dot y=(1-r)y+x,\qquad r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}.
$$
The unit circle is an orbitally asymptotically stable periodic orbit of period $2\pi$. At $x_*=(1,0)$ the affine phase $\psi_b(x,y)=x-1$ has a singular phase-bordered shooting Jacobian, while $\psi_g(x,y)=y$ is transverse and gives an invertible phase-bordered shooting Jacobian.
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: The same stable unit-circle orbit has a singular radial phase border and an invertible transverse phase border; phase conditioning is separate from orbital stability.
selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 The identities $\dot r=(xx'+yy')/r$ and $\dot\vartheta=(xy'-yx')/r^2$ give $\dot r=r(1-r)$ and $\dot\vartheta=1$. Thus $r=1$ is invariant and $\vartheta(t)=\vartheta(0)+t$, so the least period is $2\pi$. Differentiating $r(1-r)$ at $r=1$ gives the radial variational equation $\dot\rho=-\rho$, whose multiplier is $e^{-2\pi}<1$; the angular variational equation is $\dot\alpha=0$, whose multiplier is $1$. Because the polar-coordinate Jacobian at times $0$ and $2\pi$ is the same invertible matrix, the Cartesian monodromy is conjugate to $\operatorname{diag}(e^{-2\pi},1)$. For $r<1$ the radial derivative is positive, and for $r>1$ it is negative, so nearby radii move monotonically toward $1$ and cannot leave their initial radial interval. Their distance to the unit circle therefore tends to zero while remaining small. This proves orbital asymptotic stability and shows the neutral multiplier is simple. [given, algebra]

2.1 At $(1,0)$ the vector field is $(0,1)$. For $\psi_b=x-1$, $c_b=(1,0)$ and $c_b^\top f(x_*)=0$, so [F2] gives a singular shooting Jacobian. For $\psi_g=y$, $c_g=(0,1)$ and $c_g^\top f(x_*)=1$; the phase multiplier is simple by step 1.1, so [F2] gives an invertible Jacobian. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 The identities $\dot r=(xx'+yy')/r$ and $\dot\vartheta=(xy'-yx')/r^2$ give $\dot r=r(1-r)$ and $\dot\vartheta=1$. Thus $r=1$ is invariant and $\vartheta(t)=\vartheta(0)+t$, so the least period is $2\pi$. Differentiating $r(1-r)$ at $r=1$ gives the radial variational equation $\dot\rho=-\rho$, whose multiplier is $e^{-2\pi}<1$; the angular variational equation is $\dot\alpha=0$, whose multiplier is $1$. Because the polar-coordinate Jacobian at times $0$ and $2\pi$ is the same invertible matrix, the Cartesian monodromy is conjugate to $\operatorname{diag}(e^{-2\pi},1)$. For $r<1$ the radial derivative is positive, and for $r>1$ it is negative, so nearby radii move monotonically toward $1$ and cannot leave their initial radial interval. Their distance to the unit circle therefore tends to zero while remaining small. This proves orbital asymptotic stability and shows the neutral multiplier is simple. [given, algebra]

$$

additional_source_clauses.text:
Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, let $c:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be smooth (that is, $C^\infty$) with $1\le m<d$, let $M$ be a constant symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix, and let $V:U\to\mathbb R$ be smooth. A **holonomic constraint** is the position condition $c(q)=0$. Write $J(q)=Dc(q)$, let $Q=\{q\in U:c(q)=0\}$, and define its regular part by $Q_{\mathrm{reg}}=\{q\in Q:\operatorname{rank}J(q)=m\}$. For $q\in Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$, $A(q)=J(q)M^{-1}J(q)^T$ is positive definite. On a compact regular chart $K\subset Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$, $A^{-1}$ is uniformly bounded: $\sup_{q\in K}\|A(q)^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}<\infty$.

A position-momentum pair $(q,p)$ is **consistent** when $q\in Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$ and $J(q)M^{-1}p=0$. The **regular constrained phase manifold** is
$$\mathcal M=\{(q,p)\in U\times\mathbb R^d:c(q)=0,\ J(q)M^{-1}p=0,\ q\in Q_{\mathrm{reg}}\}.$$
The ambient canonical two-form is $\omega_0=\sum_{i=1}^d dq_i\wedge dp_i$; its restriction to $\mathcal M$ is denoted $\omega_{\mathcal M}$.

For $v=M^{-1}p$, the constrained Hamilton equations are
$$\dot q=v,\qquad \dot p=-\nabla V(q)-J(q)^T\lambda,$$
with multiplier
$$\lambda=A(q)^{-1}\bigl(D^2c(q)[v,v]-J(q)M^{-1}\nabla V(q)\bigr).$$
Here $D^2c(q)[v,v]\in\mathbb R^m$ has components $v^TD^2c_j(q)v$. This multiplier is the one that keeps both $c(q)=0$ and $J(q)M^{-1}p=0$ satisfied.

Put $h=T/N$ and suppose the exact-solve RATTLE iterates from the common initial state stay in $\mathcal C_0$ for the grids considered. Suppose every finite RATTLE solve succeeds, its branch iterates stay in the selected local balls over $\mathcal C_1$, and its scaled residuals are bounded by a fixed sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0$. After each output apply the consistency retraction from [[lem-regular-holonomic-phase-residuals-control-distance-to-phase-manifold]] before the next step. For sufficiently small $h$, the restored trajectory stays in $\mathcal C_1$ and has an $O(T\varepsilon)$ global error envelope relative to exact-solve RATTLE; refinement alone does not force this upper bound to vanish. If both scaled residual tolerances are instead $O(h^2)$, the global solver contribution is $O(h^2)$, while the unprojected solver outputs have position and tangency residuals $O(h^4)$ and $O(h^3)$. These are upper bounds; they do not assert a matching lower bound or that residual tolerances alone certify forward error.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Consider the two-cell no-flux graph diffusion matrix
$$L=\begin{pmatrix}-1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$$
and the linear reaction-diffusion semidiscretization $y'=\rho y+D Ly$ with reaction rate $\rho=1$, diffusion coefficient $D=10$. Treat reaction explicitly and diffusion implicitly in [[def-ars222-additive-tableau-and-stages]]. The constant mode has amplification $221/200>1$, matching its reaction growth. With step $h=1/10$, the nonconstant mode has amplification
$$R(1/10,-2)=\frac{661/200-(11/5)\sqrt2}{11-6\sqrt2},$$
which lies strictly between $0$ and $9/80$. This is a two-mode scalar calculation for a finite grid; it makes no nonnormal-matrix or PDE stability assertion.

actualproofparagraphs.2.1: On each span $\mathbb Rv_j$, every stage equation in [F1] remains in that span. The implicit denominators are $1$ on $v_0$ and $1+20\gamma h>0$ on $v_1$, so the stage solves are unique there. Hence [F2] applies with $z_a=h$ and $z_b=0$ or $z_b=-20h$, respectively. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]
actualproofparagraphs.3.1: For $v_0$ and $h=1/10$, $z_b=0$, so [F2] gives $R(1/10,0)=1+\frac1{10}+\frac1{200}=\frac{221}{200}>1.$ This mode grows under the positive reaction term. [F2, step 2.1, algebra]

review_basis.full_actual_interface:
Consider $n=14$ one-dimensional examples, seven with feature $a_i=1$ and label $y_i=1$, and seven with $a_i=1$ and $y_i=-1$. With unit $\ell_2$ regularization, define

$f_i(w)=\log(1+\exp(-y_iw))+\frac12w^2,\qquad F(w)=\frac1{14}\sum_{i=1}^{14}f_i(w).$
Here $\log$ denotes the natural logarithm.

Then each component is convex with $5/4$-Lipschitz gradient, $F$ is $1$-strongly convex, and its unique minimizer is $w^*=0$. An SVRG epoch from snapshot $\widetilde w=1$ with $\eta=2/25$ and $m=28$ therefore satisfies

$$\mathbb E[F(w_J)-F(0)]\le\frac{181}{224}\,[F(1)-F(0)],\qquad F(1)-F(0)=\frac12\log(2+e+e^{-1})+\frac12-\log 2.$$
