Let $M=mI_2$, $m,\ell,\omega>0$, $V=0$, and $c(q)=(\|q\|_2^2-\ell^2)/2$. Start from $q_0=(\ell,0)$ and $p_0=(0,m\omega\ell)$, and take $0<h\omega\le\frac12$. The selected exact RATTLE step has
$$q_1=\ell\bigl(\sqrt{1-h^2\omega^2},h\omega\bigr),\qquad p_1=m\omega\ell\bigl(-h\omega,\sqrt{1-h^2\omega^2}\bigr).$$
Its position constraint and momentum tangency are exact. The exact constrained flow rotates by angle $h\omega$, whereas RATTLE rotates by $\arcsin(h\omega)$, so the one-step phase defect is $O(h^3)$ as $h\omega\to0$.

Let $M=mI_2$, $m,\ell,\omega>0$, $V=0$, and $c(q)=(\|q\|_2^2-\ell^2)/2$. Start from $q_0=(\ell,0)$ and $p_0=(0,m\omega\ell)$, and take $0<h\omega\le\frac12$. The selected exact RATTLE step has
$$q_1=\ell\bigl(\sqrt{1-h^2\omega^2},h\omega\bigr),\qquad p_1=m\omega\ell\bigl(-h\omega,\sqrt{1-h^2\omega^2}\bigr).$$
Its position constraint and momentum tangency are exact. The exact constrained flow rotates by angle $h\omega$, whereas RATTLE rotates by $\arcsin(h\omega)$, so the one-step phase defect is $O(h^3)$ as $h\omega\to0$.

proofparagraphs.text: The initial data are consistent because $\|q_0\|_2=\ell$ and $q_0^Tp_0=0$. The position multiplier equation gives $q_1=q_0+\frac hm(p_0-h\lambda q_0)$; choosing $\lambda=m(1-\sqrt{1-h^2\omega^2})/h^2=m\omega^2/(1+\sqrt{1-h^2\omega^2})$ yields the stated $q_1$, whose squared norm is $\ell^2$. This multiplier tends to $m\omega^2/2$, the position branch center. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

The continuous multiplier is $\lambda_c=m\omega^2$, hence the exact flow is $q(t)=\ell(\cos\omega t,\sin\omega t)$ and $p(t)=m\omega\ell(-\sin\omega t,\cos\omega t)$. This solves [F3] and agrees with the initial data. The RATTLE position angle is $\theta_h=\arcsin(h\omega)$. Taylor's theorem [F4] on $0\le h\omega\le1/2$ gives $\arcsin(h\omega)-h\omega=O((h\omega)^3)$. Since $\omega$ is fixed, the angle defect is $O(h^3)$ as stated. [F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Take $n=2$, $r=1$, overlap $S=I_2$, Cholesky factor $L=I_2$, $h=0$, and
$E_{xc}=0$ in [[def-finite-basis-projector-energy-model]]. Define
$G:\mathbb H_2\to\mathbb H_2$ by $G(X)=\operatorname{diag}(X_{11},X_{22})$.
Here matrix-entry labels $1,2$ mean the first and second rows/columns, corresponding to canonical indices $0,1$.
The associated response map is $F(P)=G(P)$. Let
$$P_0=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad P_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.$$
For the undamped occupied-projector iteration, $P_0$ and $P_1$ form a strict
two-cycle even though the occupied/unoccupied eigenvalue gap equals $1$ at both
iterates.

actualproofparagraphs.1.1: For Hermitian $X,Y$, the diagonal entries are real and $\langle G(X),Y\rangle_F=X_{11}Y_{11}+X_{22}Y_{22}=\langle X,G(Y)\rangle_F.$ Thus $G$ is real-linear, Hermitian-valued, and self-adjoint for the Frobenius inner product, so the stated data satisfy [F1]. Each $P_i$ is Hermitian, idempotent, and has trace $1$, hence lies in $\mathcal P_1$. [given, F1, algebra]
actualproofparagraphs.1.2: Direct substitution gives $F(P_0)=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$ and $F(P_1)=\operatorname{diag}(0,1)$. Each matrix has eigenvalues $0<1$, so the strict occupied gap is $1$. By [F2], the lowest eigenspace of $F(P_0)$ is $\operatorname{span}\{(0,1)^T\}$ and that of $F(P_1)$ is $\operatorname{span}\{(1,0)^T\}$; [F4] guarantees these give the unique projectors $\Phi(P_0)=P_1$ and $\Phi(P_1)=P_0$. [given, F2, F4, algebra]

source_evidence.case_anchor: Proof step 1.1 constructs both admissible projectors; Proof step 1.2 computes each unique occupied eigenspace. No unprovided state or empty spectral block is used.

multiplier contraction factor while worsening the inner Hessian condition
number to $1+\rho$.

Consider the design problem
$$\min_{x\in\mathbb R^2}\frac12(x_1^2+x_2^2) \quad\text{subject to }1-x_1-x_2\le0.$$
At $x_0=(0,0)$, use $B=I$ in the SQP quadratic subproblem. The exact
active-set solve returns $p=(1/2,1/2)$, and $x_0+p$ is the unique global

$f(x)=2(x_1^2+x_2^2-1)-x_1$. At a feasible point
$x=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)=(c,s)$, use multiplier estimate $\nu=-3/2$
and SQP Hessian model $B=I$. For nonzero sufficiently small $\theta$, the
SQP step $p=(s^2,-sc)$ has predicted decrease $D_\rho=s^2>0$, but its full
step increases the L1 merit for every $\rho>0$. The minimum-norm SOC
correction makes the full corrected step pass the Armijo test with
$\sigma=1/4$ for every fixed $\rho>0$ and all sufficiently small nonzero
$\theta$.

correction makes the full corrected step pass the Armijo test with
$\sigma=1/4$ for every fixed $\rho>0$ and all sufficiently small nonzero

proofparagraphs.text: Since $x^Tp=0$ and $\|p\|_2^2=s^2$, $h(x+p)=s^2$. Also $\nabla f(x)^Tp=-s^2$, so [F2] gives $D_\rho=s^2$. The objective changes by $s^2$, while the equality violation changes from zero to $s^2$; hence the full-step merit change is $(1+\rho)s^2>0$, which fails the Armijo right side $-\sigma s^2<0$. Divide the corrected merit change plus $\sigma D_\rho$ by $s^2$. With $\sigma=1/4$, the result is $-1+c/2+s^2(1/2+\rho/4)+1/4$, which tends to $-1/4$ as $\theta\to0$. It is therefore negative for all sufficiently small nonzero $\theta$, proving the SOC Armijo test passes. The explicit correction also has the $O(s^2)$ norm and $O(s^4)$ residual predicted by [F4]. [A1, F4, F5, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

source_evidence.fullclaim: Take the scalar decay equation $y'=-\kappa y$ with $\kappa>0$ and $y_0=1$. Treat the whole stiff term explicitly, so $a(y)=-\kappa y$ and $b(y)=0$. IMEX Euler gives amplification $1-h\kappa$; for $h\kappa>2$ its magnitude exceeds one although the exact solution $e^{-\kappa t}$ decays. If instead this same term is implicit, the amplification is $(1+h\kappa)^{-1}$, which lies in $(0,1)$ for every $h\kappa>0$. This scalar comparison does not imply matrix stability for nonnormal operators.

actualproofparagraphs.1.2: With $a=0$ and $b(y)=-\kappa y$, the equation in [F1] becomes $(1+h\kappa)Y=y$. Since $0<1<1+h\kappa$, [F4] gives $0<(1+h\kappa)^{-1}<1$. Thus the implicit treatment damps every such scalar step, while the explicit treatment grows whenever $h\kappa>2$. [F1, F4, algebra]

source_evidence.fullclaim: Let $D=(-\pi/4,\pi/4)\times(-1/4,1/4)$, $X(s,n)=(1+n)(\cos s,\sin s)$, and $U=X(D)$. Put $a=\pi/6$, $W(s)=(s^2-a^2)^2$, and $V(X(s,n))=W(s)+n^2/2$ on $U$. The endpoints of the circular MEP are $(\cos a,-\sin a)$ and $(\cos a,\sin a)$. Their straight chord is the vertical segment $C(y)=(\cos a,y)$ for $-\sin a\le y\le\sin a$. The chord lies inside the annular sector, but it is not a MEP.
source_evidence.case_anchor: Along $C$, the first coordinate is $\cos a>0$, and $|y|/\cos a\le\tan a<1$, so the polar angle lies in $[-a,a]\subset(-\pi/4,\pi/4)$. Its radius is between $\cos a=\sqrt3/2>3/4$ and $1<5/4$. Thus the whole chord is in the declared sector. [given, algebra]

proofparagraphs.text: Along $C$, the first coordinate is $\cos a>0$, and $|y|/\cos a\le\tan a<1$, so the polar angle lies in $[-a,a]\subset(-\pi/4,\pi/4)$. Its radius is between $\cos a=\sqrt3/2>3/4$ and $1<5/4$. Thus the whole chord is in the declared sector. [given, algebra]

The chord's tangent is $e_2=(0,1)$. At its midpoint $x_0=(\cos a,0)=X(0,n_0)$ with $n_0=\cos a-1
e0$. In the chart $X_s=(1+n)T$ and $X_n=N$, where $T(0)=e_2$ and $N(0)=e_1$. The coordinate derivatives of $V$ there are $\partial_sV=W'(0)=0$ and $\partial_nV=n_0$, so by [F3] $
abla V(x_0)\cdot e_1=n_0
e0$. [F3, given, algebra]

review_basis.full_actual_interface: Let a finite sum have $n,d\ge1$ components and dimension, and let an SVRG epoch and SAGA block each have $m\ge1$ inner updates. Count component-gradient evaluations separately from scalar coordinate arithmetic, and do not cache SVRG snapshot gradients. SVRG uses $n+2m$ component-gradient evaluations per epoch, $O(nd)$ arithmetic to assemble its full gradient, $O(d)$ arithmetic per inner update, and $O(d)$ working storage. SAGA uses $n+m$ component-gradient evaluations during its initialized block and $m$ new evaluations in each later equally long block; initializing its mean takes $O(nd)$ arithmetic, each later update takes $O(d)$ arithmetic, and its table plus auxiliary vectors use $O(nd)$ storage. The cost of evaluating a component gradient is not bounded here. For $n=1000$, $d=20$, and $m=2n=2000$, the gradient counts are 5000 SVRG evaluations per epoch, 3000 SAGA evaluations in the initial block, and 2000 in a later block; the SAGA table has 20,000 scalar coordinates.

two-dimensional projected solver specified in step 1.1 with iteration count
$m=2$, returning `no-candidate` if its two-dimensional basis or projected matrix is singular
or if $M<2$.

The real family
$$
\mathcal A=\left\{A(t)=\begin{pmatrix}1&t\\t&1\end{pmatrix}:-1\le t\le1\right\}
$$
is represented by the entrywise interval box with off-diagonal entries $[-1,1]$. It contains a singular matrix, and its natural Leibniz interval evaluation $[0,2]$ does not certify uniform nonsingularity.
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: The two-by-two off-diagonal interval family includes singular endpoint members and its Leibniz interval straddles zero, preventing a uniform nonsingularity verdict.
selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 For each $t\in[-1,1]$, $\det A(t)=1-t^2\in[0,1]$. The direct interval product $[-1,1]\cdot[-1,1]=[-1,1]$ encloses $t^2$, so the Leibniz interval expression $1-[-1,1]=[0,2]$ contains every determinant. At $t=1$, $A(1)(1,-1)^{\mathsf T}=0$ with a nonzero vector, so $A(1)$ is singular. The interval $[0,2]$ includes zero and is not $\{0\}$; [F1] therefore makes no uniform nonsingularity claim from this enclosure. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 If uniform residual data with $q<1$ existed for this whole family and any nonempty right-hand-side set, [F2] would make $A(1)$ invertible. This contradicts the nonzero null vector just exhibited. Hence such a usable uniform residual certificate cannot hold for the family. [given, F2, step 1.1, contradiction] ∎

      locator: "§II, equations (2)–(6): the MEP equation and equal-arc reparameterization"
    - title: "Xuanyu Liu, Huajie Chen, and Christoph Ortner, Convergence of the Discrete Minimum Energy Path"
      url: "https://arxiv.org/pdf/2204.07467"
      locator: "§2.1–2.3: discrete convergence requires stability and a specified discretization"

## Example

Let $U=\mathbb R^2$ and $V\equiv0$. Every regular path from $A=(0,0)$ to $B=(1,0)$ satisfies the MEP equation, so there are infinitely many distinct continuum MEPs. For a finite string with $M=2$, both chains

$$R_1^{(0)}=(1/2,0),\qquad R_1^{(1)}=(1/2,1)$$

have equal adjacent segment lengths and zero projected force. The improved-tangent NEB ordinary force also vanishes for both. Thus their discrete residuals are exactly zero, although their interior images differ.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The zero potential, fixed endpoints $A,B$, two finite chains, and the definitions of the string, NEB, and stable path comparison.

[F1] [[def-regular-minimum-energy-path-in-a-collision-free-tube]]: a regular path is an MEP when the normal gradient vanishes; fixed endpoints are part of the path data.

[F2] [[alg-finite-image-string-method]]: the string stops when the projected-force and equal-spacing residuals are both within tolerance.

[F3] [[alg-improved-tangent-climbing-neb]]: the ordinary NEB force is projected gradient plus a tangential spring term.

[F4] [[thm-gauge-fixed-stable-discrete-path-comparison]]: a local path error conclusion requires an invertible residual Jacobian with a uniform inverse bound and other stated consistency/stability hypotheses.

## Proof

**Given:** The potential, endpoints, and finite chains in the Example.

1.1 For each $c\in\mathbb R$, $R_c(t)=(t,c\sin(\pi t))$ on $[0,1]$ is regular because its first coordinate derivative is $1$, and it has endpoints $A,B$. Since $\nabla V=0$, every normal gradient component is zero, so [F1] makes every $R_c$ an MEP. Distinct $c$ give distinct paths. [F1, given, algebra]

1.2 For $M=2$, each listed interior point is equidistant from $A$ and $B$: the two distances are $1/2$ when $R_1=(1/2,0)$ and both $\sqrt{5}/2$ when $R_1=(1/2,1)$. Thus the adjacent lengths agree. Since the gradient is zero, the string projected force is zero by [F2], and the ordinary NEB spring term is also zero by [F3]. Both chains therefore have exactly zero force and spacing residuals. [F2, F3, given, algebra]

2.1 The two chains differ in their interior image, and the continuum family in step 1.1 is nonunique. In this example the string residual map has no locally invertible Jacobian that can isolate a path: its force components vanish identically and its spacing equation alone cannot determine the two coordinates of the interior image. Hence the stable comparison theorem's inverse/stability premise [F4] is absent, and zero discrete residual does not imply a unique or accurate continuum path. [F4, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

source_evidence.fullclaim:
For $n\ge2$ and $1\le r<n$, the set $\mathcal D_r$ of
[[def-admissible-hermitian-density-domain]] is nonempty, closed, and convex in
$\mathbb H_n$, and complete in the Frobenius metric.

actualproofparagraphs.1.1: The diagonal matrix $D_0=\operatorname{diag}(1,\ldots,1,0,\ldots,0)$ with $r$ ones is Hermitian, satisfies $0\preceq D_0\preceq I_n$, and has trace $r$. Thus $D_0\in\mathcal D_r$, so the domain is nonempty. [given, F1, construct]
actualproofparagraphs.2.1: For every fixed $x\in\mathbb C^n$, entrywise convergence gives $x^*D_kx\to x^*Dx$ and $x^*(I_n-D_k)x\to x^*(I_n-D)x$. Since both sequences are nonnegative, their limits are nonnegative, so $0\preceq D\preceq I_n$. Finite sums commute with coordinate limits, hence $\operatorname{tr}D=\lim_k\operatorname{tr}D_k=r$. Therefore $D\in\mathcal D_r$. [step 1.2, F1, algebra]

Assume AC. Let $X,Y$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces over the same scalar
field, let $U\subseteq X$ be open, and let
$B=\overline B(x^\dagger,\rho)\subseteq U$ be convex. Let
$F:U\to Y$ continuously Fréchet differentiable over that field (bounded
complex-linear derivatives in the complex case). Set $A=F'(x^\dagger)$,
$S=A^*A$ and $y=F(x^\dagger)$. Suppose for each $x\in B$ that
$F'(x)=(I+R_x)A$ for a bounded linear $R_x:Y\to Y$ with
$\|R_x\|\le\kappa<1$, taking $R_{x^\dagger}=0$. Let $x\in B$,
$e=x-x^\dagger$, $e_0=x_0-x^\dagger=S^\nu w$, $0<\nu\le1/2$,
$\|w\|\le W$, and $\|y_\delta-y\|\le\delta$. For a single exact
anchored update with shift $\alpha>0$, define $e_+=x_+-x^\dagger$,
$v=\|Ae\|$, $v_+=\|Ae_+\|$, $R=R_x$,
$H=R+R^*+R^*R$, $\theta=2\kappa+\kappa^2$,
$d_0=2\kappa(1+\kappa)$, and $c_0=1+\kappa$. Then
$$t=F'(x)e-(F(x)-y),\quad z=(I+R)^*(y_\delta-y+t)-HAe_+,$$
$$(S+\alpha I)e_+=\alpha e_0+A^*z,\quad \|z\|\le c_0\delta+d_0v+\theta v_+.$$
Consequently
$$(1-\theta)v_+\le W\alpha^{\nu+1/2}+d_0v+c_0\delta,\qquad \|e_+\|\le W\alpha^\nu+\frac{c_0\delta+d_0v+\theta v_+}{2\sqrt\alpha}.$$
Also for $x,u\in B$,
$$(1-\kappa)\|A(x-u)\|\le\|F(x)-F(u)\|\le(1+\kappa)\|A(x-u)\|,$$
and the tangential-cone condition holds with constant $2\kappa/(1-\kappa)$. The conclusions require only the current state and segment in $B$, not the next state in $B$.

Let $L>0$, let $M\ge1$ be an integer, and let $R:[0,L]\to\mathbb R^d$ be a unit-speed $C^3$ curve with $M$ equal arc-length intervals of length $h=L/M$. Suppose $\|R''\|_2\le K_2$ and the coordinate third derivatives satisfy the bound in [[lem-centered-chord-and-unequal-step-tangent-error]] with constant $M_3$. For sufficiently small $h$, each chord length $\ell_i=\|R(ih)-R((i-1)h)\|_2$ satisfies $|\ell_i-h|\le C_1h^3$, where $C_1$ depends only on $K_2,M_3$. The piecewise-linear interpolant through the samples differs from $R$ in supremum norm by at most $C_2h^2$. If this polygon is redistributed by linear interpolation at equally spaced cumulative-length targets, the $j$th redistributed image is within $C_3h^2$ of $R(jh)$, for every $j=0,\ldots,M$.

Here $C^3$ on $[0,L]$ means that $R$ is the restriction of a $C^3$ curve on an open interval containing $[0,L]$; derivatives at the endpoints are the continuous one-sided values, and the unit-speed and derivative bounds are required on $[0,L]$.

proofparagraphs.text: Let $p_i=\sum_{m=1}^{i}\ell_m$ and $L_h=p_M$. Step 1.1 gives $|p_i-ih|\le iC_1h^3\le C_1Lh^2$ and $|L_h-L|\le C_1Lh^2$. Thus the redistributed target $q_j=jL_h/M$ satisfies $|q_j-jh|\le C_1Lh^2$. Each segment has length at least $h/2$ for small $h$. If target $q_j$ lies on segment $i$ at fraction $\theta$, then $p_{i-1}+\theta\ell_i=q_j$; combining $|p_{i-1}-(i-1)h|\le C_1Lh^2$, $|q_j-jh|\le C_1Lh^2$, and $|\ell_i-h|\le C_1h^3$ gives $|(i-1)h+\theta h-jh|\le C h^2$. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

The point on the true curve at parameter $(i-1)h+\theta h$ is within $C_2h^2$ of the redistributed polygon point by step 1.2, and it is within $C h^2$ of $R(jh)$ by unit speed and step 2.1. The triangle inequality gives the claimed $C_3h^2$ bound, including endpoints where redistribution fixes the endpoints. [F1, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

proofparagraphs.text: On each mesh interval $[s,s+h]$, apply the one-dimensional degree-two formula [F3] to each coordinate of the extended curve at $s$; the endpoint convention supplies the required derivative continuity, and [A1, F2] gives a remainder vector $r$ with $\|r\|_2\le M_3h^3/6$. Thus $R(s+h)-R(s)=hT+\frac{h^2}{2}K+r$ with $T=R'(s)$, $K=R''(s)$, and $\|K\|_2\le K_2$. Differentiating $\|R'(s)\|_2^2=1$ gives $T^TK=0$ by the chain rule [F4]. Hence $|\|R(s+h)-R(s)\|_2^2-h^2|\le C h^4$ for a constant depending only on $K_2,M_3$; for sufficiently small $h$ the chord is at least $h/2$, so division by its sum with $h$ yields $|\ell_i-h|\le C_1h^3$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, given, algebra]

For $s=ih+\theta h$ with $0\le\theta\le1$, apply the one-dimensional degree-one formula [F3] on $\lbrack ih,s\rbrack$ and $\lbrack ih,(i+1)h\rbrack$. The remainder bound in [F3] and $\|R''\|_2\le K_2$ give $R(s)=R(ih)+\theta hR'(ih)+O(K_2h^2)$ and $R((i+1)h)=R(ih)+hR'(ih)+O(K_2h^2)$. Subtracting the linear interpolant cancels the first-order term, so the pointwise interpolation error is bounded by $C_2h^2$, uniformly over all intervals. [A1, F1, F3, given, algebra]

Let $L>0$, let $M\ge1$ be an integer, and let $R:[0,L]\to\mathbb R^d$ be a unit-speed $C^3$ curve with $M$ equal arc-length intervals of length $h=L/M$. Suppose $\|R''\|_2\le K_2$ and the coordinate third derivatives satisfy the bound in [[lem-centered-chord-and-unequal-step-tangent-error]] with constant $M_3$. For sufficiently small $h$, each chord length $\ell_i=\|R(ih)-R((i-1)h)\|_2$ satisfies $|\ell_i-h|\le C_1h^3$, where $C_1$ depends only on $K_2,M_3$. The piecewise-linear interpolant through the samples differs from $R$ in supremum norm by at most $C_2h^2$. If this polygon is redistributed by linear interpolation at equally spaced cumulative-length targets, the $j$th redistributed image is within $C_3h^2$ of $R(jh)$, for every $j=0,\ldots,M$.

Here $C^3$ on $[0,L]$ means that $R$ is the restriction of a $C^3$ curve on an open interval containing $[0,L]$; derivatives at the endpoints are the continuous one-sided values, and the unit-speed and derivative bounds are required on $[0,L]$.

proofparagraphs.text: On each mesh interval $[s,s+h]$, apply the one-dimensional degree-two formula [F3] to each coordinate of the extended curve at $s$; the endpoint convention supplies the required derivative continuity, and [A1, F2] gives a remainder vector $r$ with $\|r\|_2\le M_3h^3/6$. Thus $R(s+h)-R(s)=hT+\frac{h^2}{2}K+r$ with $T=R'(s)$, $K=R''(s)$, and $\|K\|_2\le K_2$. Differentiating $\|R'(s)\|_2^2=1$ gives $T^TK=0$ by the chain rule [F4]. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, given, algebra]

For $s=ih+\theta h$ with $0\le\theta\le1$, apply the one-dimensional degree-one formula [F3] on $\lbrack ih,s\rbrack$ and $\lbrack ih,(i+1)h\rbrack$. The remainder bound in [F3] and $\|R''\|_2\le K_2$ give $R(s)=R(ih)+\theta hR'(ih)+O(K_2h^2)$ and $R((i+1)h)=R(ih)+hR'(ih)+O(K_2h^2)$. Subtracting the linear interpolant cancels the first-order term, so the pointwise interpolation error is bounded by $C_2h^2$, uniformly over all intervals. [A1, F1, F3, given, algebra]

For $\gamma=1-1/\sqrt2$ and $\delta=-1/\sqrt2$ in [[def-ars222-additive-tableau-and-stages]], one has $\gamma>0$ and
$$\delta=1-\frac1{2\gamma},\qquad \gamma(1-\delta)=\frac12,\qquad \gamma(2-\gamma)=\frac12,\qquad \gamma(1-\gamma-\delta)=\frac12-\gamma^2.$$

actualproofparagraphs.1.1: Let $r=\sqrt2$. If $r\le1$, then $0\le r\le1$ and [F3] gives $r^2\le1$, contradicting $r^2=2$ from [F2]; hence $r>1$. Applying [F4] to $0<1<r$ gives $0<1/r<1$, so $\gamma=1-1/r>0$. [F2, F3, F4, algebra]
actualproofparagraphs.2.1: By [F1] and $\gamma=(r-1)/r$ from step 1.1, $1-1/(2\gamma)=1-r/(2(r-1))=(r-2)/(2(r-1))$. Since $r^2=2$, $r(r-2)=2-2r=-2(r-1)$; dividing by the nonzero $2r(r-1)$ gives $(r-2)/(2(r-1))=-1/r=\delta$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $\gamma=1-1/\sqrt2$ as in [[def-ars222-additive-tableau-and-stages]]. For each of the two implicit stages, let $c_j$ be its center after the previous stages have been selected. Suppose $b$ is bounded by $M$ and $L$-Lipschitz on a closed ball $\overline B(c_j,R_j)\subset U$, and $|\gamma|hM\le R_j$, $|\gamma|hL<1$. Then stage $Y_j=c_j+\gamma h b(Y_j)$ has a unique root in that ball. Every candidate $\widetilde Y_j$ in the same ball with unscaled stage-equation residual $r_j$ satisfies
$$\|\widetilde Y_j-Y_j\|_2\le\frac{\|r_j\|_2}{1-|\gamma|hL}.$$
The claim is local to these stage balls; it asserts no remote-root or large-step branch.

M f(x_*)=f(x_*).
$$
In particular, $1$ is a Floquet multiplier.

selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 Nonconstancy implies $f(x_*)\ne0$: otherwise the constant curve through $x_*$ is an IVP solution, and uniqueness in [F2] forces $\gamma$ to be that constant curve. [given, F2]

2.1 Differentiate the flow identity in [F2] with respect to $s$ at $s=0$. The chain rule [F3] gives $D_x\phi_T(x_*)f(x_*)$ on the left, while the time derivative on the right is $f(\phi_T(x_*))=f(x_*)$. By [F1] the left derivative is the monodromy action, hence $Mf(x_*)=f(x_*)$. Since $f(x_*)\ne0$ by step 1.1, this is an eigenvector with eigenvalue $1$, which is a Floquet multiplier by [F4]. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1] ∎

literal_source_anchor.quote:
Let $0<\alpha<1$ and let $(\omega_j)$ be the weights from
[[alg-backward-euler-convolution-quadrature]]. Then $\omega_0=1$,
$\omega_j<0$ for every $j\ge1$, and for every complex $z$ with $|z|<1$,
$$\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\omega_jz^j=(1-z)^\alpha_{\operatorname{Log}}.$$
For $n\ge0$ define
$$p_n:=\sum_{j=0}^n\omega_j.$$
Then
$$p_n=\prod_{k=1}^n\left(1-\frac{\alpha}{k}\right) =\frac{\Gamma(n+1-\alpha)}{\Gamma(1-\alpha)\Gamma(n+1)}>0,$$
where the empty product for $n=0$ is $1$. For every $n\ge1$,
$$p_n\ge\frac{(n+1)^{-\alpha}}{\Gamma(1-\alpha)}.$$

review_basis.full_actual_interface:
Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ have continuous first and second partial derivatives. Put $g(x):=\nabla f(x)$ and $G(x):=\nabla^2 f(x)$, using the conventions of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] and [[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]]. Let $K\subseteq U$ be convex. Suppose that for every $x\in K$, $G(x)$ is symmetric and, for constants $0<\mu\le\Lambda<\infty$,
$$ \mu\|w\|_2^2\le w^TG(x)w\quad(w\in\mathbb R^n),\qquad \|G(x)\|_2\le\Lambda, $$
where $\|A\|_2:=\sup_{\|w\|_2=1}\|Aw\|_2$. Then for all $u,v\in K$, with $d:=u-v$,
$$ \|g(u)-g(v)\|_2\le\Lambda\|d\|_2, \qquad (g(u)-g(v))^Td\ge\mu\|d\|_2^2, $$
and
$$ \frac\mu2\|d\|_2^2\le f(u)-f(v)-g(v)^Td\le\frac\Lambda2\|d\|_2^2. $$
Separately, let $W\subseteq U$ be convex, let $x_*\in W$, and suppose $G$ is $L_G$-Lipschitz on $W$ in operator norm. Then for all $u,v\in W$, with $d:=u-v$,
$$ \|g(u)-g(v)-G(x_*)d\|_2 \le L_G\max\{\|u-x_*\|_2,\|v-x_*\|_2\}\,\|d\|_2. $$
review_basis.source_specific_focus: The Hessian sandwich transfers along the segment from v to u to gradient monotonicity and quadratic Taylor remainders; the separate reference-Hessian estimate uses x_star in W.

$$ m_s:=\frac{s^Ty}{\|s\|_2^2},\quad M_s:=\frac{\|y\|_2^2}{s^Ty},\quad q:=\frac{s^TBs}{\|s\|_2^2},\quad \eta:=\frac{s^TBs}{\|s\|_2\|Bs\|_2}. $$
Then $\eta>0$, $\eta\le1$, and
$$ \operatorname{tr}(B^+)=\operatorname{tr}(B)-\frac{\|Bs\|_2^2}{s^TBs} +\frac{\|y\|_2^2}{s^Ty}, \qquad \det(B^+)=\det(B)\frac{s^Ty}{s^TBs}. $$

$$ \psi(B^+)\le\psi(B)+(M_s-\log m_s-1) +h\!\left(\frac{q}{\eta^2}\right)+\log\eta^2. $$

Assume AC and the usual filtered Brownian conventions of
[[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]. Let $G$ be a predictable
$d\times m$ matrix process on $[0,T]$ with
$$\mathbb E\left(\int_0^T\|G_s\|_F^2\,ds\right)^{p/2}<\infty$$
for some real $p\ge2$, and let $M_t=\int_0^tG_s\,dW_s$ be its continuous
vector Itô integral. There is a finite constant $C_{p,d}$, independent of
$G$ and $T$, such that
$$\mathbb E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|M_t|^p\le C_{p,d}\, \mathbb E\left(\int_0^T\|G_s\|_F^2\,ds\right)^{p/2}.$$

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $s\ge1$, let $R_1,\ldots,R_s$ be complex matrices of one fixed shape,
and let $C\ge1$. Define
$$\mathcal C_{s,C}:=\{c\in\mathbb R^s:\sum_{i=1}^s c_i=1,\ \sum_{i=1}^s|c_i|\le C\}$$
and $J(c):=\|\sum_{i=1}^s c_iR_i\|_F^2$. Then $J$ attains a minimum on
$\mathcal C_{s,C}$. Among all minimizers there is a unique vector of minimum
Euclidean norm. This rule defines the exact capped DIIS coefficient vector even
when the least-squares Gram matrix is singular.

actualproofparagraphs.2.1: The map $c\mapsto\sum_i c_iR_i$ is linear and continuous in finite dimensions, and its squared Frobenius norm is continuous by [F1]. The extreme-value theorem gives a minimum; its minimizer set is closed as the inverse image of the singleton containing that minimum, hence compact as a closed subset of $\mathcal C_{s,C}$. Thus [F2] gives a nonempty compact set $M=\operatorname*{argmin}_{c\in\mathcal C_{s,C}}J(c)$. [step 1.1, F1, F2]
actualproofparagraphs.3.1: For $c,d\in\mathcal C_{s,C}$ and $0\le t\le1$, the coefficients $e=(1-t)c+td$ satisfy $\sum_i e_i=(1-t)\sum_i c_i+t\sum_i d_i=1$. By [F3], $\sum_i|e_i|\le(1-t)\sum_i|c_i|+t\sum_i|d_i|\le C$, so $\mathcal C_{s,C}$ is convex. The set $M$ is also convex: for matrices $A,B$ the identity $\|(1-t)A+tB\|_F^2=(1-t)\|A\|_F^2+t\|B\|_F^2-t(1-t)\|A-B\|_F^2$ proves convexity of the squared norm. Applying it to $A=\sum_i c_iR_i$ and $B=\sum_i d_iR_i$ shows $J((1-t)c+td)\le(1-t)J(c)+tJ(d)=\min J$, so the convex combination also minimizes. Since $M$ is compact, the continuous function $c\mapsto\|c\|_2^2$ has a minimizer $c_*\in M$. [step 2.1, F1, F3, algebra]
actualproofparagraphs.4.1: If distinct $c,d\in M$ both had minimum Euclidean norm, their midpoint would lie in $M$ and satisfy $\left\|\frac{c+d}{2}\right\|_2^2=\frac{\|c\|_2^2+\|d\|_2^2}{2}-\frac{\|c-d\|_2^2}{4}<\frac{\|c\|_2^2+\|d\|_2^2}{2},$ contradicting minimality. Thus $c_*$ is the unique minimum-norm least-squares minimizer. No nonsingularity of the Gram matrix is needed for existence or tie-breaking. [step 3.1, algebra] ∎

Let $R:J\to\mathbb R^d$ be a unit-speed $C^3$ curve on an open interval $J$ containing $[0,1]$, and suppose $\max_j\sup_{s\in J_0}|R_j'''(s)|\le M_3/\sqrt d$ on the stencil interval $J_0$. For $s-h,s+h\in J_0$, define

$$d_h:=\frac{R(s+h)-R(s-h)}{2h},\qquad \widehat t_h:=\frac{d_h}{\|d_h\|_2}.$$

If $\delta_h:=M_3h^2/6\le1/2$, then $d_h\ne0$ and

$$\|d_h-R'(s)\|_2\le\delta_h,\qquad \|\widehat t_h-R'(s)\|_2\le4\delta_h.$$

For unequal positive steps $h_-,h_+$ with $s-h_-,s+h_+\in J_0$, define

$$d_{h_-,h_+}:=\frac{h_+}{h_-(h_-+h_+)}(R(s)-R(s-h_-))+\frac{h_-}{h_+(h_-+h_+)}(R(s+h_+)-R(s)).$$

If $\delta_{h_-,h_+}:=M_3h_-h_+/6\le1/2$, then it is nonzero and its unit normalization differs from $R'(s)$ by at most $4\delta_{h_-,h_+}$. In particular, equal steps give an $O(h^2)$ unit-tangent error; quasiuniform unequal steps give an $O(h_-h_+)$ error. No second-order claim is made for a one-sided tangent branch.

The same normalization argument as in step 2.1, using $\delta_{h_-,h_+}\le1/2$, gives nonzero $d_{h_-,h_+}$ and normalized error at most $4\delta_{h_-,h_+}$. Let $N\ge1$, let $x_j=\cos(j\pi/N)$, and let $I_N^L$ denote degree-at-most-$N$ interpolation on these nodes. For every integer $n\ge0$, let $\rho_N(n)$ be the unique integer $r\in\{0,\ldots,N\}$ congruent to either $n$ or $-n$ modulo $2N$. Then
$$
I_N^L T_n=T_{\rho_N(n)}.
$$
In particular, sampling a Chebyshev series on the Lobatto grid can fold every degree $n>N$ to a degree at most $N$.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Under the pairing of [[def-chebyshev-arcsine-weighted-l2-pairing]],
$$\langle T_m,T_n\rangle_C= \begin{cases} \pi,&m=n=0,\\ \pi/2,&m=n\ge1,\\ 0,&m\ne n. \end{cases}$$
The polynomials $T_0,T_1,\ldots$ form a basis of the real polynomial space, and the pairing is positive definite on continuous real functions on $[-1,1]$. If a continuous real function $h$ satisfies $\langle h,T_n\rangle_C=0$ for every $n\ge0$, then $h=0$ on $[-1,1]$.
source_evidence.case_anchor:
Under the pairing of [[def-chebyshev-arcsine-weighted-l2-pairing]],
$$\langle T_m,T_n\rangle_C= \begin{cases} \pi,&m=n=0,\\ \pi/2,&m=n\ge1,\\ 0,&m\ne n. \end{cases}$$
The polynomials $T_0,T_1,\ldots$ form a basis of the real polynomial space, and the pairing is positive definite on continuous real functions on $[-1,1]$. If a continuous real function $h$ satisfies $\langle h,T_n\rangle_C=0$ for every $n\ge0$, then $h=0$ on $[-1,1]$.

proofparagraphs.text: By [F1]–[F2], $\langle T_m,T_n\rangle_C=\int_0^\pi\cos(m\theta)\cos(n\theta)\,d\theta$. If $m\ne n$, [F3], cosine parity [F5], and $\sin(k\pi)=0$ from [F5] make the integral of each nonzero-frequency cosine vanish by [F4]. If $m=n\ge1$, [F3] gives $\frac12(1+\cos(2m\theta))$, whose integral is $\pi/2$. If $m=n=0$, the integrand is $1$ and its integral is $\pi$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, algebra]

The recurrence [F6] shows inductively that $T_n$ has degree $n$ and nonzero leading coefficient: this holds for $T_0,T_1$, and the leading term of $2XT_n$ cannot cancel with the lower-degree $T_{n-1}$. Eliminating the leading term of any polynomial successively proves that $T_0,T_1,\ldots$ span all polynomials; their distinct degrees also give linear independence. Step 1.1 gives positive squared norms and pairwise orthogonality. [F6, step 1.1, algebra, induction]

The polynomials $T_0,T_1,\ldots$ form a basis of the real polynomial space, and the pairing is positive definite on continuous real functions on $[-1,1]$. If a continuous real function $h$ satisfies $\langle h,T_n\rangle_C=0$ for every $n\ge0$, then $h=0$ on $[-1,1]$.

proofparagraphs.text: Suppose continuous $h$ pairs to zero with every $T_n$. By step 2.1 it pairs to zero with every polynomial. Fix $\varepsilon>0$ and choose a polynomial $q$ with $\|q-h\|_\infty<\varepsilon$ by [F7]. The bound $M=\|h\|_\infty<\infty$ follows from [F8]. The pointwise bounds $-M\varepsilon\le h(\cos\theta)(h-q)(\cos\theta)\le M\varepsilon$ and [F9] give $0\le\langle h,h\rangle_C=\langle h,h-q\rangle_C\le\pi M\varepsilon.$ The lower inequality uses the nonnegative integrand $h(\cos\theta)^2$ and [F9]. Since this holds for every $\varepsilon>0$, $\langle h,h\rangle_C=0$. If $h(x_0)\ne0$ at some $x_0\in[-1,1]$, choose $\theta_0\in[0,\pi]$ with $\cos\theta_0=x_0$; continuity makes $h(\cos\theta)^2$ bounded below by a positive constant on a one-sided neighborhood if $\theta_0$ is an endpoint, or a two-sided neighborhood otherwise. [F9] then gives a positive integral, contradicting zero norm. Therefore $h=0$. [F1, F7, F8, F9, step 2.1, choose, algebra]

For any continuous $h$, if $\langle h,h\rangle_C=0$ but $h(\cos\theta_0)\ne0$ at some $\theta_0\in[0,\pi]$, continuity gives a one-sided interval at an endpoint, or a two-sided interval in the interior, on which $h(\cos\theta)^2$ is bounded below by a positive number. [F9] makes its integral positive, a contradiction. Thus $h(\cos\theta)=0$ for every $\theta$, and cosine maps $[0,\pi]$ onto $[-1,1]$, so $h=0$. Symmetry and bilinearity follow from the integral definition [F1], proving positive definiteness. [F1, F9, given, algebra] ∎

review_basis.full_actual_interface:
Let $\kappa,\theta,\sigma>0$ satisfy the Feller condition
$2\kappa\theta\ge\sigma^2$, and put
$$a=\frac{4\kappa\theta-\sigma^2}{8}.$$
For a positive local strong solution of the CIR SDE
$$dX_t=\kappa(\theta-X_t)dt+\sigma\sqrt{X_t}\,dW_t$$
on $U=(0,\infty)$, the Lamperti variable $Z_t=\sqrt{X_t}$ satisfies
$$dZ_t=\left(\frac a{Z_t}-\frac\kappa2 Z_t\right)dt+ \frac\sigma2dW_t$$
up to every compact exit time. Moreover, for every $h>0$, $z\ge0$, and
$\Delta W\in\mathbb R$, the drift-implicit step
$$z_+=z+h\left(\frac a{z_+}-\frac\kappa2z_+\right) +\frac\sigma2\Delta W$$
has exactly one positive root. It is the value defined by
[[alg-cir-lamperti-positive-implicit-scheme]]. The boundary input $z=0$ is
included for the numerical root statement; the CIR solution theorem below
uses $X_0>0$.

$$
|\lambda_k(A+E)-\lambda_k(A)|\le\|E\|_2.
$$

source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: The induced norm of a Hermitian perturbation bounds every ordered eigenvalue displacement, with no eigenvalue simplicity assumption.
selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 Realify $A$ and $E$. Their eigenvalues in decreasing order repeat each complex eigenvalue twice, so the $2k$-th eigenvalue of $\mathcal R(A)$ is $\lambda_k(A)$ and similarly for $E$ and $A+E$. By [F2] with indices $i=2k,j=1$, the upper Weyl inequality gives $\lambda_{2k}(\mathcal R(A+E))\le\lambda_{2k}(\mathcal R(A))+\lambda_1(\mathcal R(E))$. With $i=2k,j=2n$, the lower inequality gives $\lambda_{2k}(\mathcal R(A+E))\ge\lambda_{2k}(\mathcal R(A))+\lambda_{2n}(\mathcal R(E))$. [given, F1, F2]

For a Hermitian $H\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, define its inertia as $(n_+(H),n_-(H),n_0(H))$, the counts with multiplicity of positive, negative, and zero eigenvalues. If $S\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ is nonsingular, then
$$
\operatorname{inertia}(S^*HS)=\operatorname{inertia}(H).
$$
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: Nonsingular complex congruence preserves the positive, negative and zero inertia counts of a Hermitian form.

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
For a Hermitian $H\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, define its inertia as $(n_+(H),n_-(H),n_0(H))$, the counts with multiplicity of positive, negative, and zero eigenvalues. If $S\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ is nonsingular, then
$$
\operatorname{inertia}(S^*HS)=\operatorname{inertia}(H).
$$
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: Nonsingular complex congruence preserves the positive, negative and zero inertia counts of a Hermitian form.
selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 By [F1], $\mathcal R(H)$ and $\mathcal R(S^*HS)$ are real symmetric and the latter equals $\mathcal R(S)^{\mathsf T}\mathcal R(H)\mathcal R(S)$ with $\mathcal R(S)$ nonsingular. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Apply [F2] to the realification congruence in step 1.1. The real positive, negative, and zero counts agree; by [F1] each is twice the corresponding complex count, so division by $2$ gives the asserted complex inertia equality. [step 1.1, F1, F2, algebra] ∎

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
For $Z=X+iY\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ with real $X,Y$, define its realification
$$
\mathcal R(Z)=\begin{pmatrix}X&-Y\\Y&X\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb R^{2n\times2n}.
$$
Then $\mathcal R(ZW)=\mathcal R(Z)\mathcal R(W)$, $\mathcal R(Z^*)=\mathcal R(Z)^{\mathsf T}$, and $Z$ is invertible exactly when $\mathcal R(Z)$ is invertible. If $H=H^*$ is Hermitian with eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n$ counted with multiplicity, then $\mathcal R(H)$ is real symmetric with eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n,\lambda_n$. For any complex matrix $E$, $\|\mathcal R(E)\|_2=\|E\|_2$.
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: The real block representation preserves multiplication, adjoints and invertibility, duplicates Hermitian eigenvalue multiplicities and preserves induced norm.

selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 Identify $z=x+iy\in\mathbb C^n$ with $(x,y)\in\mathbb R^{2n}$. Direct multiplication gives $\mathcal R(Z)(x,y)=(\Re(Zz),\Im(Zz))$; this identity shows that realification respects composition. Writing $Z=X+iY$ gives $\mathcal R(Z^*)=\begin{pmatrix}X^{\mathsf T}&Y^{\mathsf T}\\-Y^{\mathsf T}&X^{\mathsf T}\end{pmatrix}=\mathcal R(Z)^{\mathsf T}$. [given, F2, algebra]

2.1 The identification preserves Euclidean norms. Hence, by [F4], the suprema of $\|Ez\|_2$ over complex unit vectors and of $\|\mathcal R(E)u\|_2$ over real unit vectors agree, proving the operator-norm identity. If $Z$ is invertible, $\mathcal R(Z^{-1})$ is an inverse of $\mathcal R(Z)$ by step 1.1; conversely, if $\mathcal R(Z)$ is invertible, its kernel is zero, so $Zz=0$ implies $z=0$, and [F3] makes the square matrix $Z$ invertible. [F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

proofparagraphs.text: Fix $c$ with $|c|<r_0$ and choose $R$ with $|c|<R<r_0$. For $0<|h|<R-|c|$ and each $n\ge1$, $$\frac{(c+h)^n-c^n}{h}=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}(c+h)^{n-1-j}c^j,$$ so every term has modulus at most $R^{n-1}$ and the quotient has modulus at most $nR^{n-1}$. Therefore the tail after degree $N$ of the difference-quotient series is bounded uniformly in such $h$ by $\sum_{n>N}n|a_n|R^{n-1}$. The tail of the proposed derivative series at $c$ has the same bound. [given, algebra]

Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose $N$ so both tail bounds in step 1.1 are below $\varepsilon/3$. The finite polynomial $\sum_{n=0}^N a_nx^n$ has derivative $\sum_{n=1}^Nna_nc^{n-1}$ at $c$, so choose $h$ small enough that its difference quotient differs from this derivative by less than $\varepsilon/3$. The full difference quotient and full derivative series then differ by less than $\varepsilon$ by the two tails and this finite-polynomial bound. This proves differentiability and the displayed derivative formula. [given, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

u_t$ be the finite sectional solution on the initial grid segment $G\cap[a,R]$ from $
u_0=\eta_0|_{[a,R]}$, extended by zero to $G$. Initialize the finite model's reported reservoir with $L_0=\int_{(R,\infty)}x\,\eta_0(dx)$. If $M_1=M_1(\eta_0)$, then for $0\le t\le T$,
$$d_{BL}(
u_t,\eta_t)\le e^{C_Tt}\left[ rac{M_1}{R}+ rac{2K_*M_1^2t}{aR}ight],$$
where $C_T$ is the bounded-number stability constant from [[thm-infinite-fixed-pivot-sectional-global-wellposedness-and-bl-stability]]. The reservoir records the finite model's overflow mass exactly; the estimate allows the unbounded model's above-cutoff particles to coagulate or fragment and return mass to the retained range.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $\mathcal H$, $A$, and $E_t$ be as in [[def-dirichlet-sine-mode-heat-splitting-model]]. The maps $E_t$ for $t\ge0$ satisfy $E_0=I$ and $E_{t+s}=E_tE_s$, are contractions in $\ell^2$, and are strongly continuous at $t=0$. Define the generator domain to consist of those $u\in\mathcal H$ for which the right limit
$$\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{E_tu-u}{t}$$
exists in $\mathcal H$. This domain is exactly $D(A)=\{u:\sum_{k\ge1}k^4|u_k|^2<\infty\}$, and the limit equals $Au=(-k^2u_k)_{k\ge1}$.

actualproofparagraphs.1.2: For every $x\ge0$, [F4] applied to $s\mapsto e^{-s}$ on $[0,x]$ gives $0\le1-e^{-x}\le x$: the difference is $xe^{-\xi}$ for some $\xi\in[0,x]$, and [F3] bounds $e^{-\xi}$ by $1$. For $u\in D(A)$, the $k$th coordinate of $(E_tu-u)/t$ tends to $-k^2u_k$ by the chain rule and exponential derivative in [F4]. Its difference from that limit has absolute value at most $2k^2|u_k|$, by the same bound. The squared tail of these differences is therefore at most $4\sum_{k>K}k^4|u_k|^2$, which tends to zero; on every finite head the coordinate limits give norm convergence. Hence the right limit exists in $\mathcal H$ and equals $Au$. [F1, F3, F4, algebra]
actualproofparagraphs.2.1: Fix $u\in\mathcal H$ and $\varepsilon>0$. By convergence of its square sum, choose $K$ so that $\sum_{k>K}|u_k|^2<\varepsilon^2/4$. The squared norm of the tail of $E_tu-u$ is at most this tail because $|e^{-k^2t}-1|\le1$ by [F3]; for the finitely many indices $k\le K$, continuity of the exponential at zero from [F4] makes their squared sum less than $\varepsilon^2/4$ for all sufficiently small $t>0$. Thus $\|E_tu-u\|_2<\varepsilon$, proving strong continuity at zero. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra, choose]

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $V\in C^4(U,\mathbb R)$ on an open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, let $x\in U$, and let $v\in\mathbb R^d$ satisfy $\|v\|_2=1$ and $x\pm\epsilon v\in U$ for $\epsilon>0$. Assume the segments $x+[-\epsilon,\epsilon]v$ lie in $U$. Define

$$D_\epsilon(x,v):=\frac{\nabla V(x+\epsilon v)-\nabla V(x-\epsilon v)}{2\epsilon}.$$

If approximate gradient evaluations $\widehat g_\pm$ satisfy $\|\widehat g_\pm-\nabla V(x\pm\epsilon v)\|_2\le\eta$, and $M_4$ bounds the third derivatives of each gradient coordinate in the Taylor remainders on these segments, then

$$\left\|\frac{\widehat g_+-\widehat g_-}{2\epsilon}-\nabla^2V(x)v\right\|_2\le\frac{\sqrt d\,M_4}{6}\epsilon^2+\frac{\eta}{\epsilon}.$$

Thus the deterministic truncation error is $O(\epsilon^2)$ and the force-evaluation error contributes $O(\eta/\epsilon)$. This is an error bound for the Hessian action on the supplied direction; it is not an operator-norm bound for a full Hessian approximation.

$$D_\epsilon(x,v):=\frac{\nabla V(x+\epsilon v)-\nabla V(x-\epsilon v)}{2\epsilon}.$$

If approximate gradient evaluations $\widehat g_\pm$ satisfy $\|\widehat g_\pm-\nabla V(x\pm\epsilon v)\|_2\le\eta$, and $M_4$ bounds the third derivatives of each gradient coordinate in the Taylor remainders on these segments, then

$$\left\|\frac{\widehat g_+-\widehat g_-}{2\epsilon}-\nabla^2V(x)v\right\|_2\le\frac{\sqrt d\,M_4}{6}\epsilon^2+\frac{\eta}{\epsilon}.$$

Thus the deterministic truncation error is $O(\epsilon^2)$ and the force-evaluation error contributes $O(\eta/\epsilon)$. This is an error bound for the Hessian action on the supplied direction; it is not an operator-norm bound for a full Hessian approximation.
source_evidence.case_anchor: Write $e_\pm=\widehat g_\pm-g(x\pm\epsilon v)$. Then $\|e_+-e_-\|_2\le\|e_+\|_2+\|e_-\|_2\le2\eta$, so their contribution after division by $2\epsilon$ is at most $\eta/\epsilon$. Adding this to step 1.1 proves the inequality. A bound on this single direction alone supplies no bound on an operator acting on all directions. [given, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

source_evidence.fullclaim:
For the constant forcing $f(x):=\pi/4$ on $(0,\pi)$, define its Fourier sine coefficient by
$$\widehat f_k:=\frac2\pi\int_0^\pi f(x)\sin(kx)\,dx.$$
Then $\widehat f_k=g_k$ from [[def-dirichlet-sine-mode-heat-splitting-model]]. Thus $g\in\mathcal H$ but $g$ is outside the generator domain of $A$. The constant forcing has nonzero endpoint value, while every Dirichlet sine mode vanishes at both endpoints.

actualproofparagraphs.2.1: The squared coefficients sum to $\sum_{j\ge0}(2j+1)^{-2}\le\sum_{k\ge1}k^{-2}<\infty$ by [F2], so $g\in\mathcal H$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]
actualproofparagraphs.2.2: The generator-domain sum is $\sum_{k\ge1}k^4|g_k|^2=\sum_{j\ge0}(2j+1)^2$, whose partial sums are at least the number of terms and hence unbounded. Therefore $g\notin D(A)$ by [F1]. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

source_evidence.case_anchor: Even coefficients vanish while every odd coefficient1/k is nonzero, so Proof step 2.1 proves square summability and Proof step 2.2 still obtains divergent generator weight.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $V$ be a Hilbert space and let $V_h\subseteq V$ be a subspace. Suppose the exact form $a$ is coercive with constant $\alpha>0$ in the norm $\|\cdot\|_V$. Let $a_h$ be a discrete form on $V_h$ and suppose

$$|a_h(v_h,v_h)-a(v_h,v_h)|\le\eta_h\|v_h\|_V^2\qquad(v_h\in V_h)$$

for some $\eta_h\ge0$. Then $a_h$ is coercive with constant at least $\alpha-\eta_h$ whenever $\eta_h<\alpha$. In particular, if $\eta_h\le\alpha/2$, then its coercivity constant is at least $\alpha/2$.
source_evidence.case_anchor: Let $V$ be a Hilbert space and let $V_h\subseteq V$ be a subspace. Suppose the exact form $a$ is coercive with constant $\alpha>0$ in the norm $\|\cdot\|_V$. Let $a_h$ be a discrete form on $V_h$ and suppose

proofparagraphs.text: Fix $v_h\in V_h$. By coercivity [F1] and the defect hypothesis [A1], $\operatorname{Re}a_h(v_h,v_h)=\operatorname{Re}a(v_h,v_h)+\operatorname{Re}(a_h(v_h,v_h)-a(v_h,v_h))\ge(\alpha-\eta_h)\|v_h\|_V^2$. [given, F1, A1, algebra]
If $\eta_h<\alpha$, then $\alpha-\eta_h>0$, so the inequality in step 1.1 is precisely coercivity with that constant. If $\eta_h\le\alpha/2$, then $\alpha-\eta_h\ge\alpha/2$. [step 1.1, algebra] ∎

selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 For any firmly nonexpansive $J$, its reflector $R=2J-I$ is nonexpansive: with $d=v-v'$ and $e=Jv-Jv'$, [F2] gives $$\|2e-d\|_2^2=\|d\|_2^2+4\|e\|_2^2-4\langle e,d\rangle\le\|d\|_2^2.$$ Thus $R_A R_B$ is nonexpansive because it is a composition of two nonexpansive maps. [A1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Expanding the reflectors gives $T=(I+R_A R_B)/2$. For $d=w-w'$ and $s=R_AR_Bw-R_AR_Bw'$, nonexpansiveness gives $\|s\|_2\le\|d\|_2$, and $$\left\|\frac{d+s}{2}\right\|_2^2\le\left\langle\frac{d+s}{2},d\right\rangle$$ is equivalent after multiplying by $4$ and cancelling common terms to $\|s\|_2^2\le\|d\|_2^2$. This is the firm inequality for $T$. [A1, F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Assume Countable Choice and the setting of [[def-parameterized-elliptic-variational-problem]]. On an open neighborhood $\Theta_0\subseteq\Theta$, suppose the same constants $M<\infty$ and $\alpha>0$ give boundedness and coercivity for every $a_\theta$, and $\theta\mapsto A_\theta$ and $\theta\mapsto\ell_\theta$ are operator-norm $C^1$. Then each state $u_\theta$ exists uniquely, the map $\theta\mapsto u_\theta\in V$ is $C^1$, and for each direction $\eta\in\mathbb R^m$ its derivative $w_\eta=D_\theta u_\theta[\eta]$ is the unique solution of
$$a_\theta(w_\eta,v)=D_\theta\ell_\theta[\eta](v)-D_\theta a_\theta[\eta](u_\theta,v)\qquad(v\in V).$$
Uniform coercivity is required on the parameter neighborhood; no differentiability conclusion is asserted at a loss of coercivity.

actualproofparagraphs.4.1: The solution operator $A_\theta^{-1}:V^*\to V$ has norm at most $\alpha^{-1}$. For nearby $\theta,\widetilde\theta$, the identity $A_{\widetilde\theta}^{-1}-A_\theta^{-1} =A_{\widetilde\theta}^{-1}(A_\theta-A_{\widetilde\theta})A_\theta^{-1}$ shows its operator-norm continuity. The formula in step 2.2, together with continuity of $u_\theta$, $D A_\theta$, and $D\ell_\theta$, then shows $D_\theta u_\theta$ is continuous. Hence the state map is $C^1$. [A1, F1, F2, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

source_evidence.case_anchor: Positivealpha excludes loss of coercivity; Proof step 4.1 bounds every inverse byalpha^{-1}, so no inverse atalpha=0 is asserted.

Assume Countable Choice and the setting of [[def-parameterized-elliptic-variational-problem]]. On an open neighborhood $\Theta_0\subseteq\Theta$, suppose the same constants $M<\infty$ and $\alpha>0$ give boundedness and coercivity for every $a_\theta$, and $\theta\mapsto A_\theta$ and $\theta\mapsto\ell_\theta$ are operator-norm $C^1$. actualproofparagraphs.2.1: For sufficiently small $h$ with $\theta+h\in\Theta_0$, put $\delta u=u_{\theta+h}-u_\theta$, $\delta A=A_{\theta+h}-A_\theta$, and $\delta\ell=\ell_{\theta+h}-\ell_\theta$. Subtract the two variational equations to get $a_\theta(\delta u,v)=\delta\ell(v)-(\delta A\,u_{\theta+h})(v)$. Taking $v=\delta u$, using coercivity and the dual norm, and dividing by $\|\delta u\|_V$ when it is nonzero gives $\|\delta u\|_V\le\alpha^{-1}\bigl(\|\delta\ell\|_{V^*}+\|\delta A\|\,\|u_{\theta+h}\|_V\bigr)=O(\|h\|_2)$. The same bound is immediate when $\delta u=0$. Thus the state map is locally Lipschitz. [A1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]
actualproofparagraphs.2.2: For each direction $h\in\mathbb R^m$, define $w_h$ by $a_\theta(w_h,v)=D\ell_\theta[h](v)-\bigl(DA_\theta[h]u_\theta\bigr)(v)$. The right side is a bounded linear functional, so [F1] gives a unique $w_h$. Uniqueness and linearity of the right side in $h$ show $h\mapsto w_h$ is linear. [F1, F2, step 1.1, given]

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Use the dimensions, exact interval maps $\Phi_n,K_n$, terminal and initial data, and Euclidean conventions of [[lem-local-c1-step-consistency-implies-tangent-adjoint-gradient-order]]. Let $(A,b,c)$ be a fixed explicit $s$-stage tableau with $c_i=\sum_{j<i}a_{ij}$ and $\sum_i b_i=1$. Its weights may be negative or zero. The actual numerical state and cost maps are
$$Y_i=x+h\sum_{j<i}a_{ij}f(t_n+c_jh,Y_j,\theta),$$
$$\Psi_n=x+h\sum_i b_if(t_n+c_ih,Y_i,\theta),\qquad L_n=h\sum_i b_i\ell(t_n+c_ih,Y_i,\theta).$$
These are exact finite-stage maps, not outputs of a stopped implicit solver.

Assume $f:\mathcal D\to\mathbb R^d$ and $\ell:\mathcal D\to\mathbb R$ are $C^2$ on an open convex time-state-parameter domain. On a common compact convex subset with positive margin in $\mathcal D$, their derivatives through order two are uniformly bounded. All admitted local exact trajectories, all numerical trajectories and stages, and all needed joining segments lie in this domain and common tube, uniformly over the fixed parameter neighborhood and $h\le h_0$. Stage times outside $[t_n,t_{n+1}]$ are included when the tableau has such abscissae. Unique admitted local flows are assumed as in the flow-tangent supplier.

Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper and convex. For every
$x,s\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$f(x)+f^*(s)\ge\langle s,x\rangle,$$
with extended-real interpretation. Equality holds exactly when
$x\in\operatorname{dom}f$, $f^*(s)<+\infty$, and
$s\in\partial f(x)$; equivalently, for proper convex $f$, equality itself
forces the two finiteness conditions and the subgradient membership.
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: Fenchel–Young equality forces both finite function values and the stated subgradient membership, whereas the inequality itself uses the extended-real convention.

literal_source_anchor.description: the finite triangular coefficient recursion
literal_source_anchor.quote: Seek $Y_h=X_H+\sum_{m=1}^Nh^mX_m$. The time-$h$ flow expansion is $z+\sum_{k=1}^{N+1}\frac{h^k}{k!}(Y_h\cdot\nabla)^{k-1}Y_h(z)+O(h^{N+2})$. At coefficient $h^{m+1}$, the first term $hY_h$ contributes $X_m$; every term with $k\ge2$ can involve only $X_1,\ldots,X_{m-1}$ at that degree. Thus set $X_m=d_{m+1}-P_m$, where $P_m$ is the already determined coefficient from those higher flow terms. This finite recursion matches coefficients through degree $N+1$. Since each method agrees with the exact $X_H$ flow through degree $r$, it gives $X_1=\cdots=X_{r-1}=0$. [F1, F2, F6, algebra]

Each coordinate of $F(n,L)-F(\tilde n,\tilde L)$ is a finite weighted sum of these differences; the reservoir coordinate is independent of $L$. source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: Firm nonexpansiveness and a supplied fixed point make the finite-dimensional Picard sequence converge; its zero-dimensional space is handled directly as the singleton.
selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 If $n=0$, [F3] gives $E=\{0\}$ and the nonempty fixed-point set forces $T(0)=0$; since $w_0=0$, every iterate equals the fixed point. It remains to consider $n\ge1$. Firm nonexpansiveness applied to $w_k$ and a fixed point $p$ gives $\|w_{k+1}-p\|_2^2\le\langle w_{k+1}-p,w_k-p\rangle$. Expanding $w_k-p=(w_{k+1}-p)+(w_k-w_{k+1})$ and rearranging yields $$\|w_{k+1}-p\|_2^2+\|w_{k+1}-w_k\|_2^2\le\|w_k-p\|_2^2.$$ Summing this inequality shows that the distances to $p$ are nonincreasing, the sequence is bounded, and $\sum_k\|w_{k+1}-w_k\|_2^2<\infty$, so the increments tend to zero. [A1, given, F1, F3, algebra]

Suppose $G(x)=\nabla^2 f(x)$ is $L_G$-Lipschitz in operator norm on a neighborhood of $x_*$. With $B_k:=H_k^{-1}$ and $s_k:=x_{k+1}-x_k$, the iterates satisfy
$$ \frac{\|(B_k-G_*)s_k\|_2}{\|s_k\|_2}\longrightarrow0,\qquad G_*:=G(x_*). $$
Since $s_k=\alpha_kp_k$ with $\alpha_k>0$, the same limit holds with $p_k$ in place of $s_k$. This is the Dennis–Moré condition used by the local full-memory superlinear convergence result.

For every $X\in U$ at which the response map of
[[def-self-consistent-projector-response-map]] has a strict $r$th gap,
$\Phi(X)$ is a uniquely defined member of $\mathcal P_r$. Degeneracies among
the first $r$ eigenvalues or among the remaining eigenvalues do not affect it.

actualproofparagraphs.1.1: By [F1], choose an orthonormal eigenbasis $(u_1,\ldots,u_n)$ of $F(X)$ with the eigenvalues in the given order. The strict gap prevents an eigenspace for one eigenvalue from straddling positions $r$ and $r+1$, so the sum of the first $r$ eigenspaces is the span of exactly the first $r$ basis vectors. actualproofparagraphs.2.1: Changing the orthonormal basis within a repeated eigenspace below the gap leaves that entire eigenspace in the sum; changing one within a repeated eigenspace above the gap leaves that entire eigenspace out. Thus the selected subspace does not depend on the eigenbasis chosen in step 1.1. Its orthogonal projector is $P=\sum_{j=1}^r u_ju_j^*$, which satisfies $P=P^*$ and $P^2=P$ by orthonormality. By [F3], $\operatorname{tr}P=\sum_{a=1}^n P_{aa}=\sum_{a=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^r (u_j)_a\overline{(u_j)_a}=\sum_{j=1}^r\sum_{a=1}^n|(u_j)_a|^2=\sum_{j=1}^r1=r$, since each $u_j$ is a unit vector. [step 1.1, F1, F2, F3, L1, algebra]

review_basis.full_actual_interface:
For the cubic model $m_\sigma$ of [[def-adaptive-cubic-regularization-model]],
with $\sigma>0$ and symmetric $B$, a global minimizer exists. If $g\ne0$ and
$s_*$ is any global minimizer, then $s_*\ne0$ and
$$g+Bs_*+\sigma\|s_*\|_2s_*=0,$$
$$m_\sigma(0)-m_\sigma(s_*)\ge\frac{\sigma}{6}\|s_*\|_2^3.$$

More generally, every $s$ satisfying
$$g^Ts+s^TBs+\sigma\|s\|_2^3=0,\qquad s^TBs+\sigma\|s\|_2^3\ge0$$
has $m_\sigma(0)-m_\sigma(s)\ge\frac{\sigma}{6}\|s\|_2^3$.
For $g\ne0$, put $a=\|g\|_2$ and $q=g^TBg$. The unique minimizer of
the cubic model on the negative-gradient ray $\{-tg:t\ge0\}$ is
$$s_C=-t_Cg,\qquad t_C=\frac{-q+\sqrt{q^2+4\sigma a^5}}{2\sigma a^3}>0.$$
review_basis.source_specific_focus: Positive cubic regularization makes the model coercive and gives the sigma-over-six norm-cubed decrease under its radial conditions.

Let $k\ge1$, $m\ge0$, and let $H=\begin{pmatrix}D&B^*\\B&C\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb C^{(k+m)\times(k+m)}$ be Hermitian, where $D=D^*\in\mathbb C^{k\times k}$ is nonsingular, $B\in\mathbb C^{m\times k}$, and $C=C^*\in\mathbb C^{m\times m}$. Define the Schur complement $S=C-BD^{-1}B^*$. Inertia triples are added coordinatewise, and the $0\times0$ matrix has inertia $(0,0,0)$. Then
$$
\operatorname{inertia}(H)=\operatorname{inertia}(D)+\operatorname{inertia}(S),
$$
where the triples are added coordinatewise.

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Let $k\ge1$, $m\ge0$, and let $H=\begin{pmatrix}D&B^*\\B&C\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb C^{(k+m)\times(k+m)}$ be Hermitian, where $D=D^*\in\mathbb C^{k\times k}$ is nonsingular, $B\in\mathbb C^{m\times k}$, and $C=C^*\in\mathbb C^{m\times m}$. Define the Schur complement $S=C-BD^{-1}B^*$. Inertia triples are added coordinatewise, and the $0\times0$ matrix has inertia $(0,0,0)$. Then
$$
\operatorname{inertia}(H)=\operatorname{inertia}(D)+\operatorname{inertia}(S),
$$
where the triples are added coordinatewise.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $c\in\mathbb R^d$, $R>0$, $h>0$, and let $b$ be defined on the closed Euclidean ball $\overline B(c,R)$. Suppose $\|b(z)\|_2\le M$ and $\|b(z)-b(w)\|_2\le L\|z-w\|_2$ there, with $hM\le R$ and $hL<1$. Then the IMEX Euler equation $Y=c+h b(Y)$ has exactly one solution in $\overline B(c,R)$. Every $\widetilde Y$ in that ball satisfies
$$\|\widetilde Y-Y\|_2\le\frac{\|\widetilde Y-c-hb(\widetilde Y)\|_2}{1-hL}.$$
In the algorithm [[alg-imex-euler-step]], $c=y+h a(y)$; this is a local branch result and gives no root outside the selected ball.

actualproofparagraphs.3.1: For any $\widetilde Y$ in the ball, [F4] and step 2.1 give $\|\widetilde Y-Y\|_2\le\|\widetilde Y-T(\widetilde Y)\|_2+\|T(\widetilde Y)-T(Y)\|_2\le\|\widetilde Y-c-hb(\widetilde Y)\|_2+hL\|\widetilde Y-Y\|_2$. Since $1-hL>0$, rearranging proves the residual bound. [F1, F4, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

source_evidence.fullclaim: Use the implicit Runge–Kutta residual $G(Y)=Y-\mathbf1\otimes u-h(A\otimes I_d)F(Y)$ from [[def-implicit-runge-kutta-stage-equations]] on a convex open neighborhood of an invariant stage ball. Suppose $F$ is $C^1$ there and $\|D_YF(Y)Z\|_{\infty,2}\le L\|Z\|_{\infty,2}$ for every $Y$ in the ball and every block vector $Z$. If $q=h\|A\|_\infty L<1$, then $D_YG(Y)$ is invertible at every point of the selected stage branch. The contraction hypotheses of [[lem-small-step-implicit-rk-branch-and-residual-error]] provide existence and uniqueness of the root in that ball; this lemma supplies nonsingularity for implicit differentiation.

actualproofparagraphs.1.1: Let $Y,W$ belong to the invariant ball. Its convexity puts $Y+t(W-Y)$ in the ball for $0\le t\le1$. For each block $i$, the curve $\gamma_i(t)=F_i(Y+t(W-Y))$ is continuous on $[0,1]$ and differentiable inside because $F$ is $C^1$ on an open neighborhood. Its derivative obeys $$\|\gamma_i'(t)\|_2\le\|D_YF(Y+t(W-Y))(W-Y)\|_{\infty,2}\le L\|W-Y\|_{\infty,2}.$$ Apply [F3] to each block and take the maximum. This gives $\|F(W)-F(Y)\|_{\infty,2}\le L\|W-Y\|_{\infty,2}$ using only the derivative bound on the ball. Hence [F2] applies with its invariant-ball hypotheses and the selected root exists uniquely. [given, F2, F3]

actualproofparagraphs.1.1: Let $Y,W$ belong to the invariant ball. Its convexity puts $Y+t(W-Y)$ in the ball for $0\le t\le1$. review_basis.full_actual_interface:
Let $K$ be a compact set of base points $(t,x)$ in a selected branch chart from [[thm-index-one-dae-implicit-function-reduction]], and put $z_*=\psi(t,x)$. Suppose $g(t,x,\cdot)$ is $C^2$ on $B(z_*,\rho)$ for every $(t,x)\in K$. Let $G_*(t,x)=g_z(t,x,\psi(t,x))$. Assume common constants $\gamma>0$, $\Lambda\ge0$, and $\rho>0$ satisfy

$$
\|G_*(t,x)v\|_2\ge\gamma\|v\|_2\quad(v\in\mathbb R^m),\qquad \|g_z(t,x,z)-G_*(t,x)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\Lambda\|z-\psi(t,x)\|_2
$$

for every $(t,x)\in K$ and $z\in B(\psi(t,x),\rho)$; if $\Lambda>0$, assume $\rho\le\gamma/(\sqrt m\,\Lambda)$. Then, uniformly for all such base points and candidates,

$$
\|z-z_*\|_2\le \frac{2}{\gamma}\|g(t,x,z)\|_2.
$$

The estimate is local: it applies only to candidates in the specified branch ball and does not turn a residual into a global branch or uniqueness certificate.

Fix $n,m\ge1$, constants $0<a\le b<\infty$, $C>0$, and $0<\gamma_{\min}\le\gamma_{\max}<\infty$. Suppose every stored pair in a limited-memory BFGS state satisfies
$$ a\|s_i\|_2^2\le s_i^Ty_i\le b\|s_i\|_2^2, \qquad \frac{\|y_i\|_2^2}{s_i^Ty_i}\le C, $$
and each base scale satisfies $\gamma_{\min}\le\gamma\le\gamma_{\max}$. Then the implicit SPD matrix $H_k$ represented by the two-loop recursion of [[alg-lbfgs-two-loop-with-curvature-filter]] has uniform bounds
$$ \underline\lambda I\preceq H_k\preceq\overline\lambda I, \quad T:=\frac n{\gamma_{\min}}+mC,\quad r:=\min\{1,a/T\},\quad D:=\gamma_{\max}^{-n}r^m, \quad \underline\lambda:=\frac1T,\quad \overline\lambda:=\frac{T^{n-1}}{D}. $$
Here $A\preceq B$ means $z^TAz\le z^TBz$ for all $z$. If the stored list is nonempty, the usual scale $(s_{\rm last}^Ty_{\rm last})/\|y_{\rm last}\|_2^2$ lies in $[1/C,b/a^2]$.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
For $m,n\ge0$, the polynomials of [[def-legendre-polynomial-family-and-l2-pairing]] satisfy
$$\int_{-1}^1P_n(x)P_m(x)\,dx=\frac{2}{2n+1}\,\delta_{mn}, \qquad \int_{-1}^1(1-x^2)P_n'(x)P_m'(x)\,dx=\frac{2n(n+1)}{2n+1}\,\delta_{mn},$$
where $\delta_{mn}=1$ if $m=n$ and $0$ otherwise. Each $P_n$ has degree $n$ and nonzero leading coefficient, so $P_0,\ldots,P_N$ form a basis of polynomials of degree at most $N$.

where $\delta_{mn}=1$ if $m=n$ and $0$ otherwise. Each $P_n$ has degree $n$ and nonzero leading coefficient, so $P_0,\ldots,P_N$ form a basis of polynomials of degree at most $N$.

proofparagraphs.text: The leading term of $(x^2-1)^n$ is $x^{2n}$; differentiating it $n$ times gives $(2n)!/n!$ times $x^n$ by [F3]. All other terms have lower degree after differentiation. Therefore $P_n$ has degree $n$ and leading coefficient $\kappa_n=(2n)!/(2^n(n!)^2)>0$. The distinct degrees imply the family $P_0,\ldots,P_N$ is linearly independent and spans every polynomial of degree at most $N$, by successive elimination of leading terms. [F1, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

actualproofparagraphs.4.1: Put $J_n=\int_{-1}^1(1-x^2)^n dx$. Then $J_0=2$. For $n\ge1$, the endpoint values of $x(1-x^2)^n$ are zero, so integrating its derivative gives $0=J_n-2n(J_{n-1}-J_n),\qquad J_n=\frac{2n}{2n+1}J_{n-1}.$ Induction yields $J_n=2^{2n+1}(n!)^2/(2n+1)!$. Substituting this and $\kappa_n$ from step 2.1 into step 3.1 gives $\int P_n^2=2/(2n+1)$. Together with step 1.1 this proves the first orthogonality formula, including $n=0$. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, induction, algebra]
actualproofparagraphs.5.1: When $n=0$, $P_0=1$ and $Q_0=-((1-x^2)P_0')'=0$, so $Q_0=0\cdot P_0$. Now take $n\ge1$ and define $Q_n=-((1-x^2)P_n')'$. Its leading term is $n(n+1)\kappa_nx^n$, so $Q_n-n(n+1)P_n$ has degree less than $n$. For any polynomial $q$ of degree less than $n$, two integrations by parts give $\int_{-1}^1Q_nq=\int_{-1}^1(1-x^2)P_n'q'=-\int_{-1}^1P_n((1-x^2)q')'=0,$ where both boundary terms vanish because of the factor $1-x^2$, and the last polynomial paired with $P_n$ has degree less than $n$, so step 1.1 applies. Therefore $Q_n-n(n+1)P_n$ is a lower-degree polynomial orthogonal to every lower-degree polynomial. Expand it in the basis from step 2.1; the first formula and the positive norms in step 4.1 force every coefficient to be zero. Thus $Q_n=n(n+1)P_n$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 4.1, algebra]

Let $a,b\in C^3(U,\mathbb R^d)$ on an open set and let $K_0\subset K\subset U$, where $K_0$ is compact and $K$ is compact and convex. Assume the exact subflows and their compositions from $K_0$ remain in $K$ for all sufficiently small $h>0$, and the fields and derivatives through order three are bounded on $K$. Uniformly for $y\in K_0$,
$$L_h(y)-\Phi_{a+b}^h(y)=\frac{h^2}{2}[a,b](y)+O(h^3),$$
and the Strang expansion, pointwise in $y$, is
$$S_h(y)-\Phi_{a+b}^h(y)=-\frac{h^3}{24}[a,[a,b]](y)-\frac{h^3}{12}[b,[a,b]](y)+o(h^3).$$
The Strang defect is also uniformly $O(h^3)$ on $K_0$. The maps and bracket use [[def-exact-split-flows-lie-strang-and-bracket]]; the claim is finite-dimensional.

actualproofparagraphs.3.1: For any $C^2$ scalar $q$, the chain rule gives $[L_a,L_b]q=D^2q(a,b)+Dq\,Db\,a-D^2q(b,a)-Dq\,Da\,b=Dq\,(Db\,a-Da\,b),$ where [F4] cancels the Hessian terms. Thus $[X,Y]q=L_{[a,b]}q$. Applying this to each coordinate function in step 2.1 gives the stated Lie map expansion. [F1, F4, step 2.1, algebra]
actualproofparagraphs.4.1: Step 3.1 also applies with the second field equal to $[a,b]$, which is $C^2$ under the $C^3$ hypotheses. Hence $[X,[X,Y]]=L_{[a,[a,b]]}$ and $[Y,[X,Y]]=L_{[b,[a,b]]}$. Applying step 3.2 to each coordinate yields the stated Strang coefficient and pointwise $o(h^3)$ remainder. The uniform $O(h^3)$ defect follows already from the uniform degree-two remainder in step 1.1 and the equality of all coefficients through degree two. [F1, step 1.1, step 3.1, step 3.2, algebra] ∎

Let $p\ge1$ be an integer, $T>0$, $h=T/N\le h_0\le1$, and $t_n=nh$. The state dimension $d$ and parameter dimension $m$ are fixed. All vector norms are Euclidean and all matrix norms are their induced operator norms; gradients are columns.

Consider the continuous objective
$$J(\theta)=\phi(u(T,\theta),\theta)+\int_0^T\ell(t,u(t,\theta),\theta)\,dt,$$
and the actual finite graph
$$x_{n+1}=\Psi_n(x_n,\theta),\qquad J_h(\theta)=\phi_h(x_N,\theta)+\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}L_n(x_n,\theta).$$
Assume the hypotheses of the continuous flow-tangent and adjoint-gradient results hold on a common tube. Write $\Phi_n(x,\theta)$ for the exact flow from $t_n$ to $t_{n+1}$ and
$$K_n(x,\theta)=\int_{t_n}^{t_{n+1}}\ell(t,u(t;t_n,x,\theta),\theta)\,dt.$$
These exact maps and the actual numerical maps are $C^1$ on open neighborhoods of the admitted state and parameter sets. For every relevant $n$, all states $x_n,u(t_n)$ and the segment joining them belong to a convex admitted state set. All estimates below hold uniformly on those sets and a fixed parameter neighborhood, independently of $N,n$.

actualproofparagraphs.3.2: At the terminal node, the difference of adjoint seeds is at most $Dh^p$. Subtract the two backward recurrences, splitting $A_h^Tp_h-A_e^Tp_e=A_h^T(p_h-p_e)+(A_h-A_e)^Tp_e$. The Euclidean operator norm of a transpose equals that of the matrix. For every finite-dimensional Euclidean vector $v$, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $\|v\|=\sup_{\|w\|\le1}|w^Tv|$: if $v\ne0$, equality is attained at $w=v/\|v\|$, while for $v=0$ both sides vanish, including in dimension zero. source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$ with Jacobian $J=DF$. Take $x_0\in U$ such that $A:=J(x_0)$ is invertible, and let $\beta>0$ be any bound with $\|A^{-1}\|_{\rm op}\le\beta$. Suppose $\epsilon:=\|F(x_0)\|_2>0$, set $r:=2\beta\epsilon$, and assume the open ball $B_2(x_0,2r)$ lies in $U$ and

$$\|J(x)-J(y)\|_{\rm op}\le L\|x-y\|_2\qquad(x,y\in B_2(x_0,2r))$$

for some $L\ge0$ with $\beta Lr\le\tfrac12$. Then $F$ has exactly one zero $x_*$ in the closed ball $\overline B_2(x_0,r)$, and

$$\|x_*-x_0\|_2\le2\beta\|F(x_0)\|_2.$$

If $F(x_0)=0$, then $x_0$ itself is a zero; this separate case makes no local uniqueness assertion.

Assume $B_\infty(x_0,2r)\subset U$ and

$$\|DF(x)-DF(y)\|_\infty\le L\|x-y\|_\infty\qquad(x,y\in B_\infty(x_0,2r))$$

for some $L\ge0$ with $\beta Lr\le\tfrac12$. Then $F$ has exactly one zero $x_*$ in $\overline B_\infty(x_0,r)$, and

$$\|x_*-x_0\|_\infty\le2\beta\|F(x_0)\|_\infty.$$

$$a(v_h,w_h):=\sum_K\int_KA(x)v_h'(x)w_h'(x)\,dx,\qquad a_h(v_h,w_h):=\sum_Kh_KA(m_K)v_h'|_Kw_h'|_K,$$

where $m_K$ is the cell midpoint and the cell derivatives are constant. Then

$$|a(v_h,w_h)-a_h(v_h,w_h)|\le\frac{h^2}{24}\|A''\|_{L^\infty(0,1)}\|v_h'\|_{L^2(0,1)}\|w_h'\|_{L^2(0,1)}.$$

source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: An induced Euclidean perturbation norm below one gives invertibility of identity minus the matrix and the reciprocal-one-minus-q norm bound.
selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 Since $\|{-E}\|_2=\|E\|_2\le q<1$, [F1] gives that $T=(I-E)^{-1}$ exists. [given, F1]

2.1 Put $S_N=\sum_{k=0}^N E^k$. By induction and [F2], $\|E^k\|_2\le q^k$, so $\|S_N\|_2\le\sum_{k=0}^Nq^k=(1-q^{N+1})/(1-q)$ by [F3]. The finite identity $(I-E)S_N=I-E^{N+1}$, multiplied on the left by $T$, gives $S_N=T-TE^{N+1}$ and hence $T=S_N+TE^{N+1}$. By the triangle inequality from [F3] and submultiplicativity [F2], $(1-q^{N+1})\|T\|_2\le\|S_N\|_2\le(1-q^{N+1})/(1-q)$. Since $q^{N+1}<1$, division gives $\|T\|_2\le(1-q)^{-1}$. This proves the inverse norm bound without taking a limit of matrices. [given, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $S\in C^1([0,T];\mathbb R^{d\times m})$ and $p\in C^1([0,T];\mathbb R^d)$ satisfy $S'=A S+B$ and $p'=-A^T p-g$, where $A,B,g$ are continuous and have compatible dimensions. Then
$$p(T)^T S(T)-p(0)^T S(0)=\int_0^T\bigl(-g(t)^T S(t)+p(t)^T B(t)\bigr)\,dt.$$

actualproofparagraphs.1.1: Write $p^T S=\sum_{i=1}^d p_i S_{i,\cdot}$. By [F2] coordinatewise, $(p^TS)'=(p')^TS+p^TS'$. Substituting the two equations yields $(-A^Tp-g)^TS+p^T(AS+B)=-g^TS+p^TB$, because $(A^Tp)^TS=p^TAS$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

source_evidence.case_anchor: No invertibility ofA is assumed: Proof step 1.1 cancels the twoAS terms by transposition alone, so a singular or zeroA remains admissible.

actualproofparagraphs.1.1: Write $p^T S=\sum_{i=1}^d p_i S_{i,\cdot}$. By [F2] coordinatewise, $(p^TS)'=(p')^TS+p^TS'$. Substituting the two equations yields $(-A^Tp-g)^TS+p^T(AS+B)=-g^TS+p^TB$, because $(A^Tp)^TS=p^TAS$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]
actualproofparagraphs.2.1: The right-hand side in step 1.1 is continuous and hence integrable. Apply [F3] to the scalar function $p^TS$ and integrate step 1.1 over $[0,T]$. This gives the stated endpoint identity. [F3, step 1.1] ∎

$$\|(u-I_hu)'\|_{L^2(0,1)}\le h\|u''\|_{L^\infty(0,1)}.$$

If $u(0)=u(1)=0$, then $I_hu$ also vanishes at both endpoints.

Let $E=\mathbb R^n$ with its Euclidean norm, let $D\subseteq E$, and let
$T:D\to E$ satisfy $\|T(p)-T(p')\|_2\le\|p-p'\|_2$ for all $p,p'\in D$.
For every $y\in E$ there exists $q\in E$ such that
$$\|q-T(p)\|_2\le\|y-p\|_2\qquad(p\in D).$$
Equivalently, one value can be added at the new input $y$ without violating
the Lipschitz constant $1$.

If $0$ were not in the convex hull of the finitely many gradients $2(q_0-Tp_i)$, $i\in I$, project $0$ onto that compact convex hull using [F4]. The projection vector $v\ne0$ obeys $\langle v,2(q_0-Tp_i)\rangle\ge\|v\|_2^2$ for each $i\in I$, by the variational inequality. For sufficiently small $\epsilon>0$, every active $h_i(q_0-\epsilon v)$ decreases strictly; the finitely many inactive terms have a strict gap below $H(q_0)$ and remain below it by continuity. This contradicts minimality. Therefore there are weights $\alpha_i\ge0$, supported on $I$, with $\sum_i\alpha_i=1$ and $q_0=\sum_i\alpha_i T p_i$. [A1, F1, F4, step 1.1, contradiction, algebra]

Otherwise consider any finite nonempty list $p_1,\ldots,p_m\in D$ and set $$h_i(q)=\|q-Tp_i\|_2^2-\|y-p_i\|_2^2,\qquad H(q)=\max_{1\le i\le m}h_i(q).$$ The continuous function $H$ is coercive because each $h_i(q)\to+\infty$ as $\|q\|_2\to\infty$. A nonempty sublevel $\{H\le H(0)\}$ is closed and bounded, hence compact by [F2]; [F3] gives a global minimizer $q_0$ of $H$. [A1, given, F1, F2, F3, construct]

2.1 Let $I=\{i:h_i(q_0)=H(q_0)\}$ be the nonempty active set. If $0$ were not in the convex hull of the finitely many gradients $2(q_0-Tp_i)$, $i\in I$, project $0$ onto that compact convex hull using [F4]. The projection vector $v\ne0$ obeys $\langle v,2(q_0-Tp_i)\rangle\ge\|v\|_2^2$ for each $i\in I$, by the variational inequality. For sufficiently small $\epsilon>0$, every active $h_i(q_0-\epsilon v)$ decreases strictly; the finitely many inactive terms have a strict gap below $H(q_0)$ and remain below it by continuity. This contradicts minimality. Therefore there are weights $\alpha_i\ge0$, supported on $I$, with $\sum_i\alpha_i=1$ and $q_0=\sum_i\alpha_i T p_i$. [A1, F1, F4, step 1.1, contradiction, algebra]

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Let $E=\mathbb R^n$ with its Euclidean norm, let $D\subseteq E$, and let
$T:D\to E$ satisfy $\|T(p)-T(p')\|_2\le\|p-p'\|_2$ for all $p,p'\in D$.
For every $y\in E$ there exists $q\in E$ such that
$$\|q-T(p)\|_2\le\|y-p\|_2\qquad(p\in D).$$
Equivalently, one value can be added at the new input $y$ without violating
the Lipschitz constant $1$.

literal_source_anchor.description: the reflected convolution construction on the given evolution triple
literal_source_anchor.quote: Let $\eta_\epsilon$ be a nonnegative smooth mollifier of mass one, supported in $(-\epsilon,\epsilon)$, and convolve the reflected functions in time. On a neighborhood of $[0,T]$, $u_\epsilon=\eta_\epsilon*u$ is smooth with values in $V$ by [F2]. Testing the reflected weak derivative identity against a fixed $v\in V$ and integrating by parts in the scalar variable gives $\langle u_\epsilon'(t),v\rangle=\int\langle g(s),v\rangle \eta_\epsilon(t-s)\,ds=\langle(\eta_\epsilon*g)(t),v\rangle$. The bounded inclusion $V\to V^*$ commutes with the Bochner integral by [F3], so $u_\epsilon'=\eta_\epsilon*g$ in $V^*$. [F1, F2, F3, step 3.1, construct]

literal_source_anchor.description: the real evolution-space identities for every0<=s<=t<=T
literal_source_anchor.quote:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $(V,H,V^*)$ be the real evolution triple of
[[def-parabolic-evolution-triple-and-energy-space]], and let
$u,v\in W(0,T;V)$. Each has a unique representative in $C([0,T];H)$, and
for all $0\le s\le t\le T$,
$$\|u(t)\|_H^2-\|u(s)\|_H^2 =2\int_s^t\langle u'(r),u(r)\rangle_{V^*,V}\,dr,$$
$$(u(t),v(t))_H-(u(s),v(s))_H =\int_s^t\bigl(\langle u'(r),v(r)\rangle_{V^*,V} +\langle v'(r),u(r)\rangle_{V^*,V}\bigr)\,dr.$$
Writing $c_i=\|i:V\to H\|$, the trace obeys
$$\sup_{0\le t\le T}\|u(t)\|_H^2 \le \frac{c_i^2}{T}\|u\|_{L^2(0,T;V)}^2 +2\|u'\|_{L^2(0,T;V^*)}\|u\|_{L^2(0,T;V)}.$$

literal_source_anchor.description: the fixed-map and time-dependent product formulas
literal_source_anchor.quote:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $X$ be a separable real Hilbert space and $Y$ a real Hilbert space, and
let $u\in H^1(0,T;X)$ (meaning
$u,u'\in L^2(0,T;X)$ with distribution derivative). It has a unique
continuous representative on $[0,T]$. Let
$P\in\mathcal L(X,Y)$ be a fixed bounded linear map. Then
$Pu\in H^1(0,T;Y)$ and $(Pu)'=Pu'$.

If instead $P:[0,T]\to\mathcal L(X,Y)$ is continuously differentiable in
operator norm, then $P(t)u(t)\in H^1(0,T;Y)$ and
$$\frac{d}{dt}(P(t)u(t))=P'(t)u(t)+P(t)u'(t)\quad\text{a.e.}$$
In particular, a differentiable time-dependent Ritz comparison contributes
the term $P'(t)u(t)$ to its residual derivative.

literal_source_anchor.description: the explicit zero-trial-space branch
literal_source_anchor.quote: If $V_h=\{0\}$, define $R_hu=0$; the Ritz equation, uniqueness, and norm bound are immediate. Otherwise fix a finite ordered basis $(e_1,\ldots,e_m)$ of $V_h$. Form the square matrix $K_{ij}=a(e_j,e_i)$ and vector $b_i=a(u,e_i)$. If $Kc=0$ and $x=\sum_jc_je_j$, then $a(x,e_i)=0$ for each $i$, hence $a(x,x)=\sum_i c_i a(x,e_i)=0$. Coercivity [F2] gives $x=0$, so basis independence gives $c=0$. Thus $K$ has zero kernel and, being square, is invertible. Its unique solution $Kc=b$ defines the unique $R_hu$ satisfying [F1]. [F1, F2, given, construct]

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ and $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d\times\Theta$ be open, and let $f:D\to\mathbb R^d$ be continuously differentiable. Let $V_\theta\subseteq\Theta$ be open and $u_0:V_\theta\to\mathbb R^d$ be $C^1$. Assume there is a bounded convex open set $O\subset D$ with compact closure in $D$ such that for every $\theta\in V_\theta$ the unique solution of $u'=f(t,u,\theta)$, $u(0)=u_0(\theta)$, exists on $[0,T]$, and all triples $(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)$ lie in $O$. Then $\theta\mapsto u_\theta$ is $C^1$ as a map to $C([0,T];\mathbb R^d)$. For any $\theta_0\in V_\theta$, its tangent matrix $S(t)=D_\theta u_\theta(t)|_{\theta=\theta_0}$ is the unique solution of
$$S'(t)=D_u f(t,u_{\theta_0}(t),\theta_0)S(t)+D_\theta f(t,u_{\theta_0}(t),\theta_0),\qquad S(0)=D u_0(\theta_0).$$
The result is local to the stated common compact tube and claims no differentiability outside it.

actualproofparagraphs.1.2: Put $A(t)=D_u f(t,u_{\theta_0}(t),\theta_0)$ and let $B_j(t)$ be column $j$ of $D_\theta f(t,u_{\theta_0}(t),\theta_0)$. For each parameter coordinate $j$, the augmented vector $Z_j=(S_{\cdot j},1)$ solves the homogeneous linear system $$Z_j'(t)=\begin{pmatrix}A(t)&B_j(t)\\0&0\end{pmatrix}Z_j(t),\qquad Z_j(0)=\begin{pmatrix}D u_0(\theta_0)_{\cdot j}\\1\end{pmatrix}.$$ Embed $Z_j(0)$ as one column of a square $(d+1)\times(d+1)$ initial matrix, with all other columns zero. The unique linear matrix solution supplied by [F5] has that vector solution as the selected column. Thus the tangent equation has a unique solution for each of the finitely many columns. [A1, F5, construct]

source_evidence.case_anchor: The tangent matrix need not be invertible. Proof step 1.2 constructs each column from a linear inhomogeneous equation, and no state Jacobian inverse is used.

selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 For each positive-dimensional proximal space, the optimality condition [F2] and extended-real subgradient definition [F3] give the relevant inequality. If a proximal space is zero-dimensional, [F6] says its only point is $0$; its update and test point are both $0$, so the same inequality is equality in that coordinate. Therefore in every dimension the two inequalities are $$g^*(y)-g^*(y^{k+1})\ge\left\langle\frac{y^k-y^{k+1}}\sigma+K\bar x^k,y-y^{k+1}\right\rangle,$$ $$f(x)-f(x^{k+1})\ge\left\langle\frac{x^k-x^{k+1}}\tau-K^*y^{k+1},x-x^{k+1}\right\rangle.$$ The identity $-\langle a-b,c-b\rangle=(\|c-a\|^2-\|c-b\|^2-\|b-a\|^2)/2$ applied to the primal and dual displacement terms gives the two distance differences $E_k-E_{k+1}-X_{k+1}$ and $E_k-E_{k+1}-Y_{k+1}$ in their respective coordinates. The bilinear terms from the primal inequality and the gap expand as $\langle y^{k+1},K(x-x^{k+1})\rangle+\langle Kx^{k+1},y\rangle-\langle Kx,y^{k+1}\rangle=\langle Kx^{k+1},y-y^{k+1}\rangle$. Adding the dual update term $\langle K\bar x^k,y^{k+1}-y\rangle$ gives $\langle K(\bar x^k-x^{k+1}),y^{k+1}-y\rangle$ in the upper bound for $G_{k+1}$. Moving this term to the other side yields $$E_k\ge G_{k+1}+E_{k+1}+X_{k+1}+Y_{k+1}+\langle K(x^{k+1}-\bar x^k),y^{k+1}-y\rangle,$$ where $G_{k+1}=\Phi(x^{k+1},y)-\Phi(x,y^{k+1})$, $E_j=\|x-x^j\|^2/(2\tau)+\|y-y^j\|^2/(2\sigma)$, $X_j=\|x^j-x^{j-1}\|^2/(2\tau)$, and $Y_j=\|y^j-y^{j-1}\|^2/(2\sigma)$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F5, F6, algebra]

$$
