source_evidence.full_current_interface:
At a phase-fixed periodic point $x_*$ with period $T$, let $M=D_x\phi_T(x_*)$, let $f_*=f(x_*)\ne0$, and let $c=D\psi(x_*)$ for the affine phase $\psi(x)=c^\top(x-x_{\rm ref})$. The derivative of the phase-bordered shooting residual is
$$ J=\begin{bmatrix}M-I_d&f_*\\c^\top&0\end{bmatrix}. $$
It is invertible if and only if $1$ is an algebraically simple eigenvalue of $M$ and $c^\top f_*\ne0$. In the simple case choose real left/right eigenvectors $w,f_*$ with $w^\top f_*=1$, put $Q=I-f_*w^\top$ and $W=\ker w^\top$, and let $K_W=\|((M-I_d)|_W)^{-1}\|_{2\to2}$. All vector and matrix norms below are Euclidean and induced Euclidean norms, and the product norm on $(u,\tau)\in\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R$ is Euclidean. Then
$$ \|J^{-1}\|_{2\to2}\le K_W\|Q\|_2+\|w\|_2+ \frac{\|f_*\|_2\bigl(1+\|c\|_2K_W\|Q\|_2\bigr)}{|c^\top f_*|}. $$
The period column is the exact time-sensitivity $f_*$.
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: The exact time-sensitivity column and transverse affine phase make the shooting border invertible exactly under a simple neutral multiplier, with an explicit inverse bound.
selected_current_proof_blocks: 2.1 Suppose $1$ is algebraically simple. Then [F4] implies that the complex eigenspace for eigenvalue $1$ is one-dimensional. By [F2] its spanning eigenvector $f_*$ is real, so the real kernel is $\mathbb R f_*$ and rank-nullity gives $\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb R}(M-I_d)=d-1$. Choose a real basis $v_1,\ldots,v_{d-1}$ of $\operatorname{range}(M-I_d)$. The $d-1$ real linear forms $w\mapsto v_j^\top w$ are independent: if a linear combination vanishes for every $w$, then the row $\bigl(\sum_j a_jv_j\bigr)^\top$ is zero, so $\sum_j a_jv_j=0$ and basis independence forces every coefficient $a_j$ to vanish. Rank-nullity therefore gives a nonzero real $w_0$ with $v_j^\top w_0=0$ for every $j$. Thus $w_0^\top(M-I_d)=0$. It is a compatible left eigenvector with the real right eigenvector $f_*$, so [F3], applied over $\mathbb C$, gives $w_0^\top f_*\ne0$. This pairing is real; normalize $w=w_0/(w_0^\top f_*)$, so $w$ is real, $w^\top M=w^\top$, and $w^\top f_*=1$. For $Q=I-f_*w^\top$ and $W=\ker w^\top$, one has $Qf_*=0$, $Q|_W=I_W$, and $QM=M-f_*w^\top M=M-f_*w^\top=M-Mf_*w^\top=MQ$. Hence $Q$ is the projection onto $W$, $M$ preserves $W$, and $M-I_d$ maps $W$ into $W$. Its restriction to $W$ is injective: a kernel vector there would be an eigenvector independent of $f_*$, contrary to simplicity. Since $W$ is finite dimensional, [F7] makes the restriction invertible. For $J(u,\tau)=(r,s)$, left multiplication of the first row by $w^\top$ gives $\tau=w^\top r$. Write $u=u_W+\alpha f_*$ with $u_W\in W$; applying $Q$ to the first row and using its commutation with $M$ gives $u_W=((M-I_d)|_W)^{-1}Qr$, and the phase row gives $\alpha=(s-c^\top u_W)/(c^\top f_*)$. Thus nonzero $c^\top f_*$ gives a unique solution for every right-hand side, so $J$ is invertible. source_evidence.full_current_interface: Let $v_0,\ldots,v_{m-1}\in\mathbb Q+i\mathbb Q$, $m\ge3$, be the cyclically ordered vertices of a simple strictly convex polygon whose edges are traversed counterclockwise. Let $P$ be its filled convex hull and let $\Gamma$ be the concatenation of its oriented edges. For every $z\notin\Gamma$, the winding number $n(\Gamma,z)$ is $1$ if $z\in\operatorname{int}P$ and $0$ if $z\notin P$.
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: A counterclockwise simple strictly convex rational polygon has winding one in its interior and zero outside its filled hull, excluding the contour itself.
selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 Fix an exterior point $q\notin P$. Compactness gives a nearest point $p\in P$. For every $u\in P$, convexity puts $p+t(u-p)$ in $P$ for $0\le t\le1$; minimality of $p$ gives $\|q-p\|_2^2\le\|q-p-t(u-p)\|_2^2$. Expanding, dividing by $t>0$, and letting $t\downarrow0$ yields $\langle q-p,u-p\rangle\le0$. Hence the ray $q+s(q-p)$, $s\ge0$, remains strictly in the separating half-plane and avoids $P$. Each exterior point can therefore be joined outside $P$ to a circle containing $P$ in its interior; that circle is connected, so $\mathbb C\setminus P$ is connected and unbounded. [given, construct]

3.1 Fix $z\in\operatorname{int}P$. Choose a ray from $z$ whose direction is not aimed at a vertex. Its intersection with the convex polygon is a bounded interval starting at $z$, so the ray exits at the interior $p$ of a single edge with directed tangent $v\ne0$. The polygon interior lies locally to the left of this positively oriented edge. Apply the orientation-preserving similarity $\rho(w)=\overline v(w-p)/|v|$, which sends $p$ to $0$ and the edge tangent to the positive real direction. For every $a\notin\Gamma$, put $c=\overline v/|v|$. Parametrizing the transformed contour and using [F1] gives $\int_{\rho\circ\Gamma}\frac{d\zeta}{\zeta-\rho(a)}=\int_\Gamma\frac{c\,dw}{c(w-a)}=\int_\Gamma\frac{dw}{w-a}$, so $n(\rho\circ\Gamma,\rho(a))=n(\Gamma,a)$. For sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0$, the points $\rho^{-1}(i\varepsilon)$ and $\rho^{-1}(-i\varepsilon)$ lie respectively on the interior and exterior local sides of the edge. Applying [F4] to $\rho\circ\Gamma$ gives $n(\rho\circ\Gamma,i\varepsilon)-n(\rho\circ\Gamma,-i\varepsilon)=1$; the just-proved invariance rewrites this as $n(\Gamma,\rho^{-1}(i\varepsilon))-n(\Gamma,\rho^{-1}(-i\varepsilon))=1$. The exterior-side index is zero by step 2.1. Thus an interior point near that edge has winding number one. [F1, F4, step 2.1, choose, algebra]

review_basis.full_actual_interface:
Let $B$ be the real symmetric positive-definite model matrix of
[[def-trust-region-quadratic-model-and-ratio]], with $n\ge1$, $g\in\mathbb R^n$,
and radius $\Delta>0$. There is a unique $p_N\in\mathbb R^n$ satisfying
$Bp_N=-g$. The [[alg-dogleg-trust-region-step]] procedure is well-defined on
this input and returns a feasible vector. If its boundary-intersection branch
is taken, the displayed scalar formula is the unique root $t\in(0,1)$ of
$\|p_C+t(p_N-p_C)\|_2^2=\Delta^2$. On a nonstationary input the
procedure performs one linear solve and, only on its boundary branch, one
scalar-root computation; it has no iteration loop.
review_basis.source_specific_focus: An SPD quadratic model has one Newton solution; dogleg returns Newton, Cauchy or its unique interior boundary-intersection parameter.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Every $P\in\mathcal P_r$ belongs to the admissible density domain
$\mathcal D_r$.

actualproofparagraphs.1.1: By [F2], choose a unitary eigenbasis of $P$ with real eigenvalues $\mu_j$. From $P^2=P$, each satisfies $\mu_j^2=\mu_j$, hence $\mu_j\in\{0,1\}$. Therefore every eigenvalue lies between $0$ and $1$, so for each $x$ the quadratic forms $x^*Px$ and $x^*(I-P)x$ are nonnegative. [given, F1, F2, algebra]
actualproofparagraphs.2.1: The matrix $P$ is Hermitian and has trace $r$ by [F1]; step 1.1 gives $0\preceq P\preceq I$. These are exactly the conditions in [F3], so $P\in\mathcal D_r$. [step 1.1, F1, F3] ∎

source_evidence.case_anchor: Proof step 1.1 gives every projector eigenvalue exactly0 or1; proof step 2.1 therefore includes both spectral endpoints in the semidefinite density inequalities.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $C$ be a compact subset of the regular phase manifold whose configuration projection lies in a compact regular chart. For each $(q,p)\in C$, the two scaled RATTLE equations in [[def-regular-classical-rattle-step-map]] have unique local roots in neighborhoods of
$$\lambda_0=\mu_0=\frac12A(q)^{-1}\bigl(D^2c(q)[v,v]-J(q)M^{-1}\nabla V(q)\bigr),\qquad v=M^{-1}p.$$
In local phase coordinates the position root depends smoothly on $(h,q,p)$, and the momentum root depends smoothly on $(h,q,p,\lambda)$ when the position multiplier is treated as a parameter near its selected root. The local branches agree on overlaps after shrinking their neighborhoods. A finite cover of $C$ therefore gives a common $h_0(C)>0$ for $|h|<h_0(C)$; the derivatives of each fixed finite order are uniformly bounded on this cover, and the two multiplier Jacobians remain uniformly invertible there. The exact position roots can also be kept in an ambient neighborhood of the compact regular configuration projection where $J$ has full row rank, so their constrained positions remain in $Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$. At $h=0$ both Jacobians equal $-A(q)$.

proofparagraphs.text: Put $v=M^{-1}p$ and $w(\lambda)=-M^{-1}(\frac12\nabla V(q)+J(q)^T\lambda)$. Then $q_1=q+hv+h^2w(\lambda)$. Since $c(q)=0$ and $J(q)v=0$, [F3] extends $h^{-2}c(q_1)$ smoothly, with value $F_q(0,q,p,\lambda)=\frac12D^2c(q)[v,v]-\frac12J(q)M^{-1}\nabla V(q)-A(q)\lambda$. Its $\lambda$ derivative is $-A(q)$, which is invertible. Since $A$ is smooth and invertible, $A^{-1}=\operatorname{adj}(A)/\det A$ is smooth locally, so the center $\lambda_0$ varies smoothly with the phase input. Thus [F4] gives the unique local position multiplier branch at that center. [F1, F2, F3, F4, algebra]

The branch equations are smooth in local phase coordinates, and $A^{-1}$ is uniformly bounded on the compact configuration projection of $C$. Since $J$ has full row rank on that compact projection, continuity gives an ambient neighborhood where it remains full row rank. Around each point of $C$, shrink the phase and multiplier neighborhoods so both roots remain in common IFT uniqueness neighborhoods on overlaps and exact $q_1$ remains in this regular neighborhood. These neighborhoods cover $C$; compactness gives a finite subcover and the minimum of their positive step radii is a common $h_0(C)$. The smooth branch derivatives are bounded on smaller compact neighborhoods covering $C$ for $|h|\le h_0(C)$, and continuity of the multiplier Jacobians preserves uniform invertibility after a further shrink. [F2, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, choose] ∎

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, let $c:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be smooth (that is, $C^\infty$) with $1\le m<d$, let $M$ be a constant symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix, and let $V:U\to\mathbb R$ be smooth. A **holonomic constraint** is the position condition $c(q)=0$. Write $J(q)=Dc(q)$, let $Q=\{q\in U:c(q)=0\}$, and define its regular part by $Q_{\mathrm{reg}}=\{q\in Q:\operatorname{rank}J(q)=m\}$. For $q\in Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$, $A(q)=J(q)M^{-1}J(q)^T$ is positive definite. On a compact regular chart $K\subset Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$, $A^{-1}$ is uniformly bounded: $\sup_{q\in K}\|A(q)^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}<\infty$.

A position-momentum pair $(q,p)$ is **consistent** when $q\in Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$ and $J(q)M^{-1}p=0$. The **regular constrained phase manifold** is
$$\mathcal M=\{(q,p)\in U\times\mathbb R^d:c(q)=0,\ J(q)M^{-1}p=0,\ q\in Q_{\mathrm{reg}}\}.$$
The ambient canonical two-form is $\omega_0=\sum_{i=1}^d dq_i\wedge dp_i$; its restriction to $\mathcal M$ is denoted $\omega_{\mathcal M}$.

For $v=M^{-1}p$, the constrained Hamilton equations are
$$\dot q=v,\qquad \dot p=-\nabla V(q)-J(q)^T\lambda,$$
with multiplier
$$\lambda=A(q)^{-1}\bigl(D^2c(q)[v,v]-J(q)M^{-1}\nabla V(q)\bigr).$$
Here $D^2c(q)[v,v]\in\mathbb R^m$ has components $v^TD^2c_j(q)v$. This multiplier is the one that keeps both $c(q)=0$ and $J(q)M^{-1}p=0$ satisfied.

Fix a compact regular configuration chart from [[def-regular-holonomic-phase-space-and-dynamics]] and a compact momentum set. Use the Euclidean norm on $\mathbb R^{2d}$ for phase-state differences. Each point of its consistent phase set has a neighborhood $U_j$ with a smooth retraction $\Pi_j:U_j\to\mathcal M$ such that $\Pi_j$ is the identity on $U_j\cap\mathcal M$ and
$$\|\Pi_j(q,p)-(q,p)\|\le C_j\bigl(\|c(q)\|_2+\|J(q)M^{-1}p\|_2\bigr).$$
A finite number of these neighborhoods cover the compact phase set, so one constant works for all of them. In particular, residuals of sizes $O(h^4)$ and $O(h^3)$ admit a consistent restoration at distance $O(h^3)$, uniformly on the chart.

proofparagraphs.text: At a point of the compact regular chart $K\subset Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$, permute coordinates as $q=(x,y)$ so $D_yc$ is an invertible $m\times m$ block. Apply [F2] for each finite regularity order; uniqueness makes these graphs agree locally, so the graph $y=\psi(x)$ is smooth. Write $\phi(x)=(x,\psi(x))$ and $T(x)=D\phi(x)$. Since $J(\phi(x))T(x)=0$ and both kernels have dimension $d-m$, $\operatorname{im}T=\ker J$. [F1, F2, algebra]

After shrinking to a convex coordinate neighborhood, $B(x)=D_yc(x,\psi(x))$ remains invertible and $\|B(x)^{-1}(D_yc(x,y)-B(x))\|\le\frac12$. Set $R_x(y)=c(x,y)-B(x)(y-\psi(x))$. Then $R_x(\psi(x))=0$ and the derivative of $B(x)^{-1}R_x$ has norm at most $\frac12$. The mean-value inequality [F4] gives $\|B(x)^{-1}R_x(y)\|\le\frac12\|y-\psi(x)\|$. Since $B^{-1}c=(y-\psi)+B^{-1}R_x(y)$, it follows that $\|q-\phi(x)\|=\|y-\psi(x)\|\le 2\|B(x)^{-1}\|\,\|c(q)\|$. Compactness makes the constant uniform on a finite chart cover. [F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

Since $J(\phi(x))T(x)=0$ and both kernels have dimension $d-m$, $\operatorname{im}T=\ker J$. [F1, F2, algebra]

For $\bar q=\phi(x)$, put $G=T^TMT$ and define $\bar p=MTG^{-1}T^Tp$. Positive definiteness of $M$ and injectivity of $T$ make $G$ invertible; its smooth entries and positive determinant give a smooth inverse by $G^{-1}=\operatorname{adj}(G)/\det G$. Then $J(\bar q)M^{-1}\bar p=0$ and $T^T(p-\bar p)=0$. Since $\ker T^T$ and $\operatorname{im}J(\bar q)^T$ both have dimension $m$ and the latter is contained in the former, $p-\bar p=J(\bar q)^T\eta$ for a unique $\eta$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Fix a compact regular configuration chart from [[def-regular-holonomic-phase-space-and-dynamics]] and a compact momentum set. Use the Euclidean norm on $\mathbb R^{2d}$ for phase-state differences. Each point of its consistent phase set has a neighborhood $U_j$ with a smooth retraction $\Pi_j:U_j\to\mathcal M$ such that $\Pi_j$ is the identity on $U_j\cap\mathcal M$ and
$$\|\Pi_j(q,p)-(q,p)\|\le C_j\bigl(\|c(q)\|_2+\|J(q)M^{-1}p\|_2\bigr).$$
A finite number of these neighborhoods cover the compact phase set, so one constant works for all of them. In particular, residuals of sizes $O(h^4)$ and $O(h^3)$ admit a consistent restoration at distance $O(h^3)$, uniformly on the chart.

Then $R_x(\psi(x))=0$ and the derivative of $B(x)^{-1}R_x$ has norm at most $\frac12$. The mean-value inequality [F4] gives $\|B(x)^{-1}R_x(y)\|\le\frac12\|y-\psi(x)\|$. [F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

source_evidence.fullclaim: Under the hypotheses of [[def-regular-holonomic-phase-space-and-dynamics]], let $Q_{\mathrm{reg}}=\{q\in Q:\operatorname{rank}J(q)=m\}$. It is a smooth manifold of dimension $d-m$. Choose a local configuration chart $\phi:O\subseteq\mathbb R^{d-m}\to Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$ and write $T=D\phi$, $G=T^TMT$. The cotangent coordinates $\pi=T^Tp$ identify the part of $\mathcal M$ over this chart locally with $T^*Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$: the unique consistent ambient momentum representing $\pi$ is $p=MTG^{-1}\pi$. In these coordinates the restricted canonical one-form $p^Tdq$ is $\pi^Tdx$, so the restricted two-form is $\omega_{\mathcal M}=\sum_{j=1}^{d-m}dx_j\wedge d\pi_j$. It is closed and nondegenerate, hence is symplectic on the regular phase manifold.

proofparagraphs.text: At any $q\in Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$, full row rank of $J(q)$ gives a permutation of coordinates $q=(x,y)$ for which the $m\times m$ block $D_yc(q)$ is invertible. Apply [F2] to the smooth map $c$ for each finite $k\ge1$. The resulting local graphs agree with the unique $C^1$ graph on overlaps, so that graph is $C^k$ locally for every $k$ and hence smooth. Thus locally $Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is $y=\psi(x)$; $\phi(x)=(x,\psi(x))$ parametrizes it, and $D\phi$ has rank $d-m$ with image $\ker J$. [F1, F2, construct]

Define $G(x)=D\phi(x)^TMD\phi(x)$. For every nonzero $\xi$, $D\phi\,\xi\ne0$ and $\xi^TG(x)\xi=(D\phi\,\xi)^TM(D\phi\,\xi)>0$, so $G$ is invertible. Its entries are smooth, and $G^{-1}=\operatorname{adj}(G)/\det G$ is smooth because $\det G>0$. For a cotangent coordinate $\pi\in\mathbb R^{d-m}$, put $p=MD\phi\,G^{-1}\pi$. Then $JM^{-1}p=JD\phi\,G^{-1}\pi=0$ and $D\phi^Tp=G G^{-1}\pi=\pi$. Conversely, if $JM^{-1}p=0$, then $M^{-1}p=D\phi\,\xi$ for a unique $\xi$, and $D\phi^Tp=G\xi$; hence the displayed formula gives the unique ambient $p$ representing $\pi$. Both this map and its inverse $(q,p)\mapsto(x,D\phi(x)^Tp)$ are smooth, so $(x,\pi)\mapsto(\phi(x),p)$ is a local diffeomorphism from $T^*Q_{\mathrm{reg}}$ onto the part of $\mathcal M$ over this chart. [step 1.1, F1, algebra]

Let $d\ge1$, $h,\gamma>0$, and $J,\widetilde J\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$. Set $A=I_d-\gamma hJ$ and $\widetilde A=I_d-\gamma h\widetilde J$. If both matrices are invertible, then
$$\widetilde A^{-1}-A^{-1}=\gamma h\,\widetilde A^{-1}(\widetilde J-J)A^{-1}.$$
Consequently, if $\|A^{-1}\|_2\le K$ and $\|\widetilde A^{-1}\|_2\le\widetilde K$, then
$$\|\widetilde A^{-1}-A^{-1}\|_2\le\gamma hK\widetilde K\|\widetilde J-J\|_2.$$
Here the induced matrix norm is the one defined in [[lem-rosenbrock-shifted-matrix-invertibility-bound]].

Let $d\ge1$, $M\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$, and $x,b\in\mathbb R^d$ be stored real data. Use successful sequential left-to-right dot products and componentwise subtraction in the operationwise model of [[def-operationwise-real-complex-floating-point-model-with-sqrt-and-fma]], with unit roundoff $u>0$ and $du<1$. Put
$$\widehat v_i:=\operatorname{fl}\Bigl(\sum_{j<d}M_{ij}x_j\Bigr),\qquad \widehat r:=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat v-b),\qquad \gamma_d:=\frac{du}{1-du}.$$
For $\|M\|_F=(\sum_{i,j<d}M_{ij}^2)^{1/2}$, define
$$W:=\gamma_d\|M\|_F\|x\|_2+u(\|\widehat v\|_2+\|b\|_2).$$
Then
$$\|\widehat r-(Mx-b)\|_2\le W,\qquad \|Mx-b\|_2\le\|\widehat r\|_2+W.$$
If a norm in these formulas is replaced by an exact or certified upper bound, the resulting value of $\|\widehat r\|_2+W$ remains a certified upper bound for the exact residual.

Let f_i:R^d->R be convex and continuously differentiable with L-Lipschitz gradients, set F=n^{-1}sum_i f_i, and let x* satisfy grad F(x*)=0. Conditional on the current iterate x_k and table alpha_i^k, assume an independent uniform index I_k and finite second moments. Put

$$S_k=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\|\alpha_i^k-\nabla f_i(x^*)\|_2^2,\quad \bar\alpha_k=\frac1n\sum_i\alpha_i^k,\quad v_k=\nabla f_{I_k}(x_k)-\alpha_{I_k}^k+\bar\alpha_k.$$

Then

$$\mathbb E[v_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=\nabla F(x_k),\qquad \mathbb E[\|v_k\|_2^2\mid\mathcal F_k]\le6L(F(x_k)-F(x^*))+6S_k,$$

and, for the SAGA table replacement in [[alg-saga-finite-sum-method]],

$$
\mathbb E[S_{k+1}\mid\mathcal F_k]\le(1-1/n)S_k+\frac{2L}{n}(F(x_k)-F(x^*)).
$$

Let f_i:R^d->R be convex and continuously differentiable with L-Lipschitz gradients, set F=n^{-1}sum_i f_i, and let x* satisfy grad F(x*)=0. Conditional on the current iterate x_k and table alpha_i^k, assume an independent uniform index I_k and finite second moments. Put

$$S_k=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\|\alpha_i^k-\nabla f_i(x^*)\|_2^2,\quad \bar\alpha_k=\frac1n\sum_i\alpha_i^k,\quad v_k=\nabla f_{I_k}(x_k)-\alpha_{I_k}^k+\bar\alpha_k.$$

Then

$$\mathbb E[v_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=\nabla F(x_k),\qquad \mathbb E[\|v_k\|_2^2\mid\mathcal F_k]\le6L(F(x_k)-F(x^*))+6S_k,$$

and, for the SAGA table replacement in [[alg-saga-finite-sum-method]],

$$
\mathbb E[S_{k+1}\mid\mathcal F_k]\le(1-1/n)S_k+\frac{2L}{n}(F(x_k)-F(x^*)).
$$

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Let $p(z)=z^n+a_{n-1}z^{n-1}+\cdots+a_0$ be a real monic polynomial of
degree $n\ge1$ with $|a_0|<1$. Define the reversed polynomial
$p^\#(z)=z^np(1/z)$ and
$$q(z)=\frac{p(z)-a_0p^\#(z)}{z(1-a_0^2)}.$$
If every zero of $p$ lies strictly inside the unit disk, then every zero of
$q$ does too.
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: The real monic polynomial reduction divides by a positive one-minus-constant-square factor and transfers strict unit-disk root inclusion to the reduced degree.
selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 On $|z|=1$, real coefficients give $p^\#(z)=z^n\overline{p(z)}$, so $|p^\#(z)|=|p(z)|$. The strict root hypothesis makes $p$ nonzero on the unit circle, and $|a_0p^\#(z)|<|p(z)|$. Apply [F1] to $p$ and $-a_0p^\#$; $p-a_0p^\#$ has the same $n$ zeros in the disk as $p$. [A1, given, F1, algebra]

2.1 The polynomial $p-a_0p^\#$ has constant term zero and leading coefficient $1-a_0^2\ne0$, so it is $z$ times a degree-$(n-1)$ polynomial. One of its $n$ disk zeros is the factor zero at $z=0$; the remaining $n-1$ zeros are exactly those of the quotient. Dividing by the nonzero scalar $1-a_0^2$ changes no roots. Hence all zeros of $q$ lie strictly inside the disk. [A1, given, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

$$\int_{(R,\infty)}x\,\mu(dx)\le\frac{M_2(\mu)}R,\qquad \mu((R,\infty))\le\frac{M_1(\mu)}R.$$
In particular, for the bounded-kernel solution of [[thm-continuous-coagulation-fragmentation-moment-bounds]], these tails are uniform on every finite time interval after substituting the theorem's mass and second-moment bounds.

Let $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ have an algebraically simple eigenvalue $\lambda_0$, with right vector $v$ normalized by $\|v\|_2=1$ and compatible left vector $w$ normalized by $w^*v=1$. Put $Q=I-vw^*$, $W=\ker w^*$, $q=\|Q\|_2$, and $\kappa=\|w\|_2$. The restriction $A_W=A|_W$ is well-defined. Let $D=\{\lambda:|\lambda-\lambda_0|\le\rho\}$ be a disk such that every $\lambda\in D$ makes $\lambda I_W-A_W$ invertible and
$$R\ge\sup_{\lambda\in D}\| (\lambda I_W-A_W)^{-1}\|_2<\infty.$$
If $n\ge2$, $\|E\|_2\le\delta$, and $Rq^2\delta<1$, then every eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $A+E$ in $D$ satisfies
$$
|\lambda-\lambda_0|\le \kappa\delta+\frac{\kappa qR\delta^2}{1-Rq^2\delta}.
$$
When $A$ is a monodromy matrix, this bounds the corresponding Floquet multiplier. The formula is a finite nonnormal perturbation enclosure; an unseparated cluster requires the contour-count route instead.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Use the dyadic composite-Simpson hierarchy of
[[def-smolyak-univariate-level-hierarchy]]. Let $d\ge1$. For
$S=\{j_1<\cdots<j_k\}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}$, define
$$D_Sf:=\partial_{x_{j_k}}^4\cdots\partial_{x_{j_1}}^4f,$$
so these derivatives are applied in increasing coordinate order; set
$D_\varnothing f=f$. Assume every $D_Sf$ is continuous on the closed cube,
with the one-sided endpoint convention of
[[def-higher-derivatives-and-smoothness]], and choose finite bounds $M_S\ge0$
such that $|D_Sf(x)|\le M_S$ on $[0,1]^d$. For
$\ell\in\mathbb N_0^d$, put $S(\ell):=\{j:\ell_j\ge1\}$ and
$$\delta_\ell(f):=(\Delta_{\ell_1}^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes\Delta_{\ell_d}^{(d)})(f).$$
Then
$$|\delta_\ell(f)|\le M_{S(\ell)}\left(\frac{17}{2880}\right)^{|S(\ell)|}16^{-\sum_{j\in S(\ell)}\ell_j}.$$
Moreover, for every finite $F\subseteq\mathbb N_0^d$,
$$\sum_{\ell\in F}|\delta_\ell(f)|\le\sum_{S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}}M_S\left(\frac{17}{43200}\right)^{|S|}<\infty.$$

actualproofparagraphs.1.1: For $\ell\ge1$, use [F2] on levels $\ell$ and $\ell-1$, inserting the exact integral between their values. With panel counts $2^{\ell+1}$ and $2^\ell$, [F5] gives $|\Delta_\ell g|\le(2^{-4(\ell+1)}/180+2^{-4\ell}/180)\|g^{(4)}\|_\infty=(17/2880)16^{-\ell}\|g^{(4)}\|_\infty$. For $\ell=0$, [F3] gives $|\Delta_0g|=|Q_0g|\le\|g\|_\infty$. [given, F1, F2, F3, F5, algebra]
actualproofparagraphs.3.1: Fix finite $F$ and group indices by $S=S(\ell)$. For a fixed nonempty $S$, enlarge its levels to the finite box $1\le\ell_j\le R_j$ where $R_j$ is the largest such coordinate level in that group. By step 2.1 and [F6], the sum over that box is at most $M_S\prod_{j\in S}((17/2880)\sum_{r=1}^{R_j}16^{-r})\le M_S(17/43200)^{|S|}$, using [F7]. For $S=\varnothing$, the only possible index is $0$ and its term is at most $M_\varnothing$. Summing over all subsets proves the finite-subsum claim; the right side is finite. [given, step 2.1, F6, F7, algebra] ∎

source_evidence.case_anchor: Statement explicitly defines D_empty f=f. For the level vector zero, S(ell) is empty, so the product factor is one and the estimate is |Q_0 tensor ... tensor Q_0(f)|<=M_empty. Proof steps 1.1 and 3.1 handle this case. If the finite subsum set F is empty its sum is zero and the same nonnegative bound holds.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $d\ge1$ and $m=(m_1,\ldots,m_d)\in\mathbb N_0^d$. For
$R_m:=\{\ell\in\mathbb N_0^d:0\le\ell_j\le m_j\text{ for every }j\}$ and
the details of [[def-smolyak-univariate-level-hierarchy]],
$$\sum_{\ell\in R_m}\Delta_\ell=Q_{m_1}^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes Q_{m_d}^{(d)}.$$

actualproofparagraphs.1.1: Fix any one-dimensional input $g$ and coordinate $j$, and put $c_r:=Q_r(g)$. By [F3], $\sum_{r=1}^{m_j}(c_r-c_{r-1})=c_{m_j}-c_0$; for $m_j=0$ this is the empty-sum identity. Adding $Q_0(g)$ and using [F1] yields $\sum_{r=0}^{m_j}\Delta_r(g)=Q_{m_j}(g)$. Since $g$ was arbitrary, this is equality of functionals. [given, F1, F3, algebra]
actualproofparagraphs.2.1: Expand $\bigotimes_{j=1}^d\left(\sum_{r=0}^{m_j}\Delta_r^{(j)}\right)$ by distributing each finite coordinate sum. By [F3]–[F4] the resulting terms are exactly the tensor details indexed once by $R_m$, which is the Smolyak sum $Q_{R_m}$ by [F2]. Applying step 1.1 in every coordinate identifies this expansion with $Q_{m_1}^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes Q_{m_d}^{(d)}$, as claimed. [given, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

source_evidence.case_anchor: Proof step 1.1 explicitly treats m_j=0: the sum from r=1 through m_j is empty and zero, and adding Q_0 gives Q_{m_j}. Thus the rectangle R_m still contains the zero vector when all m_j vanish; proof step 2.1 distributes the nonempty coordinate sums without requiring a positive level.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $P\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $r\in\{1,2\}$ and $k\ge1$, and let $f:(-\delta,\delta)\times P\to\mathbb R^m$ be $C^{k+r}$. Suppose $\partial_h^j f(0,\alpha)=0$ for every $\alpha\in P$ and $0\le j<r$. Then $f(h,\alpha)/h^r$, initially defined for $h\ne0$, has a $C^k$ extension $F$ to $(-\delta,\delta)\times P$. Its mixed derivatives at zero satisfy
$$\partial_h^\ell\partial_\alpha^\beta F(0,\alpha)=\frac{\ell!}{(r+\ell)!}\partial_h^{r+\ell}\partial_\alpha^\beta f(0,\alpha)\qquad(\ell+|\beta|\le k).$$
source_evidence.case_anchor:
Let $P\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $r\in\{1,2\}$ and $k\ge1$, and let $f:(-\delta,\delta)\times P\to\mathbb R^m$ be $C^{k+r}$. Suppose $\partial_h^j f(0,\alpha)=0$ for every $\alpha\in P$ and $0\le j<r$. Then $f(h,\alpha)/h^r$, initially defined for $h\ne0$, has a $C^k$ extension $F$ to $(-\delta,\delta)\times P$. Its mixed derivatives at zero satisfy
$$\partial_h^\ell\partial_\alpha^\beta F(0,\alpha)=\frac{\ell!}{(r+\ell)!}\partial_h^{r+\ell}\partial_\alpha^\beta f(0,\alpha)\qquad(\ell+|\beta|\le k).$$

proofparagraphs.text: For each parameter multi-index $\beta$ with $|\beta|\le k$, put $k_\beta=k-|\beta|$, $N=r+k_\beta$, and $g_\beta(h)=\partial_\alpha^\beta f(h,\alpha)$. For every $s\le k_\beta$, put $m=N-s$. If $m\ge2$, apply [F1] componentwise to $g_\beta^{(s)}$ through degree $m-1$; continuity of its highest derivative lets us replace the Lagrange coefficient at $\theta h$ by its value at zero plus $o(1)$. If $m=1$, subtract the linear Taylor polynomial: the derivative of the remainder is $o(1)$ by continuity, so [F3] gives a remainder $o(|h|)$. Thus in every case $g_\beta^{(s)}(h)$ equals its Taylor polynomial through degree $m$ plus $o(|h|^m)$. By step 1.1 all coefficients of degrees below $r$ vanish. For $h\ne0$, the quotient rule expresses the $\ell$th derivative of $g_\beta/h^r$ as a finite linear combination of $h^{-r-\ell+s}g_\beta^{(s)}(h)$, $0\le s\le\ell$. Substituting the expansions shows that the remainder terms are $o(|h|^{k_\beta-\ell})$; the polynomial part has a continuous extension whose $\ell$th derivative at zero is $\ell!\partial_h^{r+\ell}\partial_\alpha^\beta f(0,\alpha)/(r+\ell)!$. Continuity of the derivatives on compact parameter neighborhoods makes these limits locally uniform in $\alpha$. [F1, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

Let $A\in\mathbb R^{r\times n}$ have full row rank, where $0\le r\le n$,
and let $H\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric and positive definite on
$\ker A$: $z^THz>0$ whenever $0\ne z\in\ker A$. Then
$$K=\begin{bmatrix}H&A^T\\A&0\end{bmatrix}$$
is nonsingular. Here the zero-row case $r=0$ is allowed.

proofparagraphs.text: Suppose $K\binom{z}{\mu}=0$. Its lower block gives $Az=0$, so $z\in\ker A$; multiplying the upper block $Hz+A^T\mu=0$ by $z^T$ gives $z^THz=0$. Positive definiteness on $\ker A$ forces $z=0$. [given, F1, algebra]

With $z=0$, the upper block gives $A^T\mu=0$. Full row rank of $A$ means $A^T$ is injective, so $\mu=0$. Thus the square matrix $K$ has trivial kernel and is nonsingular; when $r=0$, the same argument says $H$ has trivial kernel. [given, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

Let f_i:R^d->R be convex and continuously differentiable with L-Lipschitz gradients, set F=n^{-1}sum_i f_i, and let x* satisfy grad F(x*)=0. Conditional on a filtration \mathcal F_t, suppose x_t and the snapshot \tilde x are measurable, the uniform index I_t is independent of \mathcal F_t, and the relevant second moments are finite. For

$$
v_t=\nabla f_{I_t}(x_t)-\nabla f_{I_t}(\tilde x)+\nabla F(\tilde x),
$$

one has

$$\mathbb E[v_t\mid\mathcal F_t]=\nabla F(x_t),\qquad \mathbb E[\|v_t\|_2^2\mid\mathcal F_t] \le4L(F(x_t)-F(x^*))+4L(F(\tilde x)-F(x^*)).$$

literal_source_anchor.quote:
Fix an integer $N\ge r$ and a compact set $K\Subset U$ for which the method maps and their selected branches are defined on a neighborhood. Let $H_h^{[N]}$ and $X_h^{[N]}$ be the finite modified Hamiltonian and vector field from [[lem-finite-modified-hamiltonian-exists]], and let $\varphi_h^{[N]}$ be the time-$h$ flow of $X_h^{[N]}$. If the method, the comparison flow, and all Taylor segments remain in a compact $K'\Subset U$, then there are $h_0,C_N>0$ such that
$$E_K(h)\le C_N|h|^{N+2}\qquad(|h|\le h_0),$$
where $E_K(h)=0$ if $K=\varnothing$, and otherwise
$$E_K(h):=\max_{z\in K}\|\Phi_h(z)-\varphi_h^{[N]}(z)\|.$$
For nonempty $K$, this maximum exists by continuity on the compact set and equals the ordinary real supremum. In both cases $E_K(h)$ is the least nonnegative upper bound for the pointwise errors on $K$: for empty $K$ every nonnegative real is an upper bound and $0$ is the least. This convention does not assign a real supremum to an empty subset of $\mathbb R$.
The constants depend on the fixed truncation order and the compact derivative bounds; no uniformity as $N\to\infty$ is claimed.

literal_source_anchor.quote: Expand the finitely many polynomials $B_q(h,z)$ in step 1.3 and collect equal powers of $h$. Every term of degree at least $N+2$ is bounded by a fixed constant times $|h|^{N+2}$ for $|h|\le1$, because there are finitely many such terms and their coefficient functions are bounded on the compact tube. The recursion in [F1] (its coefficient construction) identifies all collected coefficients through degree $N+1$ with the method coefficients $d_q$ in step 1.2. Subtracting the two expansions leaves only their uniform remainders and the discarded higher-degree polynomial terms. Consequently $\|\Phi_h(z)-\varphi_h^{[N]}(z)\|\le C_N|h|^{N+2}$ for all $z\in K$, after increasing $C_N$ to a positive constant. Taking the attained maximum from step 1.1 proves the asserted estimate; step 1.1 already covers empty $K$. [F1, F4, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, algebra] ∎

In the quadratic model of [[def-trust-region-quadratic-model-and-ratio]],
let $g\ne0$, let $B$ be symmetric, and let $\Delta>0$. Write
$M:=\|B\|_2$ for the induced Euclidean matrix norm, with the convention
$\min\{\Delta,\|g\|_2/M\}=\Delta$ when $M=0$. The Cauchy step
$p_C$ of [[alg-trust-region-cauchy-step]] minimizes the model on the
negative-gradient segment $\{-tg:0\le t\le\Delta/\|g\|_2\}$ and satisfies
$$m(0)-m(p_C)\ge\tfrac12\|g\|_2 \min\{\Delta,\|g\|_2/M\}.$$

review_basis.full_actual_interface:
Let $m$ be the model of
[[def-trust-region-quadratic-model-and-ratio]], with $g\ne0$, symmetric
$B$, and radius $\Delta>0$. Suppose $\|B\|_2\le M_B$ for a declared
$M_B\ge0$, and $f$ is $C^1$ on an open set containing the segment from $x$
to $x+p$. Suppose the gradient of $f$ is $L$-Lipschitz on that segment,
meaning
$$\|\nabla f(u)-\nabla f(v)\|_2\le L\|u-v\|_2$$
there. Let $0<\theta\le1$, let $p$ be feasible, and suppose
$$m(0)-m(p)\ge\theta\,[m(0)-m(p_C)]$$
for the Cauchy step $p_C$ of [[alg-trust-region-cauchy-step]]. Interpret
$\|g\|_2/(2M_B)=+\infty$ if $M_B=0$, and assume
$\Delta\le\|g\|_2/(2M_B)$. Then the predicted reduction is positive and
$$|\rho(p)-1|\le\frac{2(L+M_B)\Delta}{\theta\|g\|_2}.$$
Consequently, for $0<\eta_2<1$, if $L+M_B>0$ and
$$\Delta\le\frac{\theta(1-\eta_2)\|g\|_2}{2(L+M_B)},$$
then $\rho(p)\ge\eta_2$. If $L+M_B=0$, then $\rho(p)=1$.

review_basis.full_actual_interface:
Let $B\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric, let $g\in\mathbb R^n$, and
let $\Delta>0$. Every global minimizer $p_*$ of
$$q(p):=\langle g,p\rangle+\tfrac12p^TBp\quad\text{over }\|p\|_2\le\Delta$$
has a multiplier $\lambda\ge0$ such that
$$(B+\lambda I)p_*=-g,\qquad B+\lambda I\succeq0,\qquad \lambda(\Delta-\|p_*\|_2)=0.$$
Conversely, every feasible $p_*$ satisfying these conditions is a global
minimizer. A global minimizer always exists.

The singular hard case is included as follows. Let $\mu$ be the least
eigenvalue of $B$ and $E_\mu$ its eigenspace. If $\mu<0$, $g\perp E_\mu$,
and the solution $p_0$ of
$(B-\mu I)p_0=-g$, $p_0\perp E_\mu$, has $\|p_0\|_2\le\Delta$, then
$$p_*=p_0+z,\qquad z\in E_\mu,\qquad \|z\|_2^2=\Delta^2-\|p_0\|_2^2$$
is a global minimizer with the singular multiplier $\lambda=-\mu$. If
$\|p_0\|_2<\Delta$, both signs of any chosen nonzero $z$ of the required
length give distinct minimizers.

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Suppose proper closed convex $f,g$ have a saddle point $(x_*,z_*,y_*)$ for the
Lagrangian in [[alg-two-block-admm-scaled]], with $Kx_*+Lz_*=c$, and every
subproblem in the exact ADMM sequence is attained. Put
$\Delta z^{k+1}=z^{k+1}-z^k$ and
$$V^k=\frac1\rho\|y^k-y_*\|_2^2+\rho\|L(z^k-z_*)\|_2^2.$$
For every $k\ge1$,
$$V^{k+1}\le V^k-\rho\|r^{k+1}\|_2^2-\rho\|L\Delta z^{k+1}\|_2^2.$$
The index begins at $k=1$: an arbitrary initial $z^0$ need not satisfy a
previous $z$-subproblem optimality condition. Also, with $p_k=f(x^k)+g(z^k)$
and $p_*=f(x_*)+g(z_*)$, every exact sweep satisfies
$$p_{k+1}-p_*\le-\langle y^{k+1},r^{k+1}\rangle+ \rho\langle L\Delta z^{k+1},r^{k+1}-L(z^{k+1}-z_*)\rangle,$$
$$p_*-p_{k+1}\le\langle y_*,r^{k+1}\rangle.$$

selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 For every $x\in\operatorname{dom}f$, the right saddle inequality at $(x,z_*)$ and feasibility give $f(x)\ge f(x_*)+\langle-K^*y_*,x-x_*\rangle$; the same argument with $(x_*,z)$ gives $-L^*y_*\in\partial g(z_*)$. Thus [F4] gives both saddle subgradient inclusions. For $k\ge1$, the preceding exact sweep also gives $-L^*y^k\in\partial g(z^k)$ from [F2]. The inequalities at $z^{k+1}$ and $z^k$ read $g(z^{k+1})-g(z^k)\le-\langle y^{k+1},L\Delta z^{k+1}\rangle$ and $g(z^{k+1})-g(z^k)\ge-\langle y^k,L\Delta z^{k+1}\rangle$. Combining them gives $\langle y^{k+1}-y^k,L\Delta z^{k+1}\rangle\le0$. This is the sign needed below and is why the estimate starts at $k=1$. [A1, F2, F3, F4, F5, given, algebra]

2.1 Adding the two defining subgradient inequalities shows subgradient monotonicity. At the $f$-block this gives $0\le\langle a^{k+1}+K^*y_*,x^{k+1}-x_*\rangle=-\langle y^{k+1}-y_*,K(x^{k+1}-x_*)\rangle+\rho\langle L\Delta z^{k+1},K(x^{k+1}-x_*)\rangle.$ At the $g$-block it gives $0\le\langle b^{k+1}+L^*y_*,z^{k+1}-z_*\rangle=-\langle y^{k+1}-y_*,L(z^{k+1}-z_*)\rangle$. Add the two inequalities and use $Kx_*+Lz_*=c$ to obtain $\langle y^{k+1}-y_*,r^{k+1}\rangle\le\rho\langle L\Delta z^{k+1},K(x^{k+1}-x_*)\rangle.$ Substitute $K(x^{k+1}-x_*)=r^{k+1}-L(z^{k+1}-z_*)$. [A1, F2, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Suppose proper closed convex $f,g$ have a saddle point $(x_*,z_*,y_*)$ for the
Lagrangian in [[alg-two-block-admm-scaled]], with $Kx_*+Lz_*=c$, and every
subproblem in the exact ADMM sequence is attained. Put
$\Delta z^{k+1}=z^{k+1}-z^k$ and
$$V^k=\frac1\rho\|y^k-y_*\|_2^2+\rho\|L(z^k-z_*)\|_2^2.$$
For every $k\ge1$,
$$V^{k+1}\le V^k-\rho\|r^{k+1}\|_2^2-\rho\|L\Delta z^{k+1}\|_2^2.$$
The index begins at $k=1$: an arbitrary initial $z^0$ need not satisfy a
previous $z$-subproblem optimality condition. Also, with $p_k=f(x^k)+g(z^k)$
and $p_*=f(x_*)+g(z_*)$, every exact sweep satisfies
$$p_{k+1}-p_*\le-\langle y^{k+1},r^{k+1}\rangle+ \rho\langle L\Delta z^{k+1},r^{k+1}-L(z^{k+1}-z_*)\rangle,$$
$$p_*-p_{k+1}\le\langle y_*,r^{k+1}\rangle.$$

review_basis.full_actual_interface:
Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be open, $f:D\to\mathbb R^d$ be $C^2$, and $y(s)$ solve $y'=f(s,y)$ on $[t,t+h]$. Assume a compact convex tube $Q\subset D$ contains the trajectory, the stage midpoint segments, and all vectors used below. On $Q$, suppose
$$
\|f\|_2\le F,\quad \|D_yf\|_2\le L,\quad \|f_t\|_2\le T_0,\quad \|D^2f\|_{\rm op}\le H,
$$
where $D^2f$ is the second total derivative on the joint variable $(t,y)$, and $\|D^2f\|_{\rm op}:=\sup_{\|u\|=\|v\|=1}\|D^2f[u,v]\|_2$ for the Euclidean product norm. Fix $\alpha=1-1/\sqrt2$, and suppose $\|\widetilde J\|_2\le B_J$, $\|\widetilde T\|_2\le B_T$, and $\|\alpha h\widetilde J\|_2\le q<1$. Put $\kappa=(1-q)^{-1}$ and $M=T_0+LF$. The shifted inverse has norm at most $\kappa$ by [[lem-rosenbrock-shifted-matrix-invertibility-bound]].

For exact-arithmetic stages $k_1,q_2,k_2$ of [[alg-two-stage-rosenbrock-w-method]] (with its exact-storage checks successful), define
$$C_1=B_JF+B_T,\quad K_1=F+\alpha h\kappa C_1,\quad C_F=\frac{\alpha\kappa L C_1}{2}+\frac{H(1+K_1^2)}{8}.$$
$$C_K=\alpha^2\kappa^2B_JC_1+\frac{\alpha\kappa B_JM}{2}+\kappa C_F, \qquad M_2=H(1+F^2)+LT_0+L^2F.$$
Then the exact one-step defect is at most
$$
\|y(t)+hk_2-y(t+h)\|_2\le (C_K+M_2/6)h^3.
$$
If the computed first and second shifted solves have certified update-residual bounds $\rho_1$ and $\rho_2$, then the computed update satisfies
$$\|\widehat y_+-y(t+h)\|_2\le (C_K+M_2/6)h^3+C_rh^2\rho_1+\kappa h\rho_2, \qquad C_r:=\kappa^2(L/2+\alpha B_J).$$
Thus $\rho_1=O(h)$ and $\rho_2=O(h^2)$ preserve a cubic local defect. These are equation-residual conditions, not stage forward-error claims without the inverse bound.

At any base point in the tube, the same two-stage residual perturbation argument gives the solver-to-exact-map bound $\|\widehat\Phi_h(t,y)-\Phi_h(t,y)\|_2\le C_rh^2\rho_1+\kappa h\rho_2$, whenever both midpoint evaluations lie in $Q$.

source_evidence.case_anchor: Let $(\eta_n)$ be Cauchy in total variation. Choose increasing indices $n_j$ with $\|\eta_{n_{j+1}}-\eta_{n_j}\|_{TV}\le2^{-j}$, taking the least qualifying index at each step. For each Borel set $A$, the series $\eta_{n_1}(A)+\sum_{j\ge1}(\eta_{n_{j+1}}-\eta_{n_j})(A)$ converges absolutely, uniformly in $A$, because each summand is bounded by its total-variation norm. Define $\eta(A)$ by that sum. If $(A_k)$ are disjoint, the double series of absolute values is bounded by $\|\eta_{n_1}\|_{TV}+\sum_j\|\eta_{n_{j+1}}-\eta_{n_j}\|_{TV}$, so the two countable sums may be interchanged; hence $\eta$ is countably additive. The same tail bound gives $\|\eta-\eta_{n_j}\|_{TV}\le\sum_{r\ge j}2^{-r}\to0$. Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose $j$ so this is below $\varepsilon/2$ and the Cauchy property gives $\|\eta_n-\eta_m\|_{TV}<\varepsilon/2$ for all $n,m\ge n_j$. For any $n\ge n_j$, choose $n_k\ge n_j$ and pass to the limit in $\|\eta_n-\eta_{n_k}\|_{TV}<\varepsilon/2$; since $\eta_{n_k}\to\eta$, this gives $\|\eta_n-\eta\|_{TV}\le\varepsilon/2<\varepsilon$. Thus finite signed measures are complete in total variation. [given, choose]

source_evidence.case_anchor: Let $(\eta_n)$ be Cauchy in total variation. Choose increasing indices $n_j$ with $\|\eta_{n_{j+1}}-\eta_{n_j}\|_{TV}\le2^{-j}$, taking the least qualifying index at each step. For each Borel set $A$, the series $\eta_{n_1}(A)+\sum_{j\ge1}(\eta_{n_{j+1}}-\eta_{n_j})(A)$ converges absolutely, uniformly in $A$, because each summand is bounded by its total-variation norm. Define $\eta(A)$ by that sum. If $(A_k)$ are disjoint, the double series of absolute values is bounded by $\|\eta_{n_1}\|_{TV}+\sum_j\|\eta_{n_{j+1}}-\eta_{n_j}\|_{TV}$, so the two countable sums may be interchanged; hence $\eta$ is countably additive. The same tail bound gives $\|\eta-\eta_{n_j}\|_{TV}\le\sum_{r\ge j}2^{-r}\to0$. Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose $j$ so this is below $\varepsilon/2$ and the Cauchy property gives $\|\eta_n-\eta_m\|_{TV}<\varepsilon/2$ for all $n,m\ge n_j$. For any $n\ge n_j$, choose $n_k\ge n_j$ and pass to the limit in $\|\eta_n-\eta_{n_k}\|_{TV}<\varepsilon/2$; since $\eta_{n_k}\to\eta$, this gives $\|\eta_n-\eta\|_{TV}\le\varepsilon/2<\varepsilon$. Thus finite signed measures are complete in total variation. [given, choose]

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Apply [[def-ars222-additive-tableau-and-stages]] to the scalar split test equation $y'=\lambda_a y+\lambda_b y$, with $z_a=h\lambda_a$ and $z_b=h\lambda_b$ in $\mathbb C$. If $1-\gamma z_b\ne0$, the one-step amplification factor is
$$R(z_a,z_b)=\frac{1+z_a+(1-2\gamma)z_b+\frac12z_a^2+(\frac12-\gamma^2)z_az_b}{(1-\gamma z_b)^2}.$$
The exact scalar absolute-stability region for this tableau is
$$\mathcal S=\left\{(z_a,z_b)\in\mathbb C^2:1-\gamma z_b\ne0,\ \left|1+z_a+(1-2\gamma)z_b+\frac12z_a^2+(\frac12-\gamma^2)z_az_b\right|\le|1-\gamma z_b|^2\right\}.$$
On $z_b=0$ this reduces to $|1+z_a+z_a^2/2|\le1$; on $z_a=0$ it reduces to $|1+(1-2\gamma)z_b|\le|1-\gamma z_b|^2$. This is a scalar, two-variable region; it makes no matrix-nonnormality or PDE stability claim.

actualproofparagraphs.1.1: Substituting $a(y)=\lambda_a y$ and $b(y)=\lambda_b y$ into [F1] gives $Y_2/y=(1+\gamma z_a)/(1-\gamma z_b)$ whenever the denominator is nonzero. The third stage then satisfies $\frac{Y_3}{y}=\frac{1+\delta z_a+[(1-\delta)z_a+(1-\gamma)z_b](Y_2/y)}{1-\gamma z_b}.$ These formulas are linear coefficient identities, so they also define the amplification when $y=0$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]
actualproofparagraphs.4.1: Repeated application to the scalar test equation multiplies its state by $R$ at each step, so nonincrease of the absolute value is exactly $|R|\le1$. Since $| (1-\gamma z_b)^2|=|1-\gamma z_b|^2$, this is precisely the displayed set $\mathcal S$, with the pole excluded because the implicit stage equation is singular there. Setting either variable to zero gives the stated axis sections by substitution. [F3, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

source_evidence.case_anchor: Proof step 1.1 treats the ratios as linear coefficient identities even at y=0, avoiding division by zero initial data. Proof step 4.1 separately excludes the true pole1-gamma z_b=0.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $L>0$, let $M\ge2$ be an integer, and let $R$ be a regular MEP as in [[def-regular-minimum-energy-path-in-a-collision-free-tube]], now parameterized by arc length on $[0,L]$, with $R\in C^3$ under the endpoint convention of [[lem-arc-length-polyline-interpolation-error]] and the bounds of [[lem-centered-chord-and-unequal-step-tangent-error]] and [[lem-arc-length-polyline-interpolation-error]]. Let $R_i=R(ih)$ for $i=0,\ldots,M$, $Mh=L$, and assume every interior centered chord is nonzero. Suppose $\|\nabla V(R(s))\|_2\le G$ along the curve and $0<h\le1$. Use the centered unit tangent $\widehat t_i=(R_{i+1}-R_{i-1})/\|R_{i+1}-R_{i-1}\|_2$. Then the projected string force at each interior sample satisfies

$$\|(I-\widehat t_i\widehat t_i^T)\nabla V(R_i)\|_2\le C_Fh^2.$$

If the equal-spacing spring residual $k(\ell_i^+-\ell_i^-)\widehat t_i$ is also evaluated on these samples, then its norm is at most $C_Sh^3$ for fixed $k$. Equal-length polyline redistribution of the exact samples changes each image by at most $C_Rh^2$. The constants depend on the stated derivative bounds, $G$, $k$, and the path, not on $M$. The projected-force conclusion is for the centered-tangent string residual; it does not assert second-order consistency for the improved energy-selected NEB tangent.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $L>0$, let $M\ge2$ be an integer, and let $R$ be a regular MEP as in [[def-regular-minimum-energy-path-in-a-collision-free-tube]], now parameterized by arc length on $[0,L]$, with $R\in C^3$ under the endpoint convention of [[lem-arc-length-polyline-interpolation-error]] and the bounds of [[lem-centered-chord-and-unequal-step-tangent-error]] and [[lem-arc-length-polyline-interpolation-error]]. Let $R_i=R(ih)$ for $i=0,\ldots,M$, $Mh=L$, and assume every interior centered chord is nonzero. Suppose $\|\nabla V(R(s))\|_2\le G$ along the curve and $0<h\le1$. Use the centered unit tangent $\widehat t_i=(R_{i+1}-R_{i-1})/\|R_{i+1}-R_{i-1}\|_2$. Then the projected string force at each interior sample satisfies

$$\|(I-\widehat t_i\widehat t_i^T)\nabla V(R_i)\|_2\le C_Fh^2.$$

If the equal-spacing spring residual $k(\ell_i^+-\ell_i^-)\widehat t_i$ is also evaluated on these samples, then its norm is at most $C_Sh^3$ for fixed $k$. Equal-length polyline redistribution of the exact samples changes each image by at most $C_Rh^2$. The constants depend on the stated derivative bounds, $G$, $k$, and the path, not on $M$. The projected-force conclusion is for the centered-tangent string residual; it does not assert second-order consistency for the improved energy-selected NEB tangent.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
For the data of [[def-finite-basis-projector-energy-model]], $E(P)$ is real
and $C^2$ on its stated neighborhood. For every Hermitian $P$ in that
neighborhood and every Hermitian direction $H$,
$$DE(P)[H]=\operatorname{tr}\big((h+G(P)+\nabla E_{xc}(P))H\big)=\langle F(P),H\rangle_F.$$
Thus $F(P)$ is the Hermitian Frobenius gradient of $E$.

actualproofparagraphs.1.2: For real $t$, real-linearity gives $G(P+tH)=G(P)+tG(H)$. Expanding and collecting the coefficient of $t$ yields $\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_{t=0}\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}((P+tH)G(P+tH))=\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(H G(P)) +\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(P G(H))$. The linear trace term differentiates to $\operatorname{tr}(hH)$ by [F1], and the $E_{xc}$ term differentiates to $\langle\nabla E_{xc}(P),H\rangle_F$ by its gradient definition. [F1, F2, F3, given, algebra]

In particular, the improved-tangent NEB force in [[alg-improved-tangent-climbing-neb]] has no general $O(h^2)$ projected-force consistency bound, even when the curve and potential are smooth and the chord is nondegenerate.

proofparagraphs.text: At $n=0$, [A1] gives $\partial_sX=T(s)$ and $\partial_nX=N(s)$, an orthonormal coordinate basis. The potential has coordinate derivatives $\partial_sV=W'(s)$ and $\partial_nV=n=0$, so $\nabla V(R(s))=W'(s)T(s)$. Therefore its component normal to $T(s)$ vanishes and $R$ is a regular MEP by [F2]. [A1, F2, given, construct, algebra]

We have $W'(s)=4s(s^2-a^2)>0$ for $-a<s<0$ and $W'(s)<0$ for $0<s<a$, so the energy is strictly increasing then decreasing. Since $V=W(s)+n^2/2\ge0$ with equality exactly at $(s,n)=(\pm a,0)$, those two endpoints are global minima on the sector. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $V\in C^4(U,\mathbb R)$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, and put $F=\nabla V$. At any accepted update of [[alg-index-one-eigenvector-following-step]], the step is the unique vector $p$ solving

$$DF(x)p=-F(x),\qquad DF(x)=\nabla^2V(x).$$

Suppose $x_*$ is a critical point, its Hessian is nonsingular with exactly one negative eigenvalue, and the Hessian is Lipschitz on a neighborhood of $x_*$. Then for all initial points in a sufficiently small ball about $x_*$, every update that the algorithm attempts before it stops is the ordinary exact-Jacobian Newton update and satisfies the local quadratic estimate supplied by [[thm-updated-jacobian-newton-local-quadratic-convergence]]. A gradient or eigensolve stopping status creates no later update, and no global-start guarantee is asserted.
source_evidence.case_anchor: Suppose $x_*$ is a critical point, its Hessian is nonsingular with exactly one negative eigenvalue, and the Hessian is Lipschitz on a neighborhood of $x_*$. Then for all initial points in a sufficiently small ball about $x_*$, every update that the algorithm attempts before it stops is the ordinary exact-Jacobian Newton update and satisfies the local quadratic estimate supplied by [[thm-updated-jacobian-newton-local-quadratic-convergence]]. A gradient or eigensolve stopping status creates no later update, and no global-start guarantee is asserted.

proofparagraphs.text: At an accepted update, [F1] supplies the exact Hessian Jacobian and gradient residual to the Newton-correction procedure, and its validated ordered enclosures put every Hessian eigenvalue at distance at least $\gamma$ from zero. Thus the Hessian is invertible; [F2] makes the returned correction the unique solution of $\nabla^2V(x)p=-\nabla V(x)$, so the selected step is exactly the vector Newton step. [F1, F2, F4]

Let $x_*$ be the critical point. By [F4], $F(x_*)=0$ and $DF(x_*)=\nabla^2V(x_*)$ is invertible by [A1]. Since $V\in C^4$, $F$ is $C^2$; the assumed local Hessian-Lipschitz bound is a local Lipschitz bound on $DF$. Thus the hypotheses of [F3] hold. [A1, F3, F4, given]

source_evidence.fullclaim:
For $0\prec D\prec I$ and every Hermitian direction $H$, let
$\mathcal S(D)=\operatorname{tr}(D\log D+(I-D)\log(I-D))$. Then
$$D\mathcal S(D)[H]=\operatorname{tr}\big(H(\log D-\log(I-D))\big).$$

actualproofparagraphs.1.1: For positive scalars the integral in [F1] converges and equals $\log x$ by integrating over $[0,R]$ and taking $R\to\infty$. Diagonalizing a positive-definite Hermitian $X$ by [F4] gives the same identity for $\log X$. If $X\succeq mI$ for some $m>0$, the resolvent $R_s=(X+sI)^{-1}$ has norm at most $(m+s)^{-1}$. [F1, F4, given, algebra]
actualproofparagraphs.2.1: In the neighborhood $X\succeq (m/2)I$, the resolvent identity gives $\frac{R_s(X+tH)-R_s(X)}{t}=-R_s(X+tH)H R_s(X)$. On every bounded interval of $s$, [F2] and continuity give uniform convergence of these difference quotients to $-R_sHR_s$. For $s\ge R\ge1$, their norm is at most $\|H\|_2/s^2$, so the integral of the tail is at most $\|H\|_2/R$, uniformly for small $t$. First differentiating on $[0,R]$ and then letting $R\to\infty$ proves $D\log(X)[H]=\int_0^\infty R_sHR_s\,ds$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, given]

source_evidence.case_anchor: In proof step 2.1 the resolvent difference quotient divides by nonzero t and takes its limit as t tends to zero; the Statement asserts a derivative, not evaluation of that quotient at t=0. Proof step 1.1 fixes a positive spectral margin m, and the neighborhood X>=(m/2)I keeps the resolvent invertible. For direction H=0 all quotients and the final trace pairing are zero.

review_basis.full_actual_interface:
Let $n\ge1$, and let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$ and bounded
below by $f_{inf}$.
Run [[alg-adaptive-cubic-regularization]] with exact Hessians and parameters
$0<\eta_1<\eta_2<1$, $\gamma_{up}>1$, $0<\gamma_{down}<1$,
$0<\kappa<1$, $0<\kappa_\theta<1$, and
$0<\sigma_{min}\le\sigma_k\le\sigma_{max}$ with $\sigma_{max}\ge3L$.
Suppose the Hessian is $L$-Lipschitz on every trial segment, and let
$0<\varepsilon\le1$. Let $R\in\mathbb N_0$ satisfy
$\gamma_{up}^R\sigma_{min}\ge3L$ (take $R=0$ if
$\sigma_{min}\ge3L$).

The algorithm has two complexity guarantees.

1. **Exact model minimizers.** If every solver call returns an exact global
   minimizer, define
   $$C_g:=\sigma_{max}+\sqrt n\,L,\qquad c_g:=\frac{\eta_1\sigma_{min}}{6C_g^{3/2}}.$$
   Through the first iterate with gradient norm at most $\varepsilon$, the
   numbers $N_s$ of accepted steps and $N_u$ of rejected trials satisfy
   $$N_s\le [f(x_0)-f_{inf}]c_g^{-1}\varepsilon^{-3/2}+1,\qquad N_u\le R N_s.$$

2. **Admissible inexact model steps.** Suppose each solver-success candidate
   passes the cubic solution, residual, and Cauchy-decrease checks in
   [[alg-adaptive-cubic-regularization]], and $\nabla f$ is $K$-Lipschitz
   on every trial segment. If the solver succeeds at every nonterminal
   trial, define
   $$D_g:=\frac{\sigma_{max}+\sqrt n\,L+\kappa_\theta K} {1-\kappa_\theta},\qquad c_a:=\frac{\eta_1\sigma_{min}}{6D_g^{3/2}}.$$
   Then the same counts satisfy
   $$N_s\le [f(x_0)-f_{inf}]c_a^{-1}\varepsilon^{-3/2}+1,\qquad N_u\le R N_s.$$

In either case the uncapped process reaches a stationary or target-achieved
iterate with gradient norm at most $\varepsilon$. For the finite-cap
algorithm, an outer cap at least
$$(R+1)\left(\frac{f(x_0)-f_{inf}}{c\,\varepsilon^{3/2}}+1\right)$$
suffices, where $c=c_g$ in case 1 and $c=c_a$ in case 2. The resulting
number of outer trials, and their function, gradient, and Hessian evaluation
counts, are $O(\varepsilon^{-3/2})$. These counts do not bound the internal
work of the model solver.
review_basis.source_specific_focus: Exact or admissible residual-controlled cubic steps reach the first-order target within inverse-three-halves outer-trial counts, excluding internal solver work.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Use the tableau and stage equations in [[def-ars222-additive-tableau-and-stages]], with $F=a+b$. Let $a,b\in C^2(U,\mathbb R^d)$ on an open set, and suppose the exact solution, exact stages, approximate candidates, and all joining line segments remain in a common compact convex tube on which $a,b$ and their first two derivatives are bounded and $a,b$ are Lipschitz with constants $L_a,L_b$. At each implicit stage assume the selected branch hypotheses of [[lem-ars222-stage-branch-and-residual-control]] hold, with $|\gamma|hL_b\le1/2$.

For exact stage roots, the exact-start one-step defect is at most $C h^3$, and the exact-root one-step map is Lipschitz with constant $1+Lh$ on the tube, for constants independent of sufficiently small $h$. If computed stages have unscaled update residuals $r_2,r_3$ satisfying
$$\|r_2\|_2\le C_2h^2,\qquad \|r_3\|_2\le C_3h^3,$$
then their output differs from the exact-root output at the same input by at most $C_{\rm alg}h^3$. Consequently, for $h=T/N$ and initial error $\|y_0-y(0)\|_2\le C_0h^2$, the computed method satisfies
$$\max_{0\le n\le N}\|y_n-y(t_n)\|_2\le C_T h^2.$$
The second-stage residual has the weaker $O(h^2)$ budget because its stage error is multiplied by $h$ in the last stage; the final-stage residual must be $O(h^3)$. All residuals are in update units.

actualproofparagraphs.1.3: Let $e_2=\|\widetilde Y_2-Y_2\|_2$. By $\gamma>0$ from [F6] and $|\gamma|hL_b\le1/2$ from [A1], subtracting the second-stage equations and using its residual gives $(1-\gamma hL_b)e_2\le\|r_2\|_2$, hence $e_2\le2\|r_2\|_2$. For the final stage, subtract the equations with the same initial input; the terms depending on $Y_2$ are bounded by $hK_s e_2$, where $K_s=|1-\delta|L_a+|1-\gamma|L_b$. The final-stage residual therefore gives $\|\widetilde Y_3-Y_3\|_2\le2\|r_3\|_2+4K_s h\|r_2\|_2.$ This is at most $C_{\rm alg}h^3$ under the two stated residual budgets. [A1, F1, F3, F6, algebra]

actualproofparagraphs.2.1: By [F2] and [A1], the selected second-stage root exists in its branch ball. Its equation in [F1] and boundedness first give $Y_2-y=O(h)$. Lipschitz continuity gives $b(Y_2)=b(y)+O(h)$, so the same equation gives $Y_2-y=\gamma hF(y)+O(h^2)$. Applying [F5] to $b(Y_2)$ then gives $b(Y_2)=b(y)+\gamma h\,Db(y)F(y)+O(h^2)$, and substitution into [F1] yields $Y_2=y+\gamma hF(y)+\gamma^2h^2Db(y)F(y)+O(h^3).$ [A1, F1, F2, F5, step 1.1, algebra]
actualproofparagraphs.3.1: By [F2] and [A1], the selected third-stage root exists after $Y_2$ is selected. Since $Y_2-y=O(h)$ and the stage equations give $Y_3-y=O(h)$, Lipschitz continuity and the weight sums $\delta+(1-\delta)=1$ and $(1-\gamma)+\gamma=1$ imply $Y_3-y=hF(y)+O(h^2)$. Taylor's formula applied to the last-stage terms gives $a(Y_2)=a(y)+\gamma h\,Da(y)F(y)+O(h^2),\quad b(Y_2)=b(y)+\gamma h\,Db(y)F(y)+O(h^2),\quad b(Y_3)=b(y)+h\,Db(y)F(y)+O(h^2).$ Substituting these expansions into [F1] and collecting the coefficients gives $Y_3=y+hF(y)+h^2\{\gamma(1-\delta)Da(y)F(y)+\gamma(2-\gamma)Db(y)F(y)\}+O(h^3).$ [A1, F1, F2, F5, step 2.1, algebra]

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $H_0\in\mathbb H_n$ have an occupied/unoccupied gap
$g=\lambda_{r+1}(H_0)-\lambda_r(H_0)>0$, and let $c,R,\Gamma$ be the circle
from [[lem-spectral-gap-persistence-and-uniform-resolvent-bound]]. For Hermitian
$H$ in the open operator-norm ball $\|H-H_0\|_{op}<g/4$, let $\Pi_r(H)$ be its
projector onto the $r$ lowest eigenvalues. Then $H\mapsto\Pi_r(H)$ is real
Frechet $C^1$ in the Frobenius norm and
$$D\Pi_r(H)[E]=\frac1{2\pi i}\int_\Gamma (zI-H)^{-1}E(zI-H)^{-1}\,dz$$
for each Hermitian direction $E$. With $\ell(\Gamma)=2\pi R$,
$$\|D\Pi_r(H)[E]\|_F\le\frac{16R}{g^2}\|E\|_F.$$
This is a block/cluster statement: no gap between eigenvalues inside either
cluster is required.

actualproofparagraphs.2.1: Integrating each diagonal entry and using [F3], linearity in [F4], and the finite spectral expansion gives $\frac1{2\pi i}\int_\Gamma R_H(z)\,dz=U\operatorname{diag}(1,\ldots,1,0,\ldots,0)U^*=\Pi_r(H).$ Thus the contour expression represents the full occupied cluster projector, including repeated eigenvalues within that cluster. [step 1.1, F3, F4, algebra]

source_evidence.case_anchor: The two spectral clusters have dimensions r and n-r with1<=r<n; Proof step 2.1 integrates the full nonempty occupied cluster.

$g=\lambda_{r+1}(H_0)-\lambda_r(H_0)>0$, and let $c,R,\Gamma$ be the circle
from [[lem-spectral-gap-persistence-and-uniform-resolvent-bound]]. For Hermitian
$H$ in the open operator-norm ball $\|H-H_0\|_{op}<g/4$, let $\Pi_r(H)$ be its
projector onto the $r$ lowest eigenvalues. Then $H\mapsto\Pi_r(H)$ is real
Frechet $C^1$ in the Frobenius norm and
$$D\Pi_r(H)[E]=\frac1{2\pi i}\int_\Gamma (zI-H)^{-1}E(zI-H)^{-1}\,dz$$
for each Hermitian direction $E$. With $\ell(\Gamma)=2\pi R$,
$$\|D\Pi_r(H)[E]\|_F\le\frac{16R}{g^2}\|E\|_F.$$
This is a block/cluster statement: no gap between eigenvalues inside either
cluster is required.

Let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^2$ on an open set $U$. Let $T_+>0$, let $W\subset U$ be open, and suppose every solution from $x\in W$ exists on an open time interval containing $[0,T_+]$ and stays in one compact convex set $K\subset U$ for all $t\in[0,T_+]$. Write $\Phi(t,x)=\phi_t(x)$. Then $\Phi$ is $C^2$ jointly in $(t,x)$ on $(0,T_+)\times W$, locally on every common-tube neighborhood in $W$, and its derivatives extend continuously in time to $[0,T_+]$. Its first state derivative $S(t,x)=D_x\Phi(t,x)$ solves
$$
\partial_t S=Df(\Phi)S,\qquad S(0,x)=I_n,
$$
and its second state derivative is the bilinear map $H(t,x)$ determined by
$$
\partial_t H[u,v]=Df(\Phi)H[u,v]+D^2f(\Phi)[S u,S v],\qquad H(0,x)[u,v]=0.
$$
In particular $\partial_t\Phi=f(\Phi)$, $\partial_{tx}\Phi=Df(\Phi)S$, and $\partial_{tt}\Phi=Df(\Phi)f(\Phi)$. The assertion is local to the stated common tube.

selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 Fix a base state $x\in W$. By [F1], $\Phi$ is $C^1$ in $x$ and $S$ solves $S'=A S$, where $A(t)=Df(\Phi(t,x))$. The coefficient is bounded on $[0,T_+]$ by [F3]; integrating the variational equation by [F6] and applying [F5] bounds $S$ uniformly in $t$. The flow itself is jointly continuous in $(t,x)$ on the common tube by [F1] and the ODE relation [F2]. [F1, F2, F3, F5, F6, given]

2.2 For small $h$ with $x+h\in W$, put $\Delta(t)=\Phi(t,x+h)-\Phi(t,x)$, $S_h(t)=S(t,x+h)$, and $A_h(t)=Df(\Phi(t,x+h))$. The uniform remainder in [F1] gives $\Delta=S h+o(\|h\|_2)$ uniformly on $J$. On each segment between $\Phi(t,x)$ and $\Phi(t,x+h)$, the chain rule [F7] and [F6] applied coordinatewise to $Df$ give $ A_h-A=\int_0^1 D^2f(\Phi+s\Delta)[\Delta,\cdot] ds. $ Uniform continuity of $D^2f$ on $K$ [F3] and $\Delta=S h+o(\|h\|)$ therefore imply $A_h-A=D^2f(\Phi)[S h,\cdot]+o(\|h\|_2)$ uniformly in $t$. [F1, F3, F6, F7, step 1.1, algebra]

Then $\Phi$ is $C^2$ jointly in $(t,x)$ on $(0,T_+)\times W$, locally on every common-tube neighborhood in $W$, and its derivatives extend continuously in time to $[0,T_+]$. Its first state derivative $S(t,x)=D_x\Phi(t,x)$ solves
$$
\partial_t S=Df(\Phi)S,\qquad S(0,x)=I_n,

[[alg-certified-scf-with-diis-safeguard]]: $\Phi$ is a $q$-contraction on the
complete invariant set $K$, its fixed point is $P_*$, the starting error is at
most $E_0$, and every baseline response error is at most $\eta_k$. Let $E_k$

$$\|P_k-P_*\|_F\le E_k\le q^kE_0+\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}q^{k-1-j}\eta_j.$$

least-squares residual alone is not used as an error bound. If the procedure is
continued indefinitely with successful certificates and $\eta_k\to0$, then
$P_k\to P_*$; a finite update cap still may return budget exhaustion.
Use the convention $q^0=1$, including when $q=0$.

actualproofparagraphs.1.1: Initially $\|P_0-P_*\|_F\le E_0$ by input. Suppose $\|P_k-P_*\|_F\le E_k$. If the algorithm accepts candidate $Y=P_{k+1}$, [F2] gives a certified upper bound $\bar\rho(Y)$ for $\|Y-\Phi(Y)\|_F$ with $\bar\rho(Y)/(1-q)\le qE_k$. Applying [F1] at $Y$ proves $\|P_{k+1}-P_*\|_F\le qE_k=E_{k+1}$. [given, F1, F2]
actualproofparagraphs.2.1: If the baseline is used, its evaluator certifies $\|P_{k+1}-\Phi(P_k)\|_F\le\eta_k$. The triangle inequality and contraction give $\|P_{k+1}-P_*\|_F\le\eta_k+\|\Phi(P_k)-\Phi(P_*)\|_F\le\eta_k+q\|P_k-P_*\|_F\le qE_k+\eta_k=E_{k+1}.$ Thus induction proves $\|P_k-P_*\|_F\le E_k$ at every step. [given, step 1.1, F2, algebra]
actualproofparagraphs.3.1: By [F2], both update branches obey $E_{k+1}\le qE_k+\eta_k$ (accepted DIIS uses $\eta_k=0$ for this upper estimate). Iterating this scalar recurrence by induction gives $E_k\le q^kE_0+\sum_{j<k}q^{k-1-j}\eta_j$. [step 2.1, F2, induction, algebra]

proofparagraphs.text: By [F1], $u-\Pi_Nu=\sum_{n>N}c_nT_n$. Orthogonality from [F2] gives $\|u-\Pi_Nu\|_C^2=\frac{\pi}{2}\sum_{n>N}|c_n|^2.$ Since $n>N$ implies $(1+n^2)^s\ge(1+(N+1)^2)^s$, this is at most $(1+(N+1)^2)^{-s}\frac{\pi}{2}\sum_{n>N}(1+n^2)^s|c_n|^2 \le(1+(N+1)^2)^{-s}\|u\|_{H_C^s}^2.$ Taking square roots proves the result for finite sums. [F1, F2, algebra]

Finite sums are dense in the completion defining $H_C^s$. The truncation $\Pi_N$ is a contraction in the coefficient norm and in the $C$-norm, so both sides of the finite-sum inequality pass to the limit along any Cauchy sequence of finite sums. This yields the stated estimate for every $u\in H_C^s$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Let $n\ge1$, let $\Gamma$ be a nonempty finite union of closed line segments in $\mathbb C$, let $\mathcal A\subseteq\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ be nonempty, and let $A_0\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$. Each segment of $\Gamma$ is assigned to one of finitely many disks $D_j=\{z:|z-z_j|\le r_j\}$ whose radius is $r_j\ge0$ and whose disk contains both endpoints of that segment. For each disk there are $R_j\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ and nonnegative bounds $e_j,\delta_A,s_j$ satisfying
$$e_j\ge\|I-R_j(z_jI-A_0)\|_{\infty,\mathbb C},\quad \delta_A\ge\sup_{A\in\mathcal A}\|A-A_0\|_{\infty,\mathbb C},\quad s_j\ge\|R_j\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}.$$
If $q_j=e_j+s_j(r_j+\delta_A)<1$ for each $j$, then every $z\in\Gamma$ and $A\in\mathcal A$ make $zI-A$ invertible, and
$$\|(zI-A)^{-1}\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}\le \max_j\frac{s_j}{1-q_j}.$$
The theorem bounds the resolvent on the supplied contour cover; it does not count enclosed eigenvalues or certify a nonnormal eigenvalue disk from a residual.
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: Endpoint-covered contour segments and strict disk Neumann bounds certify uniform resolvent invertibility and norm, without counting interior eigenvalues.
selected_current_proof_blocks: 2.1 By [F4], $\|I\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}=1$. Since $M=R_j(zI-A)$ is nonsingular, both square factors are nonsingular by [F3]. Then $(zI-A)^{-1}=M^{-1}R_j$, so [F2] gives $\|(zI-A)^{-1}\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}\le s_j/(1-q_j)$. The disk cover from step 1.1 yields the maximum bound on all of $\Gamma$, uniformly in $A$. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

[given, F1, F2, algebra]

The function $J_\varphi(x)=\beta(x)[\int\varphi\,dB_x-\varphi(x)]$ is bounded by $\beta_*(D+1)$ and Lipschitz with constant at most $L_\beta(D+1)+\beta_*(L_B+1)$, by the assumed boundedness and $d_{BL}(B_x,B_y)\le L_B|x-y|$. Thus its fragmentation derivative difference is bounded by a constant times $d_{BL}(\mu_t,\nu_t)$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

Integrating the weak equations, steps 2.1 and 1.2 give for every admissible $\varphi$ the bound $|\langle\varphi,\mu_t-

u_0)+C_T\int_0^t d_{BL}(\mu_s,

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $(K,d)$ be a nonempty complete metric space and let $\Phi:K\to K$ be a
contraction with constant $0\le q<1$. In the SCF application, $K$ is a
complete invariant subset of the response-map domain from
[[def-self-consistent-projector-response-map]], with $d(X,Y)=\|X-Y\|_F$.
Then $\Phi$ has a unique fixed point $X_*$ and exact iterates
$X_{k+1}=\Phi(X_k)$ satisfy
$$d(X_k,X_*)\le q^k d(X_0,X_*).$$
For every $X\in K$,
$$d(X,X_*)\le\frac{d(X,\Phi(X))}{1-q}.$$
If computed updates $X_{k+1}\in K$ obey
$d(X_{k+1},\Phi(X_k))\le\eta_k$, then
$$e_{k+1}\le q e_k+\eta_k,\qquad e_k\le q^k e_0+\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}q^{k-1-j}\eta_j,$$
where $e_k=d(X_k,X_*)$ and $X_0$ is the supplied initial point.
Use the convention $q^0=1$, including when $q=0$.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $K\subseteq\mathcal D_r$ be nonempty, closed, and convex in Frobenius norm.
Suppose $F$ is $C^1$ on an open neighborhood of $K$, every matrix $F(D)$ there
has a strict $r$th gap so the gapped projector map $\Phi$ is defined, and for a
fixed $\alpha\in[0,1]$ the relaxed map
$$T_\alpha(D)=(1-\alpha)D+\alpha\Phi(D)$$
satisfies $T_\alpha(K)\subseteq K$. If a certified induced-norm bound
$$\|DT_\alpha(D)\|_{F\to F}\le q\qquad(D\in K),\qquad 0\le q<1,$$
holds, where $\|A\|_{F\to F}:=\sup_{\|H\|_F=1}\|A[H]\|_F$, then
$T_\alpha$ is a contraction on $K$ and its iterates converge to a unique fixed
point. The derivative is
$$DT_\alpha(D)=(1-\alpha)I+\alpha D\Phi(D).$$
The derivative bound is a separate hypothesis; $\alpha>0$ alone does not imply
contraction.

actualproofparagraphs.1.1: For $D,E\in K$, convexity puts the segment $Z(t)=E+t(D-E)$ in $K$ for $t\in[0,1]$. By [F1] and [L1], $\Phi$ is defined along this segment; [F2] gives its local $C^1$ regularity. For an increment $H$, $T_\alpha(D+H)-T_\alpha(D)=(1-\alpha)H+\alpha(\Phi(D+H)-\Phi(D))$, so Frechet differentiability of $\Phi$ gives $DT_\alpha(D)=(1-\alpha)I+\alpha D\Phi(D)$. The chain rule [F5] on the segment gives $\frac d{dt}T_\alpha(Z(t))=DT_\alpha(Z(t))[D-E]$. Its norm is at most $q\|D-E\|_F$ by the assumed induced-norm bound; continuity follows from [F2] and [F6]. [given, F1, L1, F2, F5, F6, algebra]
actualproofparagraphs.2.1: Apply [F3] on $[0,1]$ to this path. It yields $\|T_\alpha(D)-T_\alpha(E)\|_F\le q\|D-E\|_F$, so $T_\alpha$ is a contraction on $K$. [step 1.1, F3]

Let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, and suppose its coordinate diameters
$$D_j=\sup\{|x_j-u_j|:x,u\in C\}$$
are finite. Run diagonal AdaGrad [[alg-diagonal-adagrad-online-regret]] for $T\ge1$ rounds on convex losses $\ell_t:C\to\mathbb R$, with $g_t\in\partial\ell_t(x_t)$, step size $\eta>0$, and accumulator $s_{t,j}=\sqrt{\epsilon^2+\sum_{k=1}^t g_{k,j}^2}$ for $\epsilon>0$. For every comparator $u\in C$,

$$\sum_{t=1}^T(\ell_t(x_t)-\ell_t(u))\le\sum_{j=1}^d\left(\frac{D_j^2}{2\eta}+\eta\right)s_{T,j}.$$

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Let $d\ge2$, let $V\in C^4(U,\mathbb R)$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ using the convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], and let $x_*$ be a critical point with Hessian $H_*:=\nabla^2V(x_*)$ ordered as $\lambda_1(H_*)\le\cdots\le\lambda_d(H_*)$. Suppose

$$\lambda_1(H_*)\le-2\gamma,\qquad \lambda_j(H_*)\ge2\gamma\ (j\ge2),\qquad \|H_*\|_{\rm op}\le\Lambda$$

for $\gamma>0$ and $\Lambda\ge2\gamma$. Let the closed ball $\overline B_2(x_*,r)$ lie in $U$, let the Hessian be $L$-Lipschitz there, and assume $Lr\le\gamma$. At every iterate $x$ in this ball, suppose a validated Hessian enclosure gives $\lambda_1(H(x))\le-\gamma$ and $\lambda_j(H(x))\ge\gamma$ for $j\ge2$, and accepted dimer data satisfy the hypotheses of [[thm-dimer-mode-perturbation-and-local-saddle-error]] with uniform rotation residual $\tau_{\rm rot}$ and HVP error bound $\delta\le\gamma/4$. Define

$$\alpha:=\frac{4(\tau_{\rm rot}+\delta)}{5\gamma},\qquad q:=\max\left\{|1+\sigma\lambda_1(H_*)|,\ \max_{2\le j\le d}|1-\sigma\lambda_j(H_*)|\right\},$$

where $0<\sigma<2/\Lambda$. Suppose the finite dimer saddle translation of [[alg-finite-budget-dimer-mode-following]] uses a unit direction $v$ from those accepted data and a computed gradient $\widehat g(x)$ with $\|\widehat g(x)-\nabla V(x)\|_2\le\eta$. Put

$$\kappa:=q+\frac{\sigma Lr}{2}+2\sigma\left(\alpha+\frac{Lr}{3\gamma}\right)\left(\Lambda+\frac{Lr}{2}\right).$$

If $\kappa<1$ and $\sigma\eta\le(1-\kappa)r$, then every attempted translation starting at $\|x_0-x_*\|_2\le r$ remains in the ball and obeys

$$\|x_{k+1}-x_*\|_2\le\kappa\|x_k-x_*\|_2+\sigma\eta,$$

and consequently

$$\|x_k-x_*\|_2\le\kappa^k\|x_0-x_*\|_2+\frac{\sigma\eta(1-\kappa^k)}{1-\kappa}.$$

Thus exact translation gradients give local contraction, while a fixed bounded translation-force error gives the stated finite noise floor. The conclusion is conditional on a validated gap and accepted dimer mode at every attempted iterate; a finite rotation cap or missing spectral enclosure gives no such guarantee.

Let $v$ be a unit direction accepted by the rotation test of [[alg-finite-budget-dimer-mode-following]], with paired-force estimate $D_\epsilon$ and $\|(I-vv^T)D_\epsilon\|_2\le\tau_{\rm rot}$. Suppose each force evaluation has Euclidean error at most $\eta$, the third derivatives of each gradient coordinate are bounded by $M_4$ on the dimer segments, and set

$$\delta:=\frac{\sqrt d\,M_4}{6}\epsilon^2+\frac{\eta}{\epsilon}.$$

$$\|x_*-x\|_2\le\rho=\frac{2\epsilon_g}{\gamma}.$$

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Use the setting of [[def-parameterized-finite-state-step-objective]]. Write $A_n=D_x\Psi_n(x_n,\theta)$, $B_n=D_\theta\Psi_n(x_n,\theta)$, and let $S_n=D_\theta x_n$. Then
$$S_0=D x_0(\theta),\qquad S_{n+1}=A_nS_n+B_n.$$
Define $p_N=D_x\phi(x_N,\theta)^T$ and, backward for $n=N-1,\ldots,0$,
$$p_n=D_x\ell_n(x_n,\theta)^T+A_n^Tp_{n+1}.$$
The exact gradient of the finite objective is
$$\nabla_\theta J=D_\theta\phi(x_N,\theta)^T+S_0^Tp_0+\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\bigl(D_\theta\ell_n(x_n,\theta)^T+B_n^Tp_{n+1}\bigr).$$
The recursion is the reverse derivative of the finite graph in exact real arithmetic; it makes no convergence claim about an iteration used to choose $\theta$.

actualproofparagraphs.1.2: Apply the reverse accumulation rule [F2] to the finite graph of states and objective summands in [F1]. The terminal contribution seeds $p_N=D_x\phi^T$; at each state node $x_n$, its local running-cost edge contributes $D_x\ell_n^T$, while its state-transition edge contributes $A_n^Tp_{n+1}$. Thus the accumulated state cotangent is exactly $p_n$ as defined in the Statement, and the direct parameter edges contribute $D_\theta\phi^T$ and $D_\theta\ell_n^T+B_n^Tp_{n+1}$. By [F3], reverse mode returns the exact derivative of this finite C1 graph. [F1, F2, F3]
actualproofparagraphs.3.1: The adjoint equation gives $p_n^TS_n=D_x\ell_nS_n+p_{n+1}^TA_nS_n$. Since $S_{n+1}=A_nS_n+B_n$, rearranging yields $$D_x\ell_nS_n=p_n^TS_n-p_{n+1}^TS_{n+1}+p_{n+1}^TB_n.$$ Summing over $n$ telescopes; $p_N=D_x\phi^T$ cancels the terminal tangent term in step 2.1 and leaves $S_0^Tp_0+\sum_n B_n^Tp_{n+1}$. Adding the direct parameter derivatives from step 2.1 gives the displayed adjoint formula. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

Let $J$ and $J_h$ be the continuous and finite state-step objectives of [[thm-continuous-ode-adjoint-gradient-formula]] and [[thm-discrete-adjoint-gradient-recursion]], respectively, and put $h=T/N$. Let $q(t,u,p)=D_\theta\ell(t,u,\theta)^T+D_\theta f(t,u,\theta)^Tp$ be the continuous running-gradient vector, evaluated on its exact state and adjoint as $q(t):=q(t,u(t),p(t))$. Suppose the exact and numerical state/adjoint pairs lie in a common tube and
$$\max_n\bigl(\|u_n-u(t_n)\|_2+\|p_n-p(t_n)\|_2\bigr)\le C_xh^p.$$
For the state part of this bound, it is sufficient that the hypotheses of [[thm-global-error-from-one-step-defect-and-stability]] hold with a uniform $O(h^{p+1})$ exact-start defect; the coefficient conditions of [[prop-explicit-rk-order-conditions-through-four]] supply that defect for an explicit Runge--Kutta method of order $p\le4$ under that item's $C^4$ and common-tube assumptions. No cited state-error result supplies the adjoint part, which is an independent hypothesis here. Write $b$ and $b_h$ for the column initial/terminal contribution vectors in the continuous and discrete gradient formulas. Assume the discrete running-gradient terms admit vectors $\widehat q_n$ and nonnegative weights $w_n$, $0\le n\le N$, with
$$\nabla J_h=b_h+\sum_{n=0}^N w_n\widehat q_n,\qquad \nabla J=b+\int_0^Tq(t)\,dt,\qquad \sum_{n=0}^Nw_n=T.$$
The weighted discrete representation is an explicit premise; it is not implied by the generic finite state-step adjoint recursion. Suppose
$$\|\widehat q_n-q(t_n,u_n,p_n)\|_2\le C_dh^p,\qquad \|b_h-b\|_2\le C_bh^p,$$
and that the same weights give the quadrature $Q_h(q)=\sum_{n=0}^Nw_nq(t_n)$ satisfying
$$\left\|Q_h(q)-\int_0^Tq(t)\,dt\right\|_2\le C_Qh^p.$$
If $q$ is Lipschitz in $(u,p)$ on the common tube with constant $L_q$ in the sum norm, then
$$\|\nabla J_h-\nabla J\|_2\le\bigl(C_b+T(C_d+L_qC_x)+C_Q\bigr)h^p.$$
The adjoint, derivative-data and quadrature hypotheses are separate from state accuracy; without them the state estimate alone gives no gradient error conclusion.

There is also the following independent method-consistency conclusion. Under the local $C^1$ step-and-cost consistency, derivative stability, derivative Lipschitz, initial-data, terminal-derivative and tube hypotheses of [[lem-local-c1-step-consistency-implies-tangent-adjoint-gradient-order]], the actual numerical graph satisfies
$$\max_n\|D_\theta u_n-D_\theta u(t_n)\|_2\le C_Sh^p,\qquad \max_n\|p_n-p(t_n)\|_2\le C_Ph^p,$$
$$\|\nabla J_h-\nabla J\|_2\le C_Gh^p,$$
with that lemma's explicit constants, together with its state bound. These conclusions derive the global tangent and adjoint errors from local map errors. They do not assume the preceding global state/adjoint bound or weighted representation.

In particular, [[lem-explicit-rk-differentiated-stages-give-local-c1-order]] supplies these local hypotheses for the actual explicit RK state map and the cost using the same tableau, under its common-tube, base $C^2$, and local augmented-order hypotheses. For $p\le4$, its augmented $C^4$ hypothesis and the existing coefficient conditions suffice; jointly $C^5$ base data are an explicit sufficient smoothness condition, and its displayed classical RK4 tableau gives a concrete order-four instance. Generic $p$ is retained through its genuine local augmented-order hypothesis. This branch permits negative or zero RK weights and makes no internal-stage adjoint accuracy claim.

Under the stated stability, common-tube and initial-error hypotheses, [F3] gives the state part of the asserted $C_xh^p$ bound; the adjoint part in the weighted conclusion remains the separately assumed bound. there is $p\in E$ with $0\in(A+B)(p)$, meaning that $a\in A(p)$ and
$b\in B(p)$ can be chosen with $a+b=0$. The Douglas–Rachford recurrence of
[[alg-douglas-rachford-splitting]] has a state sequence converging to a fixed
point of its map $T$, and its shadow $J_{\rho B}(w_k)$ converges to a zero of
$A+B$.

review_basis.full_actual_interface:
Assume AC. Let $d,m\ge1$ be finite, $T>0$, and consider the autonomous
SDE with $b\in C^1(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R^d)$ and globally Lipschitz
$\sigma:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}$. Suppose that for constants
$\mu\ge0$, $C<\infty$, and an integer $q\ge1$,
$$\langle x-y,b(x)-b(y)\rangle\le-\mu|x-y|^2, \qquad \|Db(x)\|\le C(1+|x|^q).$$
Let $\xi$ have all finite moments and let $X$ be the corresponding global
strong solution. For $N\ge\max(1,\lceil T\rceil)$, put $h=T/N$ and let
$Y_n$ be the exact-resolvent drift-implicit Euler–Maruyama values from
[[alg-drift-implicit-euler-sde]]. There is a constant $C_T$ independent of
$N$ such that
$$\mathbb E\max_{0\le n\le N}|X_{t_n}-Y_n|^2\le C_T h.$$
Moreover, for two such numerical sequences driven by the same Brownian
increments but with initial values $\xi,\widetilde\xi$,
$$\mathbb E|Y_n-\widetilde Y_n|^2 \le e^{L_\sigma^2t_n}\mathbb E|\xi-\widetilde\xi|^2,$$
where $L_\sigma$ is a global Lipschitz constant of $\sigma$. The second
estimate is finite-time mean-square stability; it does not claim strict
contraction when diffusion is present.
review_basis.source_specific_focus: Exact resolvent grid values have half-order strong convergence and a separate same-noise finite-time mean-square stability estimate, not strict stochastic contraction.

source_evidence.fullclaim:
Assume Countable Choice and the elliptic state setting of [[def-parameterized-elliptic-variational-problem]] and [[lem-elliptic-state-map-c1-under-uniform-coercivity]]. Let $J:V\times\Theta\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$. For a parameter $\theta$, let $p_\theta\in V$ solve the adjoint variational problem
$$a_\theta(v,p_\theta)=D_uJ(u_\theta,\theta)[v]\qquad(v\in V).$$
Then the reduced objective $j(\theta)=J(u_\theta,\theta)$ is $C^1$ and
